title: Remove namespace property from the Conduit web app
body: The servicemesh and deployments page in the Conduit web app rely on a namespace property that describes where conduit components reside in k8s. The web app uses this property to filter pods from k8s into lists that contain pods that are and aren't in the conduit namespace. The public API already does this filtering so the namespace property is no longer needed in the web app. This change has been tested in a minikube instance locally and uses the hello-world grpc example to verify the change is correct.

title: Store proxy latencies in a structure that matches controller histogram
body:
I've modified the proxy to store latency values in a structure that matches the buckets used by the controller, rather than in an `OrderMap`. I've tried to make this structure generic enough that, if we later change the bucketing strategy that the controller uses, it should be relatively easy to modify the latencies structure in the proxy, or to optimize its performance if we determine that is necessary (i.e. by turning it into a real binary tree?).

Added some tests in `tests/telemetry.rs` to assert observed latencies go into the correct buckets.

title: Add timeout to in-flight telemetry reports
body:
This PR adds a configurable timeout duration after which in-flight telemetry reports are dropped, cancelling the corresponding RPC request to the control plane. 

Right now, the default timeout is 10 seconds, but I'm not sure if this is a reasonable default value. I'd also like to add a unit test ensuring that this works.
author: hawkw

comments.author: olix0r
comments.body:
I wonder if we can do this in a more generic way so that timeouts can be added to arbitrary requests...

@carllerche @seanmonstar do you have any thoughts on what tower-timeout might look like? ;)

comments.author: seanmonstar
comments.body:
A basic version could be put next to the `Backoff` impl that's currently in tree, before we figure out exactly what tower-timeout would look like. I think the changes to timers would affect our design, so it's likely faster to just do hardcoded to the current `tokio_core::reactor::Timeout` for now...

However, I do agree that a generic solution would be best: having a `Timeout` service wrap another.

I wondered about that as well; in this case it seemed like since we already had the timestamp it was simpler to just add the if here. Can definitely write a generic timeout implementation, though.

review_threads.body:

This is also inconsistent with other timeouts like `ENV_PRIVATE_CONNECT_TIMEOUT` and `ENV_PUBLIC_CONNECT_TIMEOUT` which are set in milliseconds already.

title: Fix public-api error marshaling and unmarshaling
body:
If the public-api server encounters an error in the process of serving a request, it writes a plaintext error message back to the client, and the public-api client fails trying to unmarshal it.

With this change, the server marshals the error into a new ApiError struct and sets the `conduit-error` header. The client reads that header and unmarshals errors accordingly.

title: Proxy: Improve error reporting for invalid environment variables
body:
Previously when an environment variable had an invalid value the
process would exit with an error that did not mention which
environment variable is invalid.

Start fixing this by routing environment variable parsing through
functions that always know the name of the environment variable when
they report errors.

I validated this change manually.

title: Proxy: Use production config parsing in tests
body:
Previosuly the testing code for the proxy was sensitive to the values
of environment variables unintentionally, because `Config` looked at
the environment variables. Also, the tests were largely avoiding
testing the production configuration parsing code since they were
doing their own parsing.

Now the tests avoid looking at environment variables other than
`ENV_LOG`, which makes them more resilient. Also the tests now parse
the settings using the same code as production use uses.

I validated this manually.
author: briansmith

title: Proxy: Parse environment variables in one place
body:
Previously `Process` did its own environment variable parsing and did
not benefit from the improved error handling that `config` now has.
Additionally, future changes will need access to these same environment
variables in other parts of the proxy.

Move `Process`'s environment variable parsing to `config` to address
both of these issues. Now there are no uses of `env::var` outside of
`config` except for logging, which is the final desired state.

I validated this manually.

title: Add inject flag for skipping outbound ports
body: Add the `--skip-outbound-ports` flag to `conduit inject`.  This flag accepts a comma separated list of ports.  When the application sends traffic to one of these ports, the sidecar proxy will be bypassed and the traffic will be sent directly to the original destination.  This is useful for when an application sends traffic that the Conduit proxy does not support such as HTTP/1.1 or raw TCP.
author: adleong

comments.author: adleong
comments.body:
I spoke to @klingerf about this in person and he brought up the very good point that multiple different downstreams may all use the same port number but speak different protocols.  For example, you may have a downstream A that listens for gRPC on port 7777 and a downstream B that listens for HTTP/1.1 on port 7777.  This change doesn't allow you to differentiate between the two and forces you to skip the outbound proxy for both or neither.

An alternative to this would be to allow skipping the outbound proxy based on IP ranges instead of by port.  Unfortunately, for service-to-service traffic in scheduled environments like Kubernetes, there is no fixed IP address for a given downstream.

Given this, I think I'd like to move forward with this change as-is.  This definitely doesn't address the issue where multiple downstreams may use the same port number and can't be individually excluded from the proxy, but this is at least potentially work-around-able by changing your services to use unique ports.  A more complete solution will come later when the Conduit proxy is able to transparently proxy arbitrary TCP traffic.

comments.author: adleong
comments.body: I have added an integration test for this, but the test is not yet passing and I haven't figured out why.

comments.author: pcalcado
comments.body:
I've tested this branch like this:

```
$ minikube start
$ eval "$(minikube docker-env ) "
$ bash -x bin/docker-build-proxy-init latest
$ cd proxy-init/integration_test
$ ./run_tests.shq
```

It fails with all sorts of crazy errors.

Looking at the init-container log, I see that the iptables setup logic has failed but the container didn't abort:
```
$ kubectl logs pod-doesnt-redirect-blacklisted conduit-init
Error: unknown shorthand flag: 'i' in -i
Usage:
  proxy-init [flags]

Flags:
  -h, --help                                help for proxy-init
      --inbound-ports-to-ignore intSlice    Inbound ports to ignore and not redirect to proxy. This has higher precedence than any other parameters.
  -p, --incoming-proxy-port int             Port to redirect incoming traffic (default -1)
      --outbound-ports-to-ignore intSlice   Outbound ports to ignore and not redirect to proxy. This has higher precedence than any other parameters.
  -o, --outgoing-proxy-port int             Port to redirect outgoing traffic (default -1)
  -r, --ports-to-redirect intSlice          Port to redirect to proxy, if no port is specified then ALL ports are redirected
  -u, --proxy-uid int                       User ID that the proxy is running under. Any traffic coming from this user will be ignored to avoid infinite redirection loops. (default -1)
      --simulate                            Don't execute any command, just print what would be executed
```

I confirmed this locally:
```
 $ go run proxy-init/main.go  -p 80  -o 90 -i 7070 -u 1337 --simulate  ; echo $?
Error: unknown shorthand flag: 'i' in -i
Usage:
  proxy-init [flags]

Flags:
  -h, --help                                help for proxy-init
      --inbound-ports-to-ignore intSlice    Inbound ports to ignore and not redirect to proxy. This has higher precedence than any other parameters.
  -p, --incoming-proxy-port int             Port to redirect incoming traffic (default -1)
      --outbound-ports-to-ignore intSlice   Outbound ports to ignore and not redirect to proxy. This has higher precedence than any other parameters.
  -o, --outgoing-proxy-port int             Port to redirect outgoing traffic (default -1)
  -r, --ports-to-redirect intSlice          Port to redirect to proxy, if no port is specified then ALL ports are redirected
  -u, --proxy-uid int                       User ID that the proxy is running under. Any traffic coming from this user will be ignored to avoid infinite redirection loops. (default -1)
      --simulate                            Don't execute any command, just print what would be executed

0
```

So if the `-i` flag doesn't exist anymore, the CLI is exiting with 0 as its status. This looks similar to https://github.com/spf13/cobra/issues/582 , which makes me thing it might be an issue with Cobra.

To get this moving for the release, I've changed the `iptablestest-lab.ymnl` file to use `--inbound-ports-to-ignore` instead of `-i` and the tests now pass. I've also manually inspected the output using the `--simulate` flag nd it looks ok.

So, unless we have any other requirements for this change, I'd :+1: it for now and merge.

title: Refactor each CLI command to silently exit on uncaught errors
body: No longer display stack traces when using the CLI with incorrect flags or input. The one command that noticeably exhibit this behavior was the inject command used together with `kubectl apply -f -`
author: dadjeibaah

comments.author: dadjeibaah
comments.body: Oops, sorry about that!

comments.author: klingerf
comments.body:
We discussed this briefly in person. The issue is that piping bad input to `kubectl` causes `kubectl` to panic and dump a stack trace. For instance:

```
$ echo "not yaml" | kubectl apply -f -
panic: interface conversion: interface {} is string, not map[string]interface {}

goroutine 1 [running]:
k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubectl/cmd/util/openapi/validation.getObjectKind(0x2120c60, 0x4235acd60, 0x0, 0x0, 0x0, 0x0, 0x0, 0x0, 0xffffffffffffff01, 0x4235acac0)
	/go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/_output/dockerized/go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubectl/cmd/util/openapi/validation/validation.go:111 +0x539
```

This causes issues with the `conduit inject` command because conduit inject prints error messages to stdout instead of stderr, and those messages are then piped to kubectl. For instances:

```
$ conduit inject 2> /dev/null 
please specify a deployment file
```

The easiest fix is to ensure that that message (and others like it) is written to stderr.

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
I don't think this is the right fix for this issue unfortunately. If this method returns errors (such as those on lines 39 and 44 in this file), then we should be surfacing those errors instead of exiting silently.

By way of example, on conduit master, if I run `go run cli/main.go get foo`, then I get:

```
$ go run cli/main.go get foo
Error: invalid resource type
Usage:
  conduit get [flags] RESOURCE

Flags:
      --api-addr string     Override kubeconfig and communicate directly with the control plane at host:port (mostly for testing)
  -h, --help                help for get
      --kubeconfig string   Path to the kubeconfig file to use for CLI requests (default "/Users/kl/.kube/config")

Global Flags:
  -n, --conduit-namespace string   namespace in which Conduit is installed (default "conduit")

invalid resource type
exit status 1
```

But on your branch, I get no output:

```
$ go run cli/main.go get foo
exit status 2
```

I think the intent of exitSilentlyOnError is to suppress the help message, but that's really only appropriate for the version command, where we're not validating user input.

I think a better approach to fixing the stacktrace would be to try to figure out which code is panicking, and then add code to recover from the panic before the stacktrace is printed.

review_threads.author: dadjeibaah
review_threads.body: Ahh ok, I can revisit that, I was under the impression the `exitSilentlyOnError` was only silently erroring out on OS level errors like the ones you run into when using kubectl with the cli. Thanks for that

title: conduit inject: Configure proxy to log at "info" level
body:
Previously `conduit inject` was configuring the proxy to log a lot of
detail, most of which is probably shouldn't be relevant to Conduit
users.

Configure the proxy to log at the "info" level instead for the proxy
itself, and the "warn" level for internal components of the proxy.

Validated by manually doing a `conduit inject`, triggering some
traffic, and inspecting the logs.

title: Proxy: Map unqualified/partially-qualified names to FQDN
body:
Previously we required the service to fully qualify all service names
for outbound traffic. Many services are written assuming that
Kubernetes will complete names using its DNS search path, and those
services weren't working with Conduit.

Now add an option, used by default, to fully-qualify the domain names.
Currently only Kubernetes-like name completion for services is
supported, but the configuration syntax is open-ended to allow for
alternatives in the future. Also, the auto-completion can be disabled
for applications that prefer to ensure they're always using unambiguous
names. Once routing is implemented then it is likely that (default)
routing rules will replace these hard-coded rules.

Unit tests for the name completion logic are included.

Part of the solution for #9. The changes to `conduit inject` to
actually use this facility will be in another PR.

title: conduit inject: Enable auto name completion in proxy
body:
Previously `conduit inject` did not enable automatic name completion in
the proxy. As a result services couldn't connect to services outside
the "default" namespace without qualifying the service name with (at
least) the namespace. This is arguably safer but it isn't compatible
with the way things work in Kubernetes when the proxy isn't used.

Enable name auto-completion in the proxy so that the proxy will add
the current pod's namespace to any unqualified service name. This
depends on the feature being added to the proxy (PR #59).

Due to some issues with how zones are dealt with in the project, the
zone component isn't provided; it turns out that it doesn't matter
whether we provide the zone in the current implementation. Dealing
with the zone better will be added later.

Validated by deploying the emojivoto service with its configuration
updated to use unqualified names (`sed "s/\\.emojivoto//g"`). Before
this change this modified configuration would fail; now it succeeds.

Fixes #9.

I would like to have some automated tests for it, for sure. I spent some time today trying to write an automated test for this but it requires non-trivial infrastructure and it wouldn't be ready by the deadline for this feature.

Regarding the documentation, I think the documentation for this is roughly equivalent to the documentation for the existing configuration settings for the proxy. If we want to improve the documentation situation for the proxy configuration we should do so as a separate effort.

Anyway, again, I agree we need to improve the testing and documentation situation, generally. But, this particular issue isn't the thing that's in the most need of testing or documentation. We should get together and make a plan (resourcing, schedule, and technical design) for how we're going to do the test automation for these kinds of features.

title: Stop using "default" as default service namespace
body:
Previously the destinations service would look for services in the
"default" namespace if the service name didn't have at least two
labels. However, the "default" namespace is almost always the wrong
namespace. The only reasonable default namespace is the namespace of
the client service, which isn't given to the destinations service.
Therefore it shouldn't try to default the namespace.

Accordingly, stop defaulting the namespace to "default".

Validated by manually testing the emojivoto service before and after
the proxy implemented namespace defaulting itself.

I am working on some unit tests for the way the destination service maps its inputs to EndPoints queries generally, as part of fixing another issue. The mapping is broken very badly and this isn't the worst part of what's broken, so I think we should skip writing specific tests for this in favor of fixing the bigger problem and writing the more general tests.

title: Stop ignoring the most significant labels of Destination names
body:
Previously the destinations service was ignoring all the labels in a
destination name after the first two labels. Thus, for example,
"name.ns.another.domain.example.com" would be
considered the same as "name.ns.svc.cluster.local". This was very
wrong.

Match destination names taking into consideration every label in the
destination name.

Provisions have been made for the case where the controller and the
proxies are configured with the zone name to use. However, currently
neither the controller nor the proxies are actually configured with the
zone, so the implementation was made to work in the current
configuration too.

Unit tests are included for the new mapping rules.

title: Fix unit test runner and failing tests
body:
The canonical test command used in our `.travis.yml` passes:
```
$ go test -v ./...  --run "^(integration_test)" >/dev/null; echo $?
0
```

But I realised that even if I make a test fail on purpose, it **always** passes. So I've tried running without the `--run "^(integration_test)"` bit, and now this hangs forever:

```
$ go test -v ./...   >/dev/null; echo $?
```

So in commit e043adf907adae17d6b899013ea3bbf85fe78057 I've changed our travis file to the command above. In commit a4db27c I;'ve also made the integration tests only  `CONDUIT_INTEGRATION_TESTS_ENABLED`, removing the need for the flag on `go test`.

Now it still hangs, but before hanging it shows us that another test was broken and has never been reported as such:

```
$ go test ./...

?   	github.com/runconduit/conduit/cli	[no test files]

--- FAIL: TestSortStatsKeys (0.00s)

	Error Trace:	stat_test.go:25

	Error:		Not equal: []string{"other/grafana", "kube-system/heapster-v1.4.3", "kube-system/kubernetes-dashboard", "kube-system/l7-default-backend", "test/backend4", "test/hello10", "test/world-deploy1", "test/world-deploy2"} (expected)

			        != []string{"kube-system/heapster-v1.4.3", "kube-system/kubernetes-dashboard", "kube-system/l7-default-backend", "other/grafana", "test/backend4", "test/hello10", "test/world-deploy1", "test/world-deploy2"} (actual)

			

			Diff:

			--- Expected

			+++ Actual

			@@ -1,3 +1,2 @@

			 ([]string) (len=8 cap=8) {

			- (string) (len=13) "other/grafana",

			  (string) (len=27) "kube-system/heapster-v1.4.3",

			@@ -5,2 +4,3 @@

			  (string) (len=30) "kube-system/l7-default-backend",

			+ (string) (len=13) "other/grafana",

			  (string) (len=13) "test/backend4",

	Messages:	Not Sorted!

		

FAIL

FAIL	github.com/runconduit/conduit/cli/cmd	0.095s
```

So on commit 1c5adc67518b947e136e43d1d42b3b164eb120e5 I've fixed the bug that was causing the test to hang, and now we have a broken build, as it should the case since forever. Running locally you get this:

```
$ go test -v ./...   >/dev/null; echo $?
1
```
Subsequent commits fix tests that had been failing for a while and we didn't know about because of the problems stated above. After that we're back to a good state:

```
$ go test -v ./...   >/dev/null; echo $?
0
```

I think we should use cloneDeep rather than clone in these projects to avoid test pollution:
```
let pods = [ {name: "a", added: false}, {name: "b", added: false} ]

review_threads.author: rmars
review_threads.body:
since there are a lot of these "displays message for...." tests, it might be nice to wrap them in a Describe block, and then reword the tests to be clearer about what behaviours we're testing. In the `it()` assertions, I think it's usually clearer to describe the specific behaviours we're testing e.g. `it("displays a message when there are no deployments", ...)` but in the describe, since we're grouping these, we can write the method name e.g.
`describe("renderAddDeploymentsMessage", ...)`

In general, we should try to think about wording the tests to the specific behaviours we're testing, and try to be as descriptive as possible (which sometimes means trying to say /what/ you're testing without repeating what you're asserting in the test). E.g. with these tests, we're testing that the correct message displays in certain conditions. So we can try to reflect that in the wording of the assertion, such that the tests read something like:
```
 ServiceMesh
    renderAddDeploymentsMessage
       displays when no deployments are in the mesh
```

title: Fail the build if dep images are out of sync.
body:
Previously if dependencies changed but dep image SHAs were not updated,
the build could succeed, creating docker images with indeterminate
dependencies.

This change checks the dependency image SHAs hard-coded in Dockerfile's
against the current source tree. If the SHAs do not match, the build
fails.

Fixes #118

output if build fails:
```
$ bin/docker-build-controller latest
Tag in controller/Dockerfile does not match source tree:
gcr.io/runconduit/go-deps:41719552 (controller/Dockerfile)
gcr.io/runconduit/go-deps:151268ee (source)
```
author: siggy

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
I like that this makes it easy to validate all docker builds in one place, but I think there's an ordering issue. For instance, if I modify Gopkg.lock and then run `bin/docker-build-proxy-init latest`, that script will first build a new deps image to account for the Gopkg.lock change, even though that image isn't referenced in `proxy-init/Dockerfile`. And then validation happens only after the new, unused deps image has been built. The output of the script looks like this:

```
Successfully tagged gcr.io/runconduit/go-deps:d93a00b2
Tag in proxy-init/Dockerfile does not match source tree:
gcr.io/runconduit/go-deps:41719552 (proxy-init/Dockerfile)
gcr.io/runconduit/go-deps:d93a00b2 (source)
```

I think the validation should happen before we attempt to fetch or build the base image, in which case, the call to `validate_tags` should be happening inside the `docker-build-proxy-init` script itself. That way we're not wasting any time retrieving or building base images that aren't referenced by the dockerfile that we're trying to build.

So I'd revert the changes to this file, and update `docker-build-cli-bin`, `docker-build-controller`, `docker-build-proxy-init`, `docker-build-web`, and `bin/docker-build-proxy` accordingly.

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body:
I thought about this approach, but settled on the current implementation for a few reasons:

1. If someone modifies `Gopkg.lock`, they will need to rebuild the deps image. Whether they get a validation error before or after the deps build will not affect the time taken. If we fail the build immediately, they'll be instructed to set an image tag in a Dockerfile for an image that does not yet exist, which may be a bit confusing. I think this order of operations is more instructive to the developer:
  a. Modify `Gopkg.lock`
  b. Build deps image, see deps image, get validation error
  c. Update relevant Dockerfile to reflect new deps image that just got built on my system.

2. Putting validation at a higher level in the `docker-build-*` scripts duplicates implementation, and also runs the risk of someone forgetting to add validation into a new `docker-build-*` script.

3. Keeping the validation in `bin/_tag.sh` keeps all tag/sha-related logic in one place.

Let me know what you think (and if I'm missing something).

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
Hmm, yeah, all good points. I think either approach works. One comment regarding:

> Keeping the validation in `bin/_tag.sh` keeps all tag/sha-related logic in one place.

That file is already sourced in all of the `docker-build-*` scripts, so you could leave the validation code that you wrote in that file, and I agree that that's where it belongs. My recommendation was to remove the calls to validate from `bin/_docker.sh`, and put them in the `docker-build-*` files instead. It's a bit unexpected (to me) that, as a result of your change, the `bin/_docker.sh` script now has a dependency on the `bin/_tag.sh` script. It feels like building and tagging should be handled independently, by the `docker-build-*` scripts themselves.

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body: @klingerf per offline convo, have moved validation checks up into the `docker-build-*` files, and removed the `_docker.sh` -> `_tag.sh` dependency. i've added a note in `bin/_tag.sh` providing context on which scripts should do validation checks. we can move that information into a BUILD.md file later on.

title: Remove scheme requirement for api-addr flag in conduit CLI
body:
Conduit CLI has the option of providing a URL for a `--api-addr` flag. This option requires that the URL must contain an http scheme in order to create a Kubernetes API client. This PR removes the scheme restriction and allows for a user to enter both a `host:port` or `scheme://host:port` format

New tests were added to `api_test.go` to capture the scenario and tests were run manually with the CLI to ensure that no regression was introduced.

fixes #121

Signed-off-by: Dennis Adjei-Baah <dennis@buoyant.io>
author: dadjeibaah

comments.author: dadjeibaah
comments.body: Thanks @pcalcado  all great suggestions, I will have a commit up soon

comments.author: dadjeibaah
comments.body: @pcalcado I made the changes you suggested but I have some additional questions. For `api_test` I rearranged the test to be _table driven_. I started to think about the use case of including other scheme in the URL e.g. `tcp://`. Should the code be checking for invalid url schemes and throwing an error or should it just prepend https:// and wait for the API to fail with the invalid URL? For example, if we mistakenly send "tcp://1.2.3.4" the `Makek8sAPI` function will just tack on `https://tcp://....`try to connect and then eventually fail since that is an invalid url.

comments.author: pcalcado
comments.body:
@deebo91 😍 

> Should the code be checking for invalid url schemes and throwing an error or should it just prepend https:// and wait for the API to fail with the invalid URL?

This is a great question, and, in my experience, it is the exact kind of exploratory thinking that TDD leads to!

It seems like the reasons we'd be prepending the protocol here is for convenience, so I would suggest that we keep it simple and only add it if we see that the supplied URL doesn't contain a scheme (i.e. there's no `://` preceded by a string).

Usually, I would say that we should follow [Postel's Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Postel#Postel's_law) and don't try to guess if the protocol supplied by the user is valid (what if they are running in some weird Cloud vendor's version of Kubernetes that uses a different protocol to connect to the API?). In this case, though, we know that Conduit CLI will only work if the Kubernetes API is exposed via HTTP(S). It feels like a better UX if we just let the user know straight away that the protocol supplied isn't supported—and which ones they should be using—, instead of having them puzzled at a more cryptical error message written by the lower-level HTTP client.

We could then write a table-driven test covering all these scenarios, like the one you wrote, and another test and table that explicitly send in some bad input so that we have documented in tests what happens (e.g. `an error is returned`).

And, because this is freeform user input, don't forget to add some bad input reflecting typos :)

comments.author: dadjeibaah
comments.body: @pcalcado rejiggered the tests to try and capture what you were talking about in your previous comments.

comments.author: dadjeibaah
comments.body: @klingerf I think my recent change to this PR may have captured the use case you were looking for. I am open to hearing your feedback about the latest change.

review_threads.author: pcalcado
review_threads.body:
I am having a little trouble with this function. It seems like its role is to:
1) Reduce the repetition around the somewhat convoluted process of generating a URL so that we can reuse it
2) Assert that the generated URL is the expected

If I am correct in the thinking above, maybe a better name would be from `generateUrlTest` to `generateUrlAndAssert`. But that `and` there still smells funny to me.

In general, I would consider a good idea to limit the number of "things" a function does to a single one—which is usually said to "increase its _cohesion_". In this particular example, I would recommend that we remove the assertion from the method's body and have it done in the test body.

It feels to me that the two cases are actually the same, the only real difference is the input and expected output. I am also guessing we would need a test for `https` and whatever other protocols could make sense?

Instead, what if we adopt what is usually called _table driven tests_? Here is an example of how it's used elsewhere in this code base:

title: Add Protocol field to Transports telemetry
body:
See #132. This PR adds a `protocol` field to the `ClientTransport` and `ServerTransport` messages, and modifies the proxy to report a value for this field (currently, it's only ever `HTTP`). 

Currently, HTTP/1 and HTTP/2 are collapsed into one `Protocol` variant, see https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/issues/132#issuecomment-356716576. I expect that we can treat H1 as a subset of H2 as far as metrics goes.

Note that after discussing it with @klingerf, I learned that the control plane telemetry API currently does not do anything with the `ClientTransport` and `ServerTransport` messages, so beyond regenerating the protobuf-generated code, no controller changes were actually necessary. As we actually add metrics to TCP transports, we'll want to make some additions to the telemetry API to ingest these metrics. If any metrics are shared between HTTP and raw TCP transports (say, bytes sent), we'll want to differentiate between them in Prometheus. All the metrics that the control plane currently ingests from telemetry reports are likely to be HTTP-specific (requests, responses, response latencies), or at least, do not apply to raw TCP.

Actually adding metrics to raw TCP transports will probably have to wait until there _are_ raw TCP transports implemented in the proxy...

Can we get rid of this and use the protobuf-generated version of the struct throughout? I'd even be in favor of adding a new `CheckStatus` enum in the protobuf definition, using that in the `CheckResult` message, and removing the `CheckStatus` type alias in healthcheck.go.

review_threads.author: pcalcado
review_threads.body:
I guess it depends on how we want to handle protobuf/grpc code going forward.

My preference would be to treat all this as our Presentation Layer and avoid as much as possible using these objects directly in our main logic. The thinking here is that:

1) The code generated by protobuf/grpc is meant to be efficient for RPC, but isn't very ergonomic. Using it inside our core logic increases accidental complexity and leads to hard-to-test code, an example being [the amount of boilerplate we need to test the tap command](https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/blob/1dc1c00a2aee6f41d899ba6fb83ae065309e76ab/cli/cmd/tap_test.go#L90)
2) As more and more components use our protobuf definitions, these become increasingly hard to change. We should be free to change our internal objects whenever we feel like, but every time we change a protobuf schema we will need to be more careful, even considering backwards compatibility.

SO, at least for our server-side components, I would suggest that we follow what is sometimes called [Hexagonal Architecture](http://alistair.cockburn.us/Hexagonal+architecture), and keep our RPC code apart from our core types.

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
These are all good points. I agree that tying our internal structs too closely to our public structs could be problematic in the long run, if we need more flexibility internally, but are constrained by API compatibility requirements.

That said, I'm a bit skeptical that the hexagonal architecture is a good fit for go. The adapters described in the article end up being a lot of boilerplate in the codebase, for what is effectively a cast from the external representation to the internal representation. Coercing objects back and forth can also be error prone, especially if, say, the internal and external representations of a given int field use different bit lengths.

In my mind, it's a lot less error prone to manipulate the grpc structs directly, especially for things like enums. Maintaining one enum in the protobuf and a separate enum in the internal codebase means that you have to also supply a mapping between the two, and this leads to a lot more touch-points whenever you add another value to the enum.

Anyway, the takeaway here is that I can see the benefit to both approaches, but I would like to at least try to pursue the consolidated approach until it seems too unwieldy and we have good reason to split them up. If it works for you, I'm hoping we can ship this branch as written, and then I'd be happy to undertake the consolidation as a separate follow-up branch. Thoughts?

title: Move healthcheck proto to separate file, use throughout
body:
This is a follow-up to https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/pull/140#discussion_r161123464. I'm moving all of the healthcheck types out of common.proto, and into a separate file. And then I'm using the generated protobuf structs throughout the codebase, removing the corresponding structs that were previously defined in pkg/healthcheck/healthcheck.go.

As part of this change I'm changing the method signature for the `SelfCheck` method on the `StatusChecker` interface to be `SelfCheck() []*pb.CheckResult` (no longer return an error). None of the existing implementations of that method returned an error, and I think it's more appropriate for a check that errors to return `pb.CheckResult{Status: pb.CheckStatus_ERROR}` anyway. This also helps to clean up the code a bit.

title: Add transparent protocol detection to proxy
body:
The proxy will now try to detect what protocol new connections are
using, and route them accordingly. Specifically:

- HTTP/2 stays the same.
- HTTP/1 is now accepted, and will try to send an HTTP/1 request
  to the target.
- If neither HTTP/1 nor 2, assume a TCP stream and simply forward
  between the source and destination.

Closes #130 
Closes #131 

----

For HTTP/1 requests, it's possible there isn't an authority attached (1.0 doesn't know about `Host`, and even 1.1 is [allowed](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7230#section-5.4) to send `Host: \r\n` if it doesn't know it). In these cases, the socket's `SO_ORIGINAL_DST` will be used to adjust the request-target.

Some things that may need to be done before merging:

- [x] (https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/issues/181) Ensure the controller destination service can echo back an address when we use the `SO_ORIGINAL_DST`.
- [x] Decide if transparency should start with config flags to disable.
- [x] (https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/issues/187) Decide if HTTP/1 telemetry should be disabled until the controller can better handle the large number of unique paths.

title: Remove DOCKER_FORCE_BUILD, disable symbolic tags
body:
Remove DOCKER_FORCE_BUILD, disable symbolic tags

DOCKER_FORCE_BUILD, combined with symbolic tags, added complexity and
risk of running unintended versions of the code.

This change removes DOCKER_FORCE_BUILD, and sets all Docker tags
programmatically. The decision to pull or build has been moved up the
stack from _docker.sh to the docker-build-* scripts. Workflows that
want to favor docker pulls (like ci), can do so explicitly via
docker-pull.

fixes #141

Signed-off-by: Andrew Seigner <siggy@buoyant.io>

---

### Previous summary for posterity

DOCKER_FORCE_BUILD=1 is a common development build pattern.

Replace (and invert) DOCKER_FORCE_BUILD with DOCKER_TRY_PULL. Default behavior
(with DOCKER_TRY_PULL unset) is to only rely on local docker repo for cached
images. DOCKER_TRY_PULL is enabled in CI. Also remove
DOCKER_BUILD_CACHE_FROM_TAG as it was unused.

fixes #141

# Performance validation

Tested the build before/after code change, with and without force flag, and on empty local docker repo, and subsequent build:

|                 | 1st build | 2nd build |
|-----------------|-----------|-----------|
| no force/before |     3m35s |        8s |
| no force/after  |     3m36s |        8s |
| force/before    |     6m05s |        8s |
| force/after     |     6m03s |        8s |
author: siggy

comments.author: olix0r
comments.body:
> DOCKER_FORCE_BUILD=1 is a common development build pattern.

Can we get a bit clearer on this?

My specific concern is that the "root" build command, `bin/docker-build` with no other arguments, generally benefits from this behavior.  Should it be more common to run this command with an argument? If so, why?  What if we simply removed the tag argument to `bin/docker-build`? What are the larger workflows where this is necessary?

comments.author: siggy
comments.body:
@olix0r Per https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/issues/141#issuecomment-357296715, we discussed two approaches:

Approach 1:
```bash
git commit ...
bin/docker-build && bin/docker-retag-all $(bin/root-tag) latest
```

Approach 2:
```bash
DOCKER_FORCE_BUILD=1 bin/docker-build latest
```

The specific workflow this change is intended to target is documented at: https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/blob/master/BUILD.md#comprehensive.
The goal of this workflow is: edit code, build docker images, run, and repeat, without committing.

The goal of this PR is to slightly simplify the above workflow.

comments.author: olix0r
comments.body:
My intent with docker-build is specifically optimized for use of concrete tags, which, in my experience, reduces a _lot_ of complexity when debugging runtime issues (like docker pull policies, etc). We've all wasted way too much time testing the wrong images.

Are there impediments to adapting such a workflow? Or do others think this is generally a crazy idea?

Our dev workflow is still evolving and I'd like to converge on a best practices.  If using symbolic tags makes lives much easier, by all means let's adopt this change and move forward. @siggy and I will sit down and work through the this today and get a clear path forward.

comments.author: siggy

Goal of this change is to make edit/build/run as simple as possible:
```

# step 2: install

## Proposed changes

- remove the tag param from the `bin/docker-build` scripts. all tags are concrete, and specified by the tools.
- move implicit docker pulls out of `_docker.sh` up into higher-level scripts that explicitly want to pull, namely:
  - `docker-build-base`

  - `docker-build-proxy-deps`

title: Fix error handling for Tap CLI and public<>tap server
body:
-  first step towards #49
- closes #106

This started as an investigation of why `$ conduit tap` would abort with `unexpected EOF` at times.

To debug, I've read all the protobuf-to-http code and, while at that I've cleaned up it a bit and wrote tests for a lot of it.

I finally identified that this problem was due to us not checking when the gRPC `Tap()` returned an error (in this case because the pods didnt exist). Commit c27f400e8918d94ce566f63dea94d4af74c2ab7a  adds  this check.

The EOF goes away in the client, but the error message still wasn't great:
```
pcalcado@arbeitsziege.local:~/code/src/github.com/runconduit/conduit  $ conduit tap pod default/pod-with-no-rules  --api-addr localhost:8085
rpc error: code = Unknown desc = no pod exists for key default/pod-with-no-rules%
```

So I did some digging and realized that we haven't been using gRPC errors properly. Commit a3954e6 adds that to the tap server, and after it here is the message displayed:

```
pcalcado@arbeitsziege.local:~/code/src/github.com/runconduit/conduit  $ conduit tap pod default/pod-with-no-rules  --api-addr localhost:8085
no pod exists for key default/pod-with-no-rules%

comments.author: pcalcado
comments.body:
@deebo91 [said](https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/pull/177#discussion_r163688318):
```go
if totalBytesRead != messageLength {
 return nil, fmt.Errorf("message declared length [%d] but could only read [%d] bytes")
}
```
> Just to wrap my head around this error case, What scenarios would cause the code to reach this line when deserializing the HTTP? Proto? body.


The protocol we use here is custom, and it relies on declaring the message length using [the first four bytes of the HTTP body](https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/blob/5e6684f9f28abe46160ad2c5b8049bf9cb5b9a29/controller/api/public/proto_over_http.go#L114). If everything goes well, the server code probably uses `serializeAsPayload` to encode the message and everybody will be happy.

Unfortunately the world is a sad place. It could be that:
-  we accidentally introduce a code path on the server that doesn't call `serializeAsPayload` but rather use a copy adn paste'd version that isn't broken
- we might want to change the protocol in an upcoming version (say using more or fewer bytes than 4) and we might have a situation where the user has a CLI version that is a bit older and doesn't know about the protocol change
- When writing distributed systems, even if you have absolute control of the `from` and `to` components you still have to deal with the unreliable network. There are many pieces of middleware between the CLI and the actual server, from the k8s API to k8s itself to maybe even a web accelerator proxy thing or some corporate spyware that the user might have installed in their network. These things, especially some weird proprietary "security" tools corporations sometimes use, can do all sort of transformations with they payload. It might be the case that you hit a defective one and they strip out some bytes from your message. If we don't check this here, we will have a very confusing error when this gets unmarshalled. Instead, we should detect the error as soon as possible and inform this function's caller that something isn't cool.

EDIT--
OTOH, @peczenyj just reminded me that `ReadFull` returns an error if fewer bytes were read, so this is useless 😎

title: Rename js components to clarify component relationships
body:
Rename some components in an effort to make things clearer.

* Rename Deployment to DeploymentDetail to match PodDetail
* Rename Deployments to DeploymentsList to clarify which page this is
* Rename StatPane to EntityOverview to be a less generic name

Signed-off-by: Risha Mars <mars@buoyant.io>
author: rmars

comments.author: rmars
comments.body:
Yeah! So I'm trying to name them as concisely as possible while also being consistent and descriptive (omg naming is hard). Here are my thoughts on the suggestions above:

`DeploymentSummary -> DeploymentDetailSummary` 👎 
For `DeploymentSummary`, this component shows the essential metrics of a deployment (request rate graph, success/request rates), and is used in both the Service Mesh component and the DeploymentOverview components. So it's not a Summary meant for the deployment detail page, but rather a summary of a single deployment. (Suggestions to that end are welcome!)

`ServiceMesh` -> `ServiceMeshOverview` 🇨🇭 
I renamed `Deployments` to `DeploymentsOverview` to clarify the relationship with `DeploymentDetail` (i.e. an overview vs detail, or a list vs detail component). ServiceMesh doesn't have a ServiceMeshDetail that we really need to distinguish it from, though it is an overview of the service mesh health, so I could see ServiceMeshOverview as being a descriptive name. I think I would rather keep the shorter name until we have to change it though.

`HealthPane` -> `HealthOverview` 👍 
I think HealthOverview would be fine to use, and maybe more descriptive than "pane"! The gripe I had with StatPane was that I felt like "Stat" was not very descriptive (could be any stat). This could even be `EntityHealthOverview` to imply its usage in both Pod and Deployment Detail views.

`EntityOverview`  🇨🇭 
I agree that EntityOverview is a very generic name, though I think it's a marginal improvement over StatPane. Mostly in Stat Pane I felt like "stat" was very generic and could mean any metric, whereas "EntityOverview" at least implied there would be overall stats about an entity (this component is generic so it can be used for Deployment/Pod stats, hence "entity"), and "Overview" implying topline "request/success rate" stats. Suggestions welcome as to alternatives for this!

`EntityOverview` -> `EntityMetricOverview`
`HealthPane` -> `EntityHealthOverview`

This way, it's clear that a Pod/Deployment Entity's page would consist of a HealthOverview and a MetricOverview.

title: Classify non-gRPC status codes for HTTP telemetry
body:
Currently, all "success"/"failure" classifications in the telemetry API are made based on the `grpc-status` trailer. If the trailer is not present, then a request is assumed to have failed. As we start proxying non-gRPC traffic, the controller needs to also be aware of HTTP status codes, so that non-gRPC requests are not assumed to always fail.

I've modified the telemetry API server to classify requests based on their HTTP status codes when the `grpc-status` trailer is not present. 

I've also modified the `simulate-proxy` script to generate fake HTTP/2 traffic without the `grpc-status` trailer.

Closes #196

title: Set conduit version to match conduit docker tags
body:
In this branch I'm modifying the go `bin/docker-build*` scripts to pass the docker tag as an argument to the docker build command, and using the argument to set the conduit version in all of the binaries that are built. This allows us to stop hardcoding the conduit version in `controller/version.go`.

As part of this change I'm also changing the way in which the image tag is determined, such that if you're building from a clean commit that corresponds to a git tag, we use the git tag instead. This allows us to build stable image versions for release, corresponding to the release tag.

I've also added a `bin/conduit` script that will run the architecture-appropriate conduit executable, and I've updated the instructions in BUILD.md to use that script.

And finally, I've added command-line flags to the web and controller executables, for printing the build version and exiting.

Fixes #172.
Fixes #211.

title: proxy: fix h1 streams to trigger response end events
body:
Response End events were only triggered after polling the trailers of
a response, but when the Response is given to a hyper h1 server, it
doesn't know about trailers, so they were never polled!

The fix is that the `BodyStream` glue will now poll the wrapped body for
trailers after it sees the end of the data, before telling hyper the
stream is over. This ensures a ResponseEnd event is emitted.

Includes a proxy telemetry test over h1 connections.

title: Add ability to change the time window for metrics fetching throughout the app
body:
### Changes
- Consolidate the usage of `pathPrefix` and `metricsWindow` into `ApiHelpers.jsx`.
  - This allows us to stop passing around metricsWindow and pathPrefix in each component in the app.
  - This also allows us to set the metricsWindow and have this setting stay as we navigate around the app
- Wrap all app `Link`s in a `ConduitLink` that includes the `pathPrefix`, so that we don't need `pathPrefix` everywhere
- Add tests for ApiHelpers

![screen shot 2018-01-30 at 4 52 48 pm](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/549258/35600290-0c6d2954-05e2-11e8-9719-1b4011172b5e.png)

### Current issues
- Until the telemetry service is refactored, the 1h time window is probably never going to return metrics. Also, 10s is probably not going to make a lot of sense as an option you want to view.
- Currently, it's not super evident that your time window change has been received when you click the buttons. We could clear the metrics for the page and show a spinner immediately, which would give the user feedback. I've tried this in af320b0

### Future work enabled by this branch
- setting the `pollingInterval` based on the `metricsWindow` (#241)
- wrapping the api calls in a cancelable promise, which will allow us to stop setting state after component unmount (#242, #157)

title: Add -log-level flag for install and inject commands
body:
This branch updates the install and inject commands to add a `--log-level` flag, which can be used to set the log level of the control and data plane components.

Note that the CLI previously supported a global `--log-level` flag, but I've renamed that to `--verbose`, which can be used to turn on debug logging, as there shouldn't be any other use case for adjusting the log level of the CLI.

I'm also fixing an issue where, in certain places, we were calling `log.Fatal`, and that was causing the logged messages to be rendered with additional formatting, which seemed unintended. For instance, on master:

```
$ conduit completion asdf
2018/01/30 18:05:54 unsupported shell type (must be bash or zsh): asdf
```

Whereas with this change:

```
$ conduit completion asdf
unsupported shell type (must be bash or zsh): asdf
```

Fixes #230.
author: klingerf

comments.author: siggy
comments.body: @pcalcado i've updated #230 with more specific exit criteria for what this feature looks like.

review_threads.author: siggy
pcalcado
review_threads.body: I actually like the formatted output, but if we're going to change this then I'd prefer to have a global `log` object that is configured this way on `root`. Whatever solution we end up with, I think the important thing is that either we _only_ use the wrapper functions or we _only_ use the log object directly, which means that we'd need wrapped functions for all levels and formatted vs. `ln` versions.

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body: Cool, yeah this all makes sense. I've removed the `logFatalf` method, and changed the initializer back to setting the log level on logrus's global logger. Related to my comment above, I've also defaulted the log level to "panic" (no logging), when the `--verbose` flag is not set. As part of this change, I've converted all of the `log.Fatal` calls in this package to instead print directly to stderr (since they otherwise wouldn't be printed at the default level). This guarantees that we won't print log messages unless the `--verbose` flag is set, and when we do print messages, they'll be fully formatted with timestamps.

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body:
TIOLI, I prefer the granular control that log levels provide, though I may be in the minority. @pcalcado and I discussed this on a previous PR: https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/pull/154#issuecomment-358086195

As another example, I needed exactly this functionality today while debugging with `kubectl proxy --v=10`:

```bash
$ kubectl options
...
  -v, --v=0: log level for V logs
```

Perhaps this may be symptom of trying to solve two distinct use cases: 1) verbose information for users vs. 2) debugging information for developers. I think the line between the two cases (and users) are blurry enough that multiple log levels can satisfy both.

review_threads.author: pcalcado
review_threads.body: Although I still prefer --verbose for the UX I'd be happier keeping the --log-level as it is right now. If anything, we could add a --verbose that pretty much is an alias for --log-level DEBUG later.

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
Ah, sorry, I missed the discussion about this in #154. I agree with @pcalcado's comments in that PR. Exposing log levels to a CLI feels unintuitive to me, since I usually expect long-running processes to log, and I expect CLI commands to print stuff and exit, but not log in the traditional sense. That said, for the sake of debugging, I can totally see the value in adjusting the verbosity of the command, which, again, doesn't really feel like logging to me.

Put another way, under normal circumstances, a CLI command should _never_ log. It should only return exactly the output that it's intended to return, explicitly. Outputting messages as the byproduct of log statements seems messy. If the CLI does have the capacity to log, I'd expect the default log level to be "off". In that world, the `-log-level` flag would only ever be used to lower the log level for the sake of debugging. Hence my preference to switch this to a boolean `--verbose` flag that sets log-level=debug.

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body:
can we call this `--proxy-log-level`? with our usage of `--log-level` in other go processes, i'd prefer to be explicit that this something different from the log level for the process being executed.

also, could we provide some examples for valid inputs? for example, i used this this week: `trace,conduit_proxy=trace,hyper=trace`.

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body:
Yeah, so the way the `RUST_LOG` environment variable works is that it can take a comma separated list of { `level` | `scope` | `scope=level` }. A bare log `level` will enable that level for all modules, a bare `scope` will enable all log levels for that scope, and `scope=level` will set the log level for that scope to the given level. 

Valid log levels (see https://docs.rs/log/0.4.1/log/#use) are: 
- `trace`
- `debug`
- `info`
- `warn`
- `error`

The scopes we're probably the most likely to care about are:
- `conduit_proxy`: the proxy itself
- `h2`, `tower-h2`: the libraries we use for HTTP/2
- `hyper`: the library we used for HTTP/1
- `tower-grpc`: the gRPC library (probably will want the `h2` libs as well for debugging gRPC issues)

You can set more granular scopes as well, but this is based on the layout of the Rust modules in the proxy. 

For more in depth docs, see https://doc.rust-lang.org/log/env_logger/index.html#enabling-logging

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body: Hmm, it occurs to me that this wall of text could probably go in docs somewhere now that I think of it.

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
It seems like we might be overthinking this a bit. The help message for this flag looks like this:

```
      --proxy-log-level string          log level for the proxy (default "warn,conduit_proxy=info")
```

Including "warn,conduit_proxy=info" as the default gives the user enough of an indication that you can set both a global log level and a package-specific log level. Anybody who needs more control than that is likely familiar enough with the proxy to know which levels and packages to use. So I'm inclined to rename this flag to `--proxy-log-level` and leave it as is, if that works for you all.

title: Use a load-aware balancer
body:
Currently, the conduit proxy uses a simplistic Round-Robin load
balancing algorithm. This strategy degrades severely when individual
endpoints exhibit abnormally high latency.

This change improves this situation somewhat by making the load balancer
aware of the number of outstanding requests to each endpoint. When nodes
exhibit high latency, they should tend to have more pending requests
than faster nodes; and the Power-of-Two-Choices node selector can be
used to distribute requests to lesser-loaded instances.

From the finagle guide:

    The algorithm randomly picks two nodes from the set of ready endpoints
    and selects the least loaded of the two. By repeatedly using this
    strategy, we can expect a manageable upper bound on the maximum load of
    any server.

    The maximum load variance between any two servers is bound by
    ln(ln(n))` where `n` is the number of servers in the cluster.
author: olix0r

comments.author: dadjeibaah
comments.body: I know that conduit is supposed to be zero config. Does this mean that conduit users are always going to have to stick with the `power_of_two_choices` load balancing?

comments.author: adleong
comments.body:
Great question, @deebo91!  Power of two choices with the least loaded metrics (P2C+LL) is a very good general purpose load balancing algorithm that works pretty well for most kinds of traffic.  So I think it's a great default.  

In the future, it would be really cool to see Conduit dynamically picking an LB algorithm depending on the nature of the traffic it sees.  For example, EWMA+Latency for unary requests, P2C+LL for streaming requests, aperture when the load doesn't match the pool size, etc.

But in general, it should be possible to intelligently make these determinations based on the live data instead of needing users to configure it.

comments.author: dadjeibaah

Another useful metric to look at is `goal%`, which represents the percentage of requests actually sent, given a goal of 100rps. The p2c output shows that it came closer to reaching the goal, which means that it had higher overall throughput.

title: Move the Rust gRPC bindings into a dedicated crate
body:
The proxy depends on protoc-generated gRPC bindings to communicate with the controller. In order to generate these bindings, build-time dependencies like `tower_grpc_build` must be compiled.

In order to support a more granular, cacheable build scheme where these dependencies are not needed to build the proxy, a new crate has been created to house these gRPC bindings, `conduit-proxy-controller-grpc`.

Because `TryFrom` and `TryInto` conversions are implemented for protobuf-defined types, the `convert` module also had to be moved to into a dedicated crate.

Furthermore, because the proxy's tests require that `quickcheck::Aribtrary` be implemented for protobuf types, the `conduit-proxy-controller-grpc` crate supports an _arbitrary_ feature flag.

While we're moving these libraries around, the `tower-router` crate has been moved to `proxy/router` and renamed to `conduit-proxy-router.` `futures-mpsc-lossy` has been moved into the proxy directory but has not been renamed. It is no longer ambiguous with the crate housed in the tower-rs repo.

Finally, the proxy/Dockerfile-deps image has been updated to avoid the wasteful building of dependency artifacts, as they are not actually used by proxy/Dockerfile.

title: Remove proxy/Dockerfile-deps
body:
The current proxy Dockerfile configuration does not cache dependencies well, which can increase build times substantially.

By carefully splitting proxy/Dockerfile into several stages that mock parts of the project, dependencies may be built and cached in Docker such that changes to the proxy only require building the conduit-proxy crate.

Furthermore, proxy/Dockerfile now runs the proxy's tests before producing an artifact, unless the `SKIP_TESTS` build-arg is set and not-empty.

The `BUILD_UNOPTIMIZED` build-arg has been added to support quicker, debug-friendly builds.

`bin/docker-build-proxy` has been changed to admit arbitrary command-line arguments that are passed to `docker`.

To summarize an offline conversation with @siggy:

* `SKIP_TESTS` is enabled by default because, if we have a build artifact, we generally want to trust that it passed tests.

title: Fix bug where table data wasn't being updated
body:
Also remove unused state initializations.

*Problem*
The state of TabbedMetricsTable wasn't being updated when the metrics were updated.

*Cause*
State doesn't update with props update in the constructor
(https://reactjs.org/docs/react-component.html#constructor)

*Solution*
Don't use the state set in the constructor.

Fixes #236
author: rmars

comments.author: rmars
comments.body: The UpstreamDownstream tables receive metrics as props and pass those down to TabbedMetricsTables, also as props. Each component can decide whether to set its own state upon construction based on the props it receives (or even update the state based on new props, using componentWillReceiveProps). We don't actually change any of the data in the TabbedMetricsTable, so there's no need for it to communicate any changes back to its parents. So we can get away with it being rendered solely on its props. The rollup field doesn't get updated because once the component is constructed with `constructor` it doesn't take into account new Props. It doesn't get overridden with empty data, it just decides not to do anything with the new data.

review_threads.author: franziskagoltz
review_threads.body: Just to clarify: we don't need to have a state here with `pollingInterval`, as all parent components have it and will trigger a re-render upon fetching a new interval which will trigger down a new and updated render of `TabbedMetricsTable`, right?

review_threads.author: rmars
review_threads.body:
correct! we fetch data every pollingInterval in the parent component, and pass the data down as a prop to TabbedMetricTable. When the TabbedMetricsTable receives the new props, it will rerender. 
Previously, we were setting the state based on the props in the constructor - this doesn't update the state when new props are passed in, which is why the table wasn't updating.

title: Optimize Prometheus queries
body:
Prometheus queries from the Telemetry service were taking seconds or 10s
of seconds.

Optimize these queries:
- Move all summary queries requiring a single data point off of Prometheus'
  QueryRange() endpoint, onto Query()
- Set `defaultVectorRange` to 30s, and also use it regardless of time
  window
Also add tests for grpc_server and telemetry server

Signed-off-by: Andrew Seigner <siggy@buoyant.io>

Fixes #260

# Results

Previously we had 12 variants of Prometheus query with p50's ranging from 4s to 8s. After these changes, all queries are < 3s, and all but 9 are < 300ms. p95 and p99 are also cut in half.

All results were generated using https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/tree/siggy/viz

## Average latency across all Prometheus queries

### Before

![sum_avg_baseline](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/236915/35950577-111ff256-0c2c-11e8-9c42-560c54737ac0.png)

### After

![screen shot 2018-02-07 at 10 15 26 am](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/236915/35950578-156c5a84-0c2c-11e8-9397-4cfd45d7dafb.png)

## Latency per Prometheus query

### Before

![avg_baseline_step](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/236915/35950449-7cfeecee-0c2b-11e8-9c73-c7637a0ba6fd.png)

### After

![avg_query_step](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/236915/35950451-80280edc-0c2b-11e8-9779-befaeac28d97.png)
author: siggy

review_threads.author: adleong
review_threads.body: Much of the behavior of this method switches depending on if start/stop/step is set or not.  Would it make sense to split this into two methods, `QueryTs` and `QuerySummary` or something like that?

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body: I agree, now that the telemetry service's `Query()` endpoint is supporting two distinct use cases, this warrants modifying the API to be more explicit about it. This will require a protobuf change in the telemetry service, which is better done in a separate PR, I've filed #312 to track.

review_threads.author: adleong
review_threads.body: This is "summary" mode?  Does that means this gets the single most recent datapoint or does it summarize over some range?

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body:
Correct this is "summary" mode, which means return the single most recent data point. We pass in `time.Time{}` as a way to indicate we want the most recent data point:
https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/api/#instant-queries

We were previously doing this manually by querying the full timeseries, and then calling `filterQueryRsp` to filter to the latest data point.

For a bit more context, here is where the `timeseries` param in the `web` API translates into `Summarize` in the public API (perhaps as part of #312 we could make these terms more consistent):
https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/blob/2f114e69fad36c7eb40aefcbccf301a6c30470c6/web/srv/api_handlers.go#L140

review_threads.author: adleong
review_threads.body: this is not specific to this change, but I'm struggling a bit to understand the API.  Is a "Sample" a timeseries?  and each sample contains the data points for that timeseries?  and in summary mode each Sample will only have one data point?

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body: correct, a `read.Sample` represents a single metric over time, and, in summary mode `read.Sample` will contain one data point. this is another artifact of telemetry's `Query()` endpoint supporting both timeseries and non-timeseries data (so it always returns a timeseries-like data structure). this is another area to clean up in #312.

review_threads.author: rmars
review_threads.body: I might be missing something, but this test (and the one in the next section) passes even if you don't include a time range. are we just testing that it accepts such an input without error?

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body:
Really good catch !

I had previously implemented telemetry service's `Query()` endpoint to handle all querying first, then all data processes second. I felt these edge cases were worth the trade off to make the code a bit easier to read. Following your comment here, I've reconsidered, and have reorganized `Query()` to handle timeseries request/process in one block, and non-timeseries in another. This produces slightly more repeated code, but as you've pointed out, is more correct. I've modified the tests as well to validate these additional edge cases. Thanks!

title: Fix pointer copying
body:
The Public APIs stat endpoint copies a slice of values to a slice of
pointers prior to gRPC response. Go's range clause re-uses the same
pointer for each iteration of the loop, causing a slice of {1,2,3}
becoming {3,3,3}.

Fix the range loop to directly reference pointers in the slice of
values, ignoring the range variable. Also add tests to catch this case.

Signed-off-by: Andrew Seigner <siggy@buoyant.io>

Here's a concrete demonstration of the issue:
https://play.golang.org/p/aLpyKktq24K

title: Use Prometheus to track added data plane pods.
body:
The instance cache that powers the ListPods API is stored in memory in the telemetry service. This means that when there are multiple replicas of the telemetry service, each replica will have a distinct, incomplete view of the added pods based on which pods report to that telemetry replica. This causes the data plane bubbles on the dashboard to not all be filled in, and to flicker with each data refresh.

We create a Prometheus counter called `reports_total` which has `pod` as a label.  Whenever a telemetry service instance receives a report from a pod, it increments `reports_total` for that pod.  This allows us to remove the in-memory instance cache and instead query Prometheus to see if each pod has had a report in the last 30 seconds.

Fixes #337 

Signed-off-by: Alex Leong <alex@buoyant.io>
author: adleong

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body: we were previously doing `expiry := time.Now().Add(-10 * time.Minute)` ... i believe `reports_total[30s]` means we're expiring after 30s?

review_threads.author: adleong
review_threads.body: that's right.  Given that reports are supposed to come at least every 10s, a 30s TTL seemed more reasonable to me than 10m.  WDYT?

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body: i think `s.Values[len(s.Values)-1].Timestamp` is already a `time.Time`?

review_threads.author: adleong
review_threads.body: it's a `model.Time` from Prometheus, which is a type alias for `int64`.

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
There's no need to split the timestamp when calling `time.Unix` -- from the godoc:

> It is valid to pass nsec outside the range [0, 999999999]

So you could instead write this as:

```
		reports[labels["pod"]] = time.Unix(0, int64(timestamp)*int64(time.Millisecond))
```

I also recommend using the [duration constants](https://golang.org/pkg/time/#Duration), instead of hardcoding 1000, 1000000, etc.

title: Require timestamp on all telemetry requests
body:
PR #298 moved summary (non-timeseries) requests to Prometheus' Query
endpoint, with no timestamp provided. This Query endpoint returns a
single data point with whatever timestamp was provided in the request.
In the absense of a timestamp, it uses current server time. This causes
the Public API to return discreet data points with slightly different
timestamps, which is unexpected behavior.

Modify the Public API -> Telemetry -> Prometheus request path to always
require a timestamp for single data point requests.

Fixes #340

Signed-off-by: Andrew Seigner <siggy@buoyant.io>
author: siggy

title: Ensure latency quantile queries match timestamps
body:
In PR #298 we moved time window parsing (10s => (time.now - 10s,
time.now) down the stack to immediately before the query. This had the
unintended effect of creating parallel latency quantile requests with
slightly different timestamps.

This change parses the time window prior to latency quantile fan out,
ensuring all requests have the same timestamp.

title: Base control plane Docker images on scratch instead of base.
body:
The control plane is proxied through the Conduit proxy. The Conduit
proxy is based on the base image, and the control plane containers
and the proxy share a networking namespace. This means we don't
need the extra base utilities in the controller images since we can
use the utilties in the proxy image.

This is a step towards building the initial no-networking Conduit CA
pod. Since the Conduit CA will not do any networking of its own, we
networking debugging utilties are not helpful for it. They are
actually an unnecessary risk because they could facilitate the
exfiltration of the private key of the CA. (The Conduit CA pod won't
have the Conduit Proxy injected into it either.)

This also simplifies & slightly speeds up the building of the
controller images. This is a stepping stone towards being able to
build the controller images without `docker build` to improve build
times.

Signed-off-by: Brian Smith <brian@briansmith.org>

title: Add ability to cancel promises via a wrapper
body:
Fixes react setSate warnings when we navigate between components.
Follows advice of https://reactjs.org/blog/2015/12/16/ismounted-antipattern.html

Problem: if a component has initiated a fetch that has not yet completed, and you navigate to another component in the meantime, when the fetch completes, the previous component will try to call a `setState`. However, that component has already been unmounted, which causes a `Warning: Can only update a mounted or mounting component` error.

Solution: wrap the promise, adding a `cancel()` method that will reject the promise

Fixes #242
Fixes #157
author: rmars

review_threads.author: dadjeibaah
review_threads.body: Just curious about what this is used for. Is function created for testability?

review_threads.author: rmars
review_threads.body:
this is the function that wraps a promise and makes it a cancelable promise. there's no way to actually cancel a fetch request (currently), but we'd like a way to stop caring about the result of an unresolved promise. so we wrap a regular promise in an object, such that we now have:
```
{
  promise: ... // our original promise with some handlers,
  cancel: ... // a method allowing us to say when we don't care about the results of the resolve promise any more
}
```

On line 55, you can see we're using this to wrap our fetch calls:
```
return makeCancelable(fetch(path), r => r.json());
```

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
In playing around with this locally, I realized that there isn't a "Completed" status, unfortunately. The five [pod phases](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-phase) are: Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed, and Unknown. We've also added Terminating for pods that are terminating.

I haven't thought about this too much, but I think we should categorize pods as follows:

* `p.added && p.status == "Running"` => "good"
* `p.status == "Pending"` => "neutral"
* `p.status == "Failed"` => "bad"
* `p.status == "Terminating" || p.status == "Succeeded" || p.status == "Unknown"` => remove

But I'd also be up for other suggestions of how to categorize and filter.

title: proxy: use original dst if authority doesnt look like local service
body:
The proxy will check that the requested authority looks like a local service, and if it doesn't, it will no longer ask the Destination service about the request, instead just using the `SO_ORIGINAL_DST`, enabling egress naturally.

The rules used to determine if it looks like a local service come from [this comment](https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/pull/360#issuecomment-366839073):

> If `default_zone.is_none()` and the name is in the form `$a.$b.svc`, or if `!default_zone.is_none()` and the name is in the form `$a.$b.svc.$default_zone`, for some `a` and some `b`, then use the Destination service. Otherwise, use the IP given.
author: seanmonstar

review_threads.body:
The tests show the effects, but I'll group them up here. These are all considered external names:

- `name` (no namespace, svc, or zone)
- `name.namespace.svc.cluster` (zone doesn't match `cluster.local`)
- `name.namespace.foo` (not svc)

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body:
Why don't we need `External` to be `External(Authority)` or `External(IpAddr, Authority)`?

In particular, in HTTP/1 we're generally not supposed to send requests for different `Host:`s on the same connection because not all HTTP/1 servers properly support that. This makes me think that both the authority and the IP address must be part of the key.

(OTOH, if we were already mixing requests for different hosts on the same outbound HTTP/1 connection then we can address this in a separate issue later.)

Regardless of which way we do it, let's add a comment explaining why we are doing it the way we're doing it, and not the other way.

review_threads.author: seanmonstar
review_threads.body:
The addition of the `Host` header in HTTP/1.1 is actually specifically for that purpose, to allow a server to handle requests for various authorities.

Additionally, it's possible at many stages already to find that a `Host` is found at the same address. I don't believe this PR changes anything.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body:
1. How do we know the *server* is HTTP/1.1 and not HTTP/1.0? We would have had to have previously received a HTTP/1.1 response from the server to know that; we can't know it from looking at the request.

2. Although I mostly agree with you w.r.t. what was intended in HTTP/1.1, many HTTP/1.1 servers don't properly respect `Host:` beyond the first request, which is why browsers don't (IIRC) send requests for different `Host`s on the same connection. This is why, in particular, browsers don't do connection coalescing for HTTP/1.1, but only for HTTP/2.

Regardless, you don't have to answer those questions here. I just want to point out that it is important to not regress in this respect. As long as you're sure that the behavior isn't changed from before, we can deal with it in another issue.

title: Limit the max number of in-flight requests in proxy.
body:
Currently, the max number of in-flight requests in the proxy is
unbounded. This is due to the `Buffer` middleware being unbounded.

This is resolved by adding an instance of `InFlightLimit` around
`Buffer`, capping the max number of in-flight requests for a given
endpoint.

Currently, the limit is hardcoded to 10,000. However, this will
eventually become a configuration value.

Fixes #287

Signed-off-by: Carl Lerche <me@carllerche.com>>

title: Add timeout to Outbound::bind_service
body:
Closes #403.

When the Destination service does not return a result for a service, the proxy connection for that service will hang indefinitely waiting for a result from Destination. If, for example, the requested name doesn't exist, this means that the proxy will wait forever, rather than responding with an error.

I've added a timeout wrapping the service returned from `<Outbound as Recognize>::bind_service`. The timeout can be configured by setting the `CONDUIT_PROXY_BIND_TIMEOUT` environment variable, and defaults to 10 seconds (because that's the default value for [a similar configuration in Linkerd](https://linkerd.io/config/1.3.5/linkerd/index.html#router-parameters)).

Testing with @klingerf's reproduction from #403:
```
curl -sIH 'Host: httpbin.org' $(minikube service proxy-http --url)/get | head -n1
HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error
```
proxy logs:
```rust
proxy-5698f79b66-8rczl conduit-proxy INFO conduit_proxy using controller at HostAndPort { host: Domain("proxy-api.conduit.svc.cluster.local"), port: 8086 }
proxy-5698f79b66-8rczl conduit-proxy INFO conduit_proxy routing on V4(127.0.0.1:4140)
proxy-5698f79b66-8rczl conduit-proxy INFO conduit_proxy proxying on V4(0.0.0.0:4143) to None
proxy-5698f79b66-8rczl conduit-proxy INFO conduit_proxy::transport::connect "controller-client", DNS resolved proxy-api.conduit.svc.cluster.local to 10.0.0.240
proxy-5698f79b66-8rczl conduit-proxy ERR! conduit_proxy::map_err turning service error into 500: Inner(Timeout(Duration { secs: 10, nanos: 0 }))
```
author: hawkw

However, I think this would involve a slightly broader set of changes to `MapErr` and to logging, so I decided to save it for a subsequent PR.
