title: Add the proxy pod owner as a Prometheus label
body:
Update the inject command to set a CONDUIT_PROMETHEUS_LABELS proxy environment variable with the name of the pod spec that the proxy is injected into.  This will later be used as a label value when the proxy is exposing metrics.

Fixes: #426

Signed-off-by: Alex Leong <alex@buoyant.io>
author: adleong

comments.author: olix0r
comments.body:
I'm curious why the proxy has to be aware of any of this.  Hear me out:

The atomic unit of Kubernetes is the Pod.  Pods can belong in a few groupings -- Services, as well as Deployments/ReplicaSets/ReplicaControlers...

I don't think the proxy itself should need to know which pod-groupings its metrics are aggregated under or whether these aggregations occur at write-time or at read-time -- that's all up to the prometheus configuration, ideally.

So, my main question is: how can we accomplish this same thing with prometheus recording rules? If we can do this via configuration (or code in prometheus), then we would not need to push these kubernetes details into the proxy.

@brancz do you have any suggestions?

comments.author: adleong
comments.body:
To give some more context here: the goal here is to have metrics of the form:

```
inbound_requests_total{target_deployment=foo}
```

Having the proxy know its own deployment would allow it to expose this metric directly.  Barring that, the proxy would need to expose a metric like

```
inbound_requests_total{target_pod=foo-12345}
```

And have some kind of Prometheus configuration that knows how to map pods to deployments and can create and populate the `target_deployment` label.  At the same time, we may wish to drop the `target_pod` label to help keep the number of timeseries manageable.  I do not know if this is possible in Prometheus or not.

comments.author: brancz
comments.body:
> At the same time, we may wish to drop the target_pod label to help keep the number of timeseries manageable.

In this case you will end up with a unique time-series per pod anyways, as Prometheus adds the `instance` label, making it unique.

Leaving the raw `pod` label also gives the advantage that without modifying the metrics code or prometheus configuration, instead you could extend this functionality to `RelicationController`s, `StatefulSet`s, and so on simply by querying Prometheus with different queries.

comments.author: adleong
comments.body:
Thanks, @brancz!  A couple follow-up questions:

If we leave the pod/instance labels in, how is it possible to query this data by Deployment/ReplicaSet/etc?  Does the query need to have the mapping of pod->deployment built into the query itself?  Is it possible to do write-time aggregation with a recording rule?  What about as the deployment's membership changes over time?

If we do write-time aggregations on all the grouping that we care about, does it make sense to drop the pod and instance labels?  Is this a bad idea?

comments.author: brancz
comments.body:
> If we leave the pod/instance labels in, how is it possible to query this data by Deployment/ReplicaSet/etc? Does the query need to have the mapping of pod->deployment built into the query itself?

kube-state-metrics for example has metrics that you could use to join pod identity to deployment/statefulset/etc through the `kube_pod_owner` metrics. But for a start you could even just use `label_replace` functions in your query replacing `pod` labels with `deployment` labels with a regex . In the latter case you would indeed need a query per type of object to aggregate by, but in the first case the type of object would be selectable in the query. I would go for the latter option at first though as what this PR proposed would also only work for Deployments as I understand. Realistically you likely only have to support StatefulSets and Deployments anyways.

> Is it possible to do write-time aggregation with a recording rule?

Recording rules aren't exactly "write-time", but for the purpose that you want to use it for it is. Just for the whole picture, the scrape interval is independent of the evaluation interval (which is when recording rules are evaluated and written to storage), so worst case the time series populated by a recording rule lags worst case the smaller of the two intervals behind, in reality it's less than a few seconds, and you could configure rule evaluation to be more aggressive if necessary.

> What about as the deployment's membership changes over time?

Can you explain what you mean by membership?

> If we do write-time aggregations on all the grouping that we care about, does it make sense to drop the pod and instance labels? Is this a bad idea?

If you do an aggregation like `sum(inbound_requests_total) by(deployment)` then the aggregation by definition only retains the `deployment` dimension, so the other dimensions are automatically dropped.

comments.author: olix0r
comments.body:
I view "deployments" as only one way to group pods. Kubernetes label selectors are the core abstraction provided for selecting over resources, so I want to make sure that we're able to address this larger set of queries; and if/when we collapse data under deployments (i.e. by dropping the _instance_ prom labels) we lose the ability to issue such granular queries.

The fact that the conduit UIs want to discuss "deployments" isn't all that relevant to the proxy itself. 

In fact, even without supporting granular label-based queries, I think tracking "deployments" exclusively is lossy and insufficient: Kubernetes Deployments manage one or more ReplicaSets.  [We're currently losing this information](https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/issues/508), so it's not possible to differentiate two versions of a deployment during a rolling update.  So, we _really_ need to track both a replicaset and deployment label for all pods!  And what happens when additional pod-management primitives are added to Kubernetes?  Will the proxy need to be updated to have all of this additional context?

I'd prefer that the controller/prometheus own the operational context, rather than the proxy. After all, prometheus is already using the kubernetes api to determine which pods to read from.

If we are going to configure the proxy to export additional labels on all metrics, which I'm not opposed to, I think we should support an arbitrary set of prom labels so the proxy need not know anything about "deployments", etc.

---

_Edit_: Take my comments about label-selection only as high-level guidance and not specific requirements.  I think the most important thing to focus on in the short-term is properly reflecting the kubernetes resource model.

title: proxy: preserve body headers in http1
body:
As a goal of being a transparent proxy, we want to proxy requests and
responses with as little modification as possible. Basically, servers
and clients should see messages that look the same whether the proxy was
injected or not.

With that goal in mind, we want to make sure that body headers (things
like `Content-Length`, `Transfer-Encoding`, etc) are left alone. Prior
to this commit, we at times were changing behavior. Sometimes
`Transfer-Encoding` was added to requests, or `Content-Length: 0` may
have been removed. While RC 7230 defines that differences are
semantically the same, implementations may not handle them correctly.

Now, we've added some fixes to prevent any of these header changes
from occurring, along with tests to make sure library updates don't
regress.

For requests:

- With no message body, `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` should no longer be
added.
- With `Content-Length: 0`, the header is forwarded untouched.

For responses:

- Tests were added that responses not allowed to have bodies (to HEAD
requests, 204, 304) did not have `Transfer-Encoding` added.
- Tests that `Content-Length: 0` is preserved.
- Tests that HTTP/1.0 responses with no body headers do not have
`Transfer-Encoding` added.
- Tests that `HEAD` responses forward `Content-Length` headers (but not
an actual body).

Closes #447

comments.author: briansmith
seanmonstar
comments.body:
> Why is that logic still needed when we have this new logic?

It was actually added because it regressed, hyper 0.11.0 handled that exact case before (GET or HEAD without content-length). It's existence is because a user reported the regression.

As to what exactly it does: it's really just a hack to protect people who do `Request::new(Get, uri).with_body("")`. That sets the internal body to `Some(B::from(""))`. And without a `Content-Length` header, hyper knows it must be chunked (but cannot ask the body anything about it, since its generic over `B: Stream<Item=impl AsRef<[u8]>>`. 

> Why isn't the fix in this PR a generalization of the logic in that code?

Because it's hacky and wrong in other cases. The code in hyper protects two request methods which should 99.9% contain no body. But many other request methods *can* have a body without a content-length, and so it would be wrong to assume otherwise.

-----

The problem we were hitting in the proxy is this:

1. To merge the hyper server (for h1) and tower-h2 server (for h2), the requests have a unified body type, `HttpBody`. 
2. The body is always set, since we use `http::Request<B>`, which does not have an optional body.
3. The `hyper::Request<B>` has an internal `Option<B>`.
4. When converting `http::Request<B>` into `hyper::Request<B>`, since the `http` has no concept of the body not existing, means `hyper::Request` has its body set to `Some(HttpBody)`.
5. When finally passed of the hyper's client, where it no longer knows anything about the body except that it's `impl Stream`, it just notices that the body is set, and there is no `content-length`, so it **must** be chunked.

The solution here in the proxy is:

1. Just before giving the request to `hyper::Client`, check if `HttpBody::is_end_stream()`.
2. If it is, unset the body from `hyper::Request`.

Thus, with this patch, these are the **only** cases where `transfer-encoding: chunked` will be used:

1. The original incoming request has `transfer-encoding: chunked`.
2. The incoming request was from h2, claimed there are more data frames coming, and did not contain `content-length` header. However, we do not as-of-yet accept h2 and then send as h1.

comments.author: seanmonstar
comments.body:
OK, so I think I finally understand the underlying motivation: being as we want to be as transparent of a proxy as possible, if reasonable, we shouldn't modify headers of requests and responses. That's what I'm going to change this PR to be about. I'll add some tests around responses, and a checklist, here's what exists so far:
- [x] requests
  - [x] with no body should not gain `Content-Length` nor `Transfer-Encoding`
  - [x] with `Content-Length: 0` should pass on the `Content-Length: 0` header
- [x] responses
  - [x] with `Content-Length: 0` should pass on the `Content-Length: 0` header
  - [x] not allowed to have bodies (`HEAD` responses, 204, 304, etc) should not have `Content-Length` or `Transfer-Encoding` added
  - [x] (`HEAD` responses should pass on `Content-Length` headers if they existed)
  - [x] HTTP/1.0 with a body and no `Content-Length` should not add `Transfer-Encoding`

There's an outstanding question: should HTTP/1.1 responses with no body headers but with a body be converted into chunked?

- **Pro**: This allows the client to reuse the connection to the proxy, even if the proxy can't reuse the connection to the server.
- **Pro**: Length delimited responses are much more reliable: responses that end when the connection closes mean its possible to get a partial response and not know. For that reason, using EOF response bodies in HTTP/1.1 is *highly discouraged*.
- **Con**: We've modified the response, which wouldn't have happened if we weren't there.
- **Con**: Possibly the client doesn't understand chunked encoding (but if it claimed HTTP/1.1, it's supposed to!). 

This question is not referring to when the client claims `HTTP/1.0`. In that case, we definitely cannot send chunked (and this case is in the checklist above).

comments.author: briansmith
comments.body:
> OK, so I think I finally understand the underlying motivation: being as we want to be as transparent of a proxy as possible, if reasonable, we shouldn't modify headers of requests and responses.

Yes, that's right. And, also, if an input request is relying on some subset of HTTP features then we shouldn't increase the subset of HTTP that is used, whenever we can reasonably avoid doing so.

>  with Content-Length: 0 should pass on the Content-Length: 0 header

More generally, requests with any Content-length should pass on the Content-Length header; zero is just a special case we need to test for.

>  not allowed to have bodies (HEAD responses, 204, 304, etc) should not have Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding added

I think if we detect that a response has a body when it shouldn't have one, we should feel free to abort the request and close the connection because that's pretty much impossible to recover from. However, we might defer an implementation of that to another issue. For now, I would say that the goal is to preserve the Content-Length/Transfer-Encoding framing for responses exactly and irrespective of the details of what the request method (HEAD, etc.) or response code (204, etc.) is.

In the case of HEAD, for example, it's not the proxy's responsibility to strip off the body, and it can't be, because there simply can't be any body; otherwise we wouldn't parse the stream correctly. (This is probably different for HTTP/2.)

>  HTTP/1.0 with a body and no Content-Length should not add Transfer-Encoding

Right, both for requests and for responses.

> There's an outstanding question: should HTTP/1.1 responses with no body headers but with a body be converted into chunked?

> Con: We've modified the response, which wouldn't have happened if we weren't there.
> Con: Possibly the client doesn't understand chunked encoding (but if it claimed HTTP/1.1, it's supposed to!).

We have to assume that if the sender didn't use chunked encoding, and they used the worst possible framing for their message, then they probably did so to work around a receiver not supporting chunked encoding. In reality, they were probably just being sloppy, but we cannot distinguish those two cases and we have to be conservative in the interest of being transparent.

Note that Conduit itself will eventually support upgrading all the traffic within the mesh to HTTP/2, and I think we can also assume that people who really care about performance are going to implement HTTP/2 or at least do reasonable things with HTTP/1, so it's not worth trying to optimize HTTP/1 beyond what they've done, other than the basic things we do like load balancing.

The `Body::is_end_stream` for tower-h2 is an optimization: if it returns true, h2 won't wait on another poll, and just signal end of stream right away. So, it's OK for this hint to be **false**, as it means it was just call `poll_data` again.

```rust
let has_no_body = !req.headers().contains_key(CONTENT_LENGTH) && !req.headers().contains_key(TRANSFER_ENCODING) &&  req.body.is_end_stream();
```

In particular, if there is a Transfer-Encoding or Content-Length header then there is a body (maybe zero-length). If neither of those headers exist, then there *might* be a body, however if we synthesized an empty body then there isn't a body.

However, I still am not convinced that we need the `req.body.is_end_stream()` check. If the original request didn't have Transfer-Encoding or Content-Length then it doesn't have a body, because there was no way for the original request to indicate the length of the body. The only way there could be a body without a Transfer-Encoding or Content-Length  is if we synthesized a body or we removed the original Transfer-Encoding/Content-Length.

Let's say we synthesized a body. Then we need to synthesize a Content-Length for it, because we can't use Transfer-Encoding for a request, since we don't know whether the server supports Transfer-Encoding. (It might be HTTP/1.0 or an incomplete HTTP/1.1 implementation.) If we are going to synthesize a Content-Length then we need to do it here.

Let's say we removed Transfer-Encoding or Content-Length from the original request, for some reason. Then again we need to synthesize a Content-Length, because we have to conservatively assume that it had a Content-Length, and because the server might not understand Transfer-Encoding.

In other words, either there must be a Transfer-Encoding in the original request, or there must be a Content-Length, or the `req.body` must be able to tell us its length so that we can synthesize a Content-Length, or there actually isn't a body. However, whether or not there is a body can always be determined by whether or not the request we forward has Content-Length (perhaps synthesized by us) or Transfer-Encoding, right?

review_threads.author: seanmonstar
review_threads.body:
The `Transfer-Encoding` header is an HTTP/1.1 concept, removed in HTTP2. Instead of `Transfer-Encoding`, HTTP2 just signals that the body is not complete by sending `DATA` frames with the end-of-stream flag unset. While we don't *yet* translate from HTTP2 to HTTP1, the `Body::is_end_stream()` method **already** handles this distinction. And as long as we have tests for the desired behavior, the implementation can be tweaked stylistically whenever.

As for performance, I'm certain that checking `is_end_stream` first is fastest.

- Checking explicitly for `req.headers().contains_key(TRANSFER_ENCODING)` would be redundant, because in H2, it's an illegal header and wouldn't exist, and for HTTP1, hyper has already looked it up, and if it were absent, if could return `Body::empty()`.
- Checking `Body::is_end_stream()` is a simple boolean field check, whereas looking for the `CONTENT_LENGTH` requires a hashtable lookup.

In the end, I'd offer that the important part is to worry about the behavior, which we can do by defining tests.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body:
> In the end, I'd offer that the important part is to worry about the behavior, which we can do by defining tests.

I generally agree with that. I think it would be ideal if our code was structured analogously to the relevant RFC requirement. However, I understand that here it might be difficult to do that because we have to consider HTTP/2, which has its own framing.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body:
I think this should be:

```rust
assert_eq!(!req.body_mut().take().unwrap().is_empty(), req.headers().has::<hyper::header::ContentLength>());
```

Shouldn't we be considering the presence of Transfer-Encoding as an alternative to Content-Length here too?

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body:
OK, great. Can we also do this same test, but using an empty body with `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`?

Finally, could you file a follow-up issue about making the same tests, except for response bodies. That is, we should test that we preserve `Content-Length: 0` in response bodies and we shouldn't convert a non-chunked response body to a chunked one (unintentionally). (Or, add the tests to this PR, if you want.)

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: NIT: Isn't the empty default actually OK here, since it is a HEAD response? I would expect `Body::empty()` + explicitly-set `Content-Length` to result in a `Content-Length` header for a HEAD response. Something to think about for future iterations of hyper, at least.

review_threads.author: seanmonstar
review_threads.body:
Hm, that comment is actually trying to say that `Default::default() == hyper::Body::empty()`. And as I write this, I cannot recall why I opted to use this with a comment instead of just `hyper::Body::empty()` directly.

Perhaps since `hyper::Body` isn't used in the http2 server cases, and so to allow the code to adapt?

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: OK, I see I misread it. never mind my comments here.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: Again, I expect the default of `Body::empty()` should work here too. If the default works, I think it would be clearer to use it here.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: This is confusing. If there is no body then why not use `Body::empty()`, the default? If the default works, I think it would be clearer to use it.

body: Closes #434

comments.author: seanmonstar
comments.body:
I've combined the `is_eof` into an `Option<CopyBuf>`. Personally, I'm not sure that it's much better, and dropping the buf on eof was tricker thanks to mutable borrows. Still, I suppose its nice that the memory is freed sooner.

As for the shared buffer: I left it as a TODO. It does seem neat, but its also pretty easy to mess up, and the more-obvious way of doing it can result in accidentally copying bytes from the wrong connection, in the case that a copy was not saved. And the compiler wouldn't be able to catch that.

Having a safer version that the compiler *could* catch is less obvious, but I think investing in it should probably be done when metrics show that it would have a worthy impact.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body:
This doesn't seem that unlikely to me, although I do think it is not super common. `shutdown(SHUT_WR)` allows the operating system to discard/recycle the send buffer and other resources on the side calling `shutdown(SHUT_WR)`; similarly the peer can discard its receive buffer. In the case of (Linux) kernel TLS the encryption (respectively, decryption) key can also be discarded. I don't know how common it is but I don't think we should speculate on that here, so I'd at least remove the last paragraph of the comment.

Regardless, I don't understand why, if we know that `copy()` doesn't do exactly what we want, why are we using `copy()`? Is it difficult to implement the correct thing?

review_threads.author: seanmonstar
review_threads.body: I originally used `copy` since I didn't think of the half-closed case. Writing a solution isn't overly difficult, but it would require essentially copying the source of the `Copy` future, and augmenting it to be duplex. My gut said this case isn't too common, and so weighed the time to write and test versus fixing this now and filing a new bug.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body:
I think that for 0.3.1 we need to think of it this way: Is the new temporary behavior we implement going to be potentially problematic? I think it would be problematic in some cases and we don't have any good insight into how common those cases are, other than we think they are relatively very rare compared to the cases that work. But, that's not very encouraging as far as making a release that's specifically a bugfix release.

So I think we should skip to the fix that also handles the half-open case correctly, and only consider this one if the fix for the half-open case can't happen for some reason.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body:
s/afters/after/?

Please expand this comment with an explanation of *why* we're doing this.

In general, it would be good to use complete sentences in comments, so that it is clear(er) if/when a comment is complete.

review_threads.body:
The repetition here makes me thing that we should have this be something like:

```rust
struct Duplex<In, Out> {
    in: EndPoint<In>,
    out: EndPOint<Out>,
}

struct EndPoint<T> { // Probably there is a better name for this. 
    buf: CopyBuf,
    eof: bool,
    io: T,
    shutdown: bool,
}
```

Also, are some of these variables mutually exclusive with each other; i.e. should some part of this be an enum that helps enforce a well-typed state machine?

But, is there any way to factor out a large amount of this code to be a regular function(s) that is (are) used by the macro, so that we can see clearly in the macro definition what is really motivating the use of a macro and avoiding the use of `TryLock`? title: Remove connect timeouts from Bind
body:
Currently, the `Reconnect` middleware does not reconnect on connection errors (see  #491) and treats them as request errors. This means that when a connection timeout is wrapped in a `Reconnect`, timeout errors are treated as request errors, and the request returns HTTP 500. Since  this is not the desired behavior, the connection timeouts should be removed, at least until their errors can be handled differently.

This PR removes the connect timeouts from `Bind`, as described in https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/pull/483#issuecomment-369380003.

It removes the `CONDUIT_PROXY_PUBLIC_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS` environment variable, but _not_ the `CONDUIT_PROXY_PRIVATE_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS` variable, since this is also used for the TCP connect timeouts. If we want also want to remove the TCP connection timeouts, I can do that as well.

Closes #483. Fixes #491.

If so, it seems OK to remove this timeout for outbound connections since either the application we're proxying has its own timeout already or it doesn't have a timeout and presumably doesn't want one, and we have no good way to configure this timeout for an application that actually wants us to provide it as a feature. However, why did we add it in the first place, @olix0r?

comments.body:
Incidentally, in https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/pull/483#issuecomment-369380003, when I said "this timeout", I meant specifically the one controlled by `CONDUIT_PROXY_PRIVATE_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS`. However, I see that the public timeout is using the same code, so it makes sense to remove it at the same time, unless @olix0r has a reason why we need the public timeout.

I would expect that the public timeout would be more useful than the private timeout because if a particular outbound destination is super slow then we should eventually either give up or try a different outbound destination. But maybe this is better undone for now until the retry and circuit breaking features are properly designed.

comments.author: hawkw

Okay, I figured out what's going on: `tower-reconnect` only reconnects if the connection was successfully established _and then_ errored. If there was an error _while_ connecting, it propagates the error. The connect timeout occurs during the connection, therefore it does not trigger a reconnect.

So it's not so much a bug in `tower-reconnect` as it is an _interaction_ between reconnect and a timeout wrapped by the reconnect middleware. I'll open an issue on `tower` for figuring out the relationship between reconnects and retries.

comments.author: briansmith
comments.body:
So, removing the timeout for the private connection seems to make perfect sense and I have no concerns about that.

Let's think critically about whether or not we want the timeout in the public (external) connections. A point in favor of removing the public timeout is the fact that we don't have a good UX for configuring the timeout. A point against removing the public timeout is that we don't (IIUC) have any garbage collection for unused connections, so if the underlying application has a timeout and closes the outbound connection to the proxy, that will have no effect on whether we close the outbound connection to the external service. However, one could argue that the more general problem of not having garbage collection for unused connections is the real problem and having this particular timeout logic is just a band-aid that helps with a special case, and that it's not worthwhile. However, one could also argue that 0.3.1 is a stability and bug fixing release and we've not had any bug reports about the timeout for the timeout for public connections, so we shouldn't change anything w.r.t. them.

This last point is the strongest one for me: If we're not fixing something we know to be broken, and there are downsides to the change, then let's avoid making the change for 0.3.1. So, I'm included to have us keep the public timeout and remove the private timeout, probably using the technique @hawkw suggested.

I think it would be good to hear from others (@olix0r, @seanmonstar, @carllerche, @hawkw) before scrambling to update the PR, to avoid waffling further.

comments.author: olix0r
comments.body:
> A point against removing the public timeout is that we don't (IIUC) have any garbage collection for unused connections, so if the underlying application has a timeout and closes the outbound connection to the proxy, that will have no effect on whether we close the outbound connection to the external service.

I don't think that removing the public timer has any practical downside right now, though I strongly agree that we need to have a larger discussion about lifecycle/resource management moving forward.

Specifically, if the proxy attempts to connect to a peer and that peer neither opens nor resets the connection, then we'll hold that connection attempt open until the endpoint is removed from service discovery, at which point the connecting future is dropped...

Currently, if those connections timeout, we'll just try to reestablish them the next time a request is dispatched to that peer.

So, I think this is, operationally, effectively equivalent behavior.

title: Enforce that requests are mapped to connections for each Host: header values
body:
This ended up being a much bigger branch than anticipated --- sorry for so much code to review!

This PR ensures that the mapping of requests to outbound connections is segregated by `Host:` header values. In most cases, the desired behavior is provided by Hyper's connection pooling. However, Hyper does not handle the case where a request had no `Host:` header and the request URI had no authority part, and the request was routed based on the SO_ORIGINAL_DST in the desired manner. We would like these requests to each have their own outbound connection, but Hyper will reuse the same connection for such requests. 

Therefore, I have modified `conduit_proxy_router::Recognize` to allow implementations of `Recognize` to indicate whether the service for a given key can be cached, and to only cache the service when it is marked as cachable. I've also changed the `reconstruct_uri` function, which rewrites HTTP/1 requests, to mark when a request had no authority and no `Host:` header, and the authority was rewritten to be the request's ORIGINAL_DST. When this is the case, the `Recognize` implementations for `Inbound` and `Outbound` will mark these requests as non-cachable.

I've also added unit tests ensuring that A, connections are created per `Host:` header, and B, that requests with no `Host:` header each create a new connection. The first test passes without any additional changes, but the second only passes on this branch. The tests were added in PR #489, but this branch supersedes that branch.

Fixes #415. Closes #489.

title: Most controller listeners should only bind on localhost

Most controller components should only bind on localhost since they are only intended to be accessed by other controller components.

| Port | purpose | bind to |
|-----|--------|------ |
|8085 | public-api | all interfaces|
|8086 | proxy-api | all interfaces |
|8087 | telemetry | localhost|
|8088 | tap | localhost|

We can't keep code around just because we might use it later; it's trivial to do a revert to bring back the configurability. As far as docker-compose goes, at least on Linux we just need to change the docker-compose configuration so that all containers share a networking namespace, which we should do anyway to better simulate the Kubernetes pod environment. title: Add --expected-version flag for conduit check command
body:
The `conduit check` command was updated in #460 to check that the CLI and controller are both running the latest version of conduit (thanks, @ahume!). This works for stable versions, but the check command fails when testing unreleased versions of conduit. When using an unreleased version, I'd like the ability to override the expected version via a command line flag.

Running the command on this branch without adding the flag produces the same result as on master:

```
$ ./bin/go-run cli/main.go check
kubernetes-api: can initialize the client.......................................[ok]
kubernetes-api: can query the Kubernetes API....................................[ok]
kubernetes-api: is running the minimum Kubernetes API version...................[ok]
conduit-api: can query the Conduit API..........................................[ok]
conduit-api[telemetry]: control plane can use telemetry service.................[ok]
conduit-version: cli is up-to-date..............................................[FAIL]  -- is running version git-0ced3787 but the latest version is v0.3.0
conduit-version: control plane is up-to-date....................................[FAIL]  -- is running version git-0ced3787 but the latest version is v0.3.0

Status check results are [FAIL]
```

Whereas running the command with the `--expected-version` flag set produces:

```
$ ./bin/go-run cli/main.go check --expected-version git-0ced3787
kubernetes-api: can initialize the client.......................................[ok]
kubernetes-api: can query the Kubernetes API....................................[ok]
kubernetes-api: is running the minimum Kubernetes API version...................[ok]
conduit-api: can query the Conduit API..........................................[ok]
conduit-api[telemetry]: control plane can use telemetry service.................[ok]
conduit-version: cli is up-to-date..............................................[ok]
conduit-version: control plane is up-to-date....................................[ok]

Status check results are [ok]
```

I've also added a 10-second timeout on the call to versioncheck.conduit.io as part of this branch.

title: Retry k8s watch endpoints on error
body:
Shortly after conduit is installed in k8s environment. The control plane component that establishes a watch endpoint with k8s run in to networking issues during proxy initialization. During failure, each watcher fails to retry its connection to k8s watch endpoint which leads to timeouts and eventually, multiple controller pod restarts. 

This PR adds retry logic to each "watch" enabled package.

fixes #478 

Signed-off-by: Dennis Adjei-Baah <dennis@buoyant.io>
author: dadjeibaah

comments.author: briansmith
comments.body:
> Ah, it's a bit unfortunate that the method signature for i.informer.Run doesn't match the method signature for a watchInitializer (it doesn't return error).

See https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/issues/155. From reading that client-go issue it looks like the informer already handles some errors itself. It would be useful to have a comment describing why we need to have the use of the informer in a retry loop. In particular, it would be useful to give an example of an error that the informer doesn't recover from itself.

comments.author: briansmith
comments.body: Another question I have about our timeout logic: In https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/17074 client-go provided a way for us to configure timeouts for HTTP requests. It seems like here we're implementing another layer of timeout. Would it be better or worse to use the mechanism introduced in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/17074 for timeouts instead? I don't know if it is better or worse; it just seems strange to implement our own timeout logic when client-go has an API for controlling timeouts.

comments.author: dadjeibaah
comments.body: @briansmith spent a couple of minutes figuring out whether we can set up timeouts for requests to k8s with watchers. I haven't found anything that leads me to believe that it is possible but I can keep searching. @klingerf is there a way we can set timeouts for watch requests in any of our watch specific code?

comments.author: briansmith
comments.body:
> @briansmith spent a couple of minutes figuring out whether we can set up timeouts for requests to k8s with watchers. I haven't found anything that leads me to believe that it is possible but I can keep searching.

IIUC, we are doing something like "loop forever, but maybe get interrupted by a timeout" where the timeout is set to 30 seconds, somewhere. So, that's a different timeout than the HTTP timeout. AFAICT, the "loop forever, but maybe get interrupted by a timeout" is pretty much trying to implement the util.wait package of k8s.io/apimachinery. I think it makes sense to use util.wait instead so that we get the exponential backoff and so we can start with a shorter retry interval (e.g. 100ms), and so we avoid duplicating already-existing code.

Is 30 seconds enough time to wait before giving up? I guess it is possible that the proxy container image needs to be downloaded and that might reasonably take 30+ seconds. Do we want Kubernetes to kill the pod in that case? It would be useful to document the rational for how long we try before we give up with a code comment.

comments.author: dadjeibaah
briansmith
comments.body:
> @briansmith
> > I think it makes sense to use util.wait instead so that we get the exponential backoff and so we can start with a shorter retry interval (e.g. 100ms), and so we avoid duplicating already-existing code.
> 
> Using wait.Until looks almost identical to what we have currently with the added benefit of Backoff and its more descriptive nature. I am not fully opposed to using Wait but the code we have doesn't add any additional layers of complexity

The code we have now does have an additional layer of complexity that isn't seen: the 30 second timeout logic that isn't included in what you quoted.

I looked at `wait.Until` and it doesn't actually implement exponential backoff. `wait.ExponentialBackoff` implements the exponential backoff. So one question is, do you want to have exponential backoff or not. It seems to me like we should have some exponential backoff using an exponent like 1.2 or 1.5 or so. If so, then we should switch to wait.ExponentialBackoff.

> > Is 30 seconds enough time to wait before giving up? I guess it is possible that the proxy container image needs to be downloaded and that might reasonably take 30+ seconds.
> 
> Do you have other recommendation on what the timeout should be? 50 seconds could be a good number.

I don't have a specific recommendation. I don't know Kubernetes' behavior. If the timeout is reached and the container exits with a failing exit code, then does it cancel the downloading of the proxy container image? If so, then the timeout has to be pretty long. If all the container images for a pod are downloaded before the pod is attempted to be started, then the timeout is probably better to be shorter.

I also looked at the rest of your PR. One issue that was noted is that some function panics when you would rather it didn't panic. Now, I am not sure what the exact problem we are solving is. My understanding from the description "each watcher fails to retry its connection to k8s" is that sometimes a TCP `connect()` fails immediately when the proxy isn't running yet. If that is the problem, then why is the retry logic wrapped around the entire watcher, instead of just inside a custom dialer? In particular, why not ask client-go to construct an `http.Client` for us and then replace its `DialContext` with one that retries the TCP connect in a loop using `wait.ExponentialBackoff` or equivalent? That seems like it would solve the exact problem we have and avoid the other complexities.

Also, if these containers are going to retry for a long period of time then they are going to be in an unhealthy state for a long period of time during the retries. This makes me think that we also should have readiness and/or liveness probes as described at https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-probes/#define-a-liveness-http-request. (Perhaps these probes should be implemented in a separate issue/PR.)

comments.body:

To make progress, we can assume we don't need to worry about this and just use a short timeout; i.e. a minute is fine. If the Conduit proxy image is frequently taking over a minute to start then something is very wrong anyway.

If we're solving a broader issue with the watches then what we're doing here might be more appropriate.)
 
> The new issue could also take advantage of the readiness probes you mentioned so we can add some sense of dependency that can help in pod startup.

Separately from the issue for putting retry logic in the DialContext (if we even want to), I think we do need to have a separate issue for the readiness probe. Without the readiness probe, AFAICT, when we roll a new deployment of the control plane, Kubernetes will start sending traffic to the new pods before they are ready, causing failures.

title: Make absolute names truly absolute.
body:
Kubernetes will do multiple DNS lookups for a name like
`proxy-api.conduit.svc.cluster.local` based on the default search settings
in /etc/resolv.conf for each container:

1. proxy-api.conduit.svc.cluster.local.conduit.svc.cluster.local. IN A
2. proxy-api.conduit.svc.cluster.local.svc.cluster.local. IN A
3. proxy-api.conduit.svc.cluster.local.cluster.local. IN A
4. proxy-api.conduit.svc.cluster.local. IN A

We do not need or want this search to be done, so avoid it by making each
name absolute by appending a period so that the first three DNS queries
are skipped for each name.

The case for `localhost` is even worse because we expect that `localhost` will
always resolve to 127.0.0.1 and/or ::1, but this is not guaranteed if the default
search is done:

1. localhost.conduit.svc.cluster.local. IN A
2. localhost.svc.cluster.local. IN A
3. localhost.cluster.local. IN A
4. localhost. IN A

Avoid these unnecessary DNS queries by making each name absolute, so that the
first three DNS queries are skipped for each name.

title: Simplify cluster zone suffix handling in the proxy
body:
The way that Kubernetes configures DNS search suffixes has some negative consequences as some names like "example.com" are ambiguous: depending on whether there is a service "example" in the "com" namespace, "example.com" may refer to an external service or an internal service, and this can
fluctuate over time. In recognition of that we added the CONDUIT_PROXY_DESTINATIONS_AUTOCOMPLETE_FQDN setting, thinking this would be part of a solution for users to opt out of the unfortunate behavior if their applications didn't depend on the DNS search suffix feature. It turns out similar effects can be acheived using a custom dnsConfig, starting
in Kubernetes 1.10 when dnsConfig reaches the beta stability level Now any CONDUIT_PROXY_DESTINATIONS_AUTOCOMPLETE_FQDN-based solution seems duplicative. Further, attempting to support it optionally made the code complex and hard to read.

Along similar lines, the CONDUIT_PROXY_POD_ZONE setting hasn't been fully vetted. Lots of things in Conduit currently assume the cluster zone is `cluster.local`. Further, how exactly the proxy will actually learn the cluster zone hasn't been decided yet; it is likely that something other than an environment variable will be used.

Therefore, let's just remove these settings, and add then back if/when they are fully fleshed out.

Some back of the napkin math:

request_total (outbound): 1 line per dst
request_total (inbound): 1 line
request_duration (outbound): 1 line per dst per histogram bucket = 25 * dst
request_duration (inbound): 1 line per histogram bucket = 25
response_total (outbound): 1 line per dst per status = 20 * dst
response_total (inbound): 1 per status = 20
response_duration (outbound): 1 line per dst per status per histogram bucket = 20 * 25 * dst = 500 * dst
response_duration(inbound): 1 line per status per histogram bucket = 20 * 25 = 500
response_latency (outbound): 1 line per dst per status per histogram bucket = 20 * 25 * dst = 500 * dst
response_latency(inbound): 1 line per status per histogram bucket = 25 * dst

So approximately 1046 lines per service that this instance communicates with.  Each line is around 100 characters long so roughly in the neighborhood of 100kb per service before any type of compression.

title: Fix infinite loop in `tcp::HalfDuplex::copy_into()`
body:
An infinite loop exists in the TCP proxy, which could be triggered by any raw TCP connection (including HTTPS requests). The connection will be proxied successfully, but instead of closing, it will remain open, and the proxy's CPU usage will remain extremely high indefinitely.

Since `Duplex::poll` will call `half_in.copy_into()`/`half_out.copy_into()` repeatedly, even after they return `Async::Ready`, when one half has shut down and returned ready, it may still be polled again, as `Duplex::poll` waits until _both_ halves have returned `Ready`. Because of the guard that `!dst.is_shutdown`, intended to prevent the destination from shutting down twice, the function will not return if it is polled again after returning `Async::Ready` once.

I've fixed this by moving the guard against double shutdowns out of the loop, so that the function will return `Async::Ready` again if it is polled after shutting down the destination.

I've also included a unit test against regressions to this bug. The unit test fails against master.

Fixes #519

title: Fix outbound HTTP/1 requests not using Destinations
body:
Commit 569d6939a799bb0df6bd4053de7d7e8ac6b49ab6 introduced a regression that caused the proxy to stop using the Destination service for outbound HTTP/1 requests with no authority in the request URI but a valid authority in the `Host:` header. 

The bug is due to some code in `Outbound::recognize` which assumed that a request had already been passed through `normalize_our_view_of_uri`. This was valid at one point while I was writing #492, as URIs were normalized prior to `recognize` and a request `Extension` was used to mark that they had been rewritten, and the host header and request URI could be assumed to be in agreement, but after merging #514 into the dev branch for #492, this behaviour changed and I forgot to update the logic in `recognize`.

I've fixed the issue by adding the logic for routing on `Host:` headers back into `Outbound::recognize`.

@seanmonstar added a test in `discovery.rs`, `outbound_http1_asks_controller_about_host`, which should exercise this case. I've added a couple more unit tests in that file to try and ensure we cover more of the different cases that can occur here.

Fixes #552

style/tioli:

review_threads.author: adleong
review_threads.body: Is it even possible for the client to be able to handle out-of-order messages?  `[Add(1.1.1.1); Remove(1.1.1.1)]` has different semantics from `[Remove(1.1.1.1); Add(1.1.1.1)]`.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body:
> Is it even possible for the client to be able to handle out-of-order messages? [Add(1.1.1.1); Remove(1.1.1.1)] has different semantics from [Remove(1.1.1.1); Add(1.1.1.1)].

You are right; in the former case the client must calculate the set as empty; in the latter case the client must calculate the set as {1.1.1.1}. That's what the client does now. In practice the server probably won't send sequences where something is `Remove`d that isn't in the set. I've chosen to require the client to handle that case just because it's straightforward to do and there's no real good alternative thing for the client to do when it gets a nonsensical order.

review_threads.author: adleong
review_threads.body: This states that `[No_endpoints(true); Add(1.1.1.1)]` is *not* equivalent to `[Add(1.1.1.1)]`.  What is the semantic difference?

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: `[NoEndpoints(true); Add(1.1.1.1)]` will first clear the client's set of addresses and then add 1.1.1.1 to it. `[Add(1.1.1.1)]` will add 1.1.1.1 to the client's set and then remove all other entries. So, the former results in a temporary state where there are no addresses in the client's set. The latter results in there not being a temporary state where there are no addresses.

review_threads.author: adleong
review_threads.body: Gotcha.  I think this comment is confusing because the two sequences of messages are equivalent in that they both end up with the client in the same state (but go through different intermediate states).  I think it safely goes without saying that `[NoEndpoints(true)]` is not equivalent to `[Add(1.1.1.1)]`.

review_threads.author: adleong
review_threads.body: Is there a reason why we need both `[Remove(<all addresses>)]` and `[no_endpints{exists: true}]` as two different ways to signal the same thing?

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body:
The `NoEndpoints` message contains an explicit indication of whether the service exists. `Remove(...)` would be ambiguous as to whether the service exists, and that distinction is important.

Also, depending on the implementation in the server, it might be useful for the server to use the `NoEndpoints` message instead of `Remove(...)` if it is removing the endpoints for the service due to a change in the service's status observed through the `Services` API instead of the `Endpoints` API in Kubernetes. I'm not sure.

review_threads.author: adleong
review_threads.body: I had assumed that `Remove(<all addresses>)` would unambiguously indicate that the service does exist but has no endpoints.  Is that not correct?

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body:
> I had assumed that Remove(<all addresses>) would unambiguously indicate that the service does exist but has no endpoints. Is that not correct?

Yes, that's right. But one would have to read the documentation to understand what it means at the beginning of a connection before anything has been added. The proxy handles it the way you suggest mostly for completeness's sake.

Definitely this isn't the only way to formulate the API. If you have a specific change you want to make, please suggest it.

This functionality creates a server that randomly generates `response_total`, `request_totals`, `response_duration_ms` and `response_latency_ms`. title: proxy: add SIGTERM and SIGQUIT handlers
body:
When the proxy is run in a Docker container, it runs as PID 1, with
no default signal handlers setup. In order to react to signals from
Kubernetes about shutting down, we need to set up explicit handlers.

This adds handlers for SIGTERM and SIGQUIT in unix environments.

Closes #549
author: seanmonstar

review_threads.author: seanmonstar
review_threads.body: All this is just moving the creation of a `Main` into the thread, since `Main` is no longer `Send` (it owns a `Core`).

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body:
My understanding is that we only need to set a flag on the first SIGTERM or SIGINT (or equivalents, optionally, on Windows) sent to the main thread, to shut down the main thread's event loop. That is the signal is sent to the same thread that the event loop is running on, IIUC. In that case, isn't tokio-signal overkill, since it is designed to support handling arbitrary signals on arbitrary event loops? In particular, tokio-signal creates the UDS to allow this cross-thread processing that we don't need, right? And also it uses a `Stream` to support a signal being handled multiple times but we only need to handle it once.

Is this your understanding too? If so, we should consider, in the future, replacing this dependency with a simpler one.

review_threads.author: seanmonstar
review_threads.body:
Yes, much of that is true. This also factored in to my decision:

- There's a multitude of warnings about how badly signal handler functions can mess up programs, with a list of things NOT to do within them. In that case, I'd rather use at least some library where people have used care to not trigger those problems. It could be `tokio-signal`, or something much simpler, maybe `signal`.
- Having a `Future` works great with the existing system we already have in place, so `tokio-signal` providing that for us is icing.
- We do only need a `Future`, not a `Stream`, at least for right now. Though, the overhead there is minimal. And it's possible that in we may want to handle receiving multiple signals at some point, such as perhaps the second signal could imply "hurry up with the shutdown", or similar.
- Knowing that this is safe and plugs in easily gives ease-of-mind, and the overhead of receiving signals shouldn't affect the proxy, as we don't expect to be receiving and processing signals on an extremely frequent basis.

I'm not for wasting unnecessarily, and would welcome a library that perhaps did less, while still being safe and convenient to use. Probably not high priority, though. Does that all sound reasonable?

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body:
> Probably not high priority, though. Does that all sound reasonable?

Yes, that all sounds reasonable to me.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: If we're going to use tokio-signal then I'd like for us to follow up with a PR that adds the use of `tokio_signal::ctrl_c` for SIGINT so that we can trigger the same behavior on Windows with Ctrl+C too, since at least two of us develop on Windows. It would be OK to have the `tokio_signal::ctrl_c` implementation only for `not(unix)`.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: Let's add a comment explaining that we're doing this because we'll often be running in a container as PID 1, beyond our control, and the proxy can't always avoid running as PID 1 because of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/51634.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: Let's document that SIGTERM is sent by Kubernetes and Docker for graceful shutdown and we support SIGINT to allow simulating that signal easily with Ctrl+C.

title: Add request_duration_ms metric and increment request_total on request end
body:
This PR adds the `request_duration_ms` metric to the Prometheus metrics exported by the proxy. It also modifies the `request_total` metric so that it is incremented when a request stream finishes, rather than when it opens, for consistency with how the `response_total` metric is generated.

Making this change required modifying `telemetry::sensors::http` to generate a `StreamRequestEnd` event similar to the `StreamResponseEnd` event. This is done similarly to how sensors are added to response bodies, by generalizing the `ResponseBody` type into a `MeasuredBody` type that can wrap a request or response body. Since this changed the type of request bodies, it necessitated changing request types pretty much everywhere else in the proxy codebase in order to fix the resulting type errors, which is why the diff for this PR is so large.

Closes #570

title: Avoid `cargo fetch --locked` in proxy/Dockerfile.
body:
`cargo fetch` doesn't consider the target platform and downloads
all crates needed to build for any target.

Stop using `cargo fetch` and instead use the implicit fetch done
by `cargo build`, which *does* consider the target platform.

This change results in 12 (soon 15) fewer crates downloaded.
This is a non-trivial savings in build time for a full rebuild
since cargo downloads crates in parallel.

```diff
- Downloading bitflags v1.0.1
- Downloading fuchsia-zircon v0.3.3
- Downloading fuchsia-zircon-sys v0.3.3
- Downloading miow v0.2.1
- Downloading redox_syscall v0.1.37
- Downloading redox_termios v0.1.1
- Downloading termion v1.5.1
- Downloading winapi v0.3.4
- Downloading winapi-i686-pc-windows-gnu v0.4.0
- Downloading winapi-x86_64-pc-windows-gnu v0.4.0
- Downloading wincolor v0.1.6
- Downloading ws2_32-sys v0.2.1
```

I verified that no downloads are done during an incremental
build.

Signed-off-by: Brian Smith <brian@briansmith.org>
author: briansmith

comments.author: briansmith
comments.body: Note that the "real" build of conduit-proxy still uses `--frozen` and as long as that works that means the `cargo build --locked` steps downloaded all the dependencies and so we shouldn't have to  worry about downloads during incremental builds.

title: Proxy: Download fewer crates in Travis CI runs
body:
Follow up
https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/pull/593 by avoiding
`cargo fetch` in favor of the implicit fetch done in `cargo build`
to work around the lack of a `--target` flag in `cargo fetch`. This
should at least slightly improve the speed and reliability of Travis
CI runs.

Signed-off-by: Brian Smith <brian@briansmith.org>

title: Fix double comma in outbound metrics
body:
Fixes #600 

The proxy metrics endpoint has a bug where metrics recorded in the outbound direction can contain two commas in a row when no outbound label is present. This occurs because the code for formatting the outbound direction label mistakenly assumed that there would always be a destination pod owner label as well, but the proxy isn't currently aware of the destination's pod owner (waiting for #429). 

I've fixed this issue by moving the place where the comma is output from the `fmt::Display` impl for `RequestLabels` to the `fmt::Display` impl for `OutboudnLabels`. This way, the comma between the `direction` and `dst_*` labels is only output when the `dst_*` label is present. 

This bug made it to master since all of the proxy end-to-end tests for metrics only test the inbound router. I've rectified this issue by adding tests on the outbound router as well (which would fail against the current master due to the double comma bug). I've also added a test that asserts there are no double commas in exported metrics, to protect against regressions to this bug.
author: hawkw

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body:
does this imply that `dst_namespace` should never be written as the first label, because it's preceded by a comma?

to put it another way, it seems like the safest thing to do is to collect the total set of labels, and do join(",") on them, rather than rely on some kind of implicit ordering.

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body:
Theoretically, yeah, you're definitely right, and if I were writing a general-purpose Prometheus client library, that's definitely what I'd do. Here, though, we always know the set of labels on a given metric, so the values are stored in a struct rather than a collection, and this way, we can write the formatted values directly to the `Formatter` (i.e. whatever we're outputting to), rather than having to allocate a vector, put all the label value strings in it, format the labels and values values by allocating more strings, join them with commas (allocating another string) and _then_ write them to the `Formatter`, so this is much more efficient. 

I'll document the potential gotchas relating to comma-ordering in a comment.

review_threads.author: seanmonstar
review_threads.body:
I actually feel it makes sense for the `Display` implementations to not be so aware of where they are being used. I don't think `OutboundLabels` should know it needs to start with a comma, since if we change the order at some point, then we have a leading comma.

It seems probably better to check something like `outbound_labels.is_empty()` from `RequestLabels`, and add a comma if not.

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body: @seanmonstar sure, that would also work.

title: All counters in proxy telemetry wrap on overflows
body:
In #602, @olix0r suggested that telemetry counters should wrap on overflows, as "most timeseries systems (like prometheus) are designed to handle this case gracefully."

This PR changes counters to use explicitly wrapping arithmetic.

Closes #602.
author: hawkw

comments.author: briansmith
comments.body: OK, that all sounds good to me. The only thing that seems really questionable is the assertion that wrapping is actually handled OK by Prometheus and basically everything else that's like Prometheus, so it would be great to get a link to some authoritative statement on that, if there is one. However, I guess in the current releases they are already wrapping, since we ship builds built with `--release`, right? Then I understand that this entire PR is basically about documenting the wrapping behavior and preventing unintended panics in non-release builds.

comments.author: hawkw
comments.body: @briansmith I think the actual determination of whether or not wrapping is actually okay is best left to @olix0r; I was just making these changes at his request.

comments.author: olix0r
comments.body:
@briansmith 

> The only thing that seems really questionable is the assertion that wrapping is actually handled OK by Prometheus and basically everything else that's like Prometheus,

Because these systems have to be able to tolerate the process restarting without knowing that the process restarted, wrapping is generally assumed to be acceptable behavior (and indistinguishable from the process restarting in most cases) -- queries are constructed with rates so that counters are turned into windowed values.

This behavior is almost certainly better than panicking.

> so it would be great to get a link to some authoritative statement on that, if there is one.

when we consume these timeseries, we use the [`rate/irate()`](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/functions/#irate()) query functions::

> > Breaks in monotonicity (such as counter resets due to target restarts) are automatically adjusted for.

Note that the [`resets()`](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/functions/#resets) function exists to highlight this exact case.

> However, I guess in the current releases they are already wrapping, since we ship builds built with --release, right? Then I understand that this entire PR is basically about documenting the wrapping behavior and preventing unintended panics in non-release builds.

I wasn't aware of that default behavior ;)  yes to the documentation part, though.

comments.author: briansmith
comments.body:
> > The only thing that seems really questionable is the assertion that wrapping is actually handled OK by Prometheus and basically everything else that's like Prometheus,
> 
> Because these systems have to be able to tolerate the process restarting without knowing that the process restarted, wrapping is generally assumed to be acceptable behavior (and indistinguishable from the process restarting in most cases) -- queries are constructed with rates so that counters are turned into windowed values.

Consider these two cases:

1. A process increments a counter twice. Prometheus reads the value. Then it increments it 2^32 -1 times (or whatever) so that the counter's value wraps to 1. Prometheus reads the value.

2. A process increments a counter twice. Prometheus reads the value. The process restarts and then increments the counter once again, to 1. Prometheus reads the value.

In each case, the second Prometheus read is going to result in a counter of 1. In that case, does Prometheus assume the counter *wrapped* (case 1), or does it assume the counter reset (case 2)?

> This behavior is almost certainly better than panicking.

I 100% agree! Nobody is arguing in favor of panicking.

The Prometheus documentation you state says "Any decrease in the value between two consecutive samples is interpreted as a counter reset." Let's make a concrete example of what that means. Let's say that the 32-bit counter value is 0xFFFFF0000, Promemetheus reads the value, and then the counter value gets incremented by 65,536 to 0 (0x00000000). AFAICT Prometheus's metrics will not count those 65,536 increments at all, because it will assume that the counter was *reset*, instead of assuming it will *wrap*.

Thus, I think it's good to avoid counters wrapping. I think that @hawkw's most recent change does that good enough, by using only 64-bit integers for counters, including the counters in histograms.

(If we ever need to go back to using smaller integer values, then we would probably need to implement our own special wrapping mechanism that ensures that we'll never have Prometheus read a very large value that is about to wrap. That is, instead of allowing a counter to ever get to 0xFFFFF0000, we'd probably reset it to 0 on the first Prometheus read where the value is 0x80000000 or more, to minimize the chances that Prometheus would interpret a wrap as a reset.)

comments.body: @briansmith this should be ready as of 71ed7150258edb7a7757f51e92a56f5176ffc977, please let me know if there are any additional changes required!

review_threads.body:
I understand we use `Counter` to count requests and responses and histograms for latencies. It seems reasonable to me to expect that the latencies for requests could at least sometimes be put into a few buckets (not spread out across all buckets) so it's not clear to me why the type for counting total requests is twice the size of the type for measuring latencies.

Put differently, my understanding is that NUM_BUCKETS = 26 so even assuming perfect distribution within the histogram, we're using `Counter` as 64-bits to handle the difference between supporting ~4 billion requests and ~104 billion requests before wrapping. But if wrapping is OK and we expect wrapping to be rare then why not just wrap all the counters at 4 billion increments, i.e. use a 32-bit type for them? I don't really have a strong opinion about it, but my point is that I don't understand the thinking behind the disparity in the first place.

I'd be happy to make them 64-bit values as well when the push metrics reporter is removed. I suppose I could also modify the push metrics reporter to accept 64-bit counts and cast them to `u32`, but I'd prefer to not touch that code at all, as it's slated to be removed very soon.

review_threads.body: Hmm. The `sum` is incremented by the value of an observation, not by 1. My intention in having `prometheus::Counter` expose a public `.incr()` method but no `Add`/`AddAssign` impls was to constrain the possible operations on a counter. review_threads.body:
1. Why isn't `Item`'s type `Wrapping<u32>` or `prometheus::Counter`?

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body:

review_threads.body:
> suppose another option --- possibly a better separation of concerns? --- would be to have Histogram::into_iter handle the joining of the bucket count values with the associated upper bounds, so the return type of the iterator was (Latency, Counter)? That behaviour is currently implemented in the fmt::Display impl, which seems like the wrong place for it...

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body:
> The users of the IntoIterator implementation don't do arithmetic on the values, so having Item be a Wrapping type or anything else would just be annoying for them, without any gain.

Yeah, that's more or less the rationale behind the current code. Will probably revisit this in an additional PR, as you requested. 

Note also that some of the ugliness here is because the `latency` module's API is consumed by both `prometheus` _and_ the push metrics reporter, which --- although slated for removal --- is still in the codebase. When that goes away and `latency` only has to support the prometheus server, this code will be much easier to refactor.

title: Move injected data from env var to k8s labels
body:
The inject code detects the object it is being injected into, and writes
self-identifying information into the CONDUIT_PROMETHEUS_LABELS
environment variable, so that conduit-proxy may read this information
and report it to Prometheus at collection time.

This change puts the self-identifying information directly into
Kubernetes labels, which Prometheus already collects, removing the need
for conduit-proxy to be aware of this information. The resulting label
in Prometheus is recorded in the form `conduit_io_proxy_deployment`.

Signed-off-by: Andrew Seigner <siggy@buoyant.io>

This change is a follow up to #448.

![screen shot 2018-03-22 at 4 42 07 pm](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/236915/37804373-2c7135e2-2df1-11e8-8206-694b44eecc2e.png)

![screen shot 2018-03-22 at 4 43 27 pm](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/236915/37804374-2ebf11fc-2df1-11e8-8055-90bc4b8c706c.png)
author: siggy

comments.author: olix0r
comments.body:
how do values not known at inject-time get manifested into these labels?

My understanding is that, specifically for deployments, which instantiate replica sets, we need to use the environment approach (via the downward api).  would these be added as labels somehow? or do these need to be added via the environment?

comments.author: siggy
comments.body:
@olix0r Values not known at inject time should still get communicated to the proxy via downward api and environment variables, and then be exported by the proxy via a `/metrics` endpoint.

The intent of this PR is to move any data that _is_ known at inject time out of the proxy, and allow Prometheus to collect it directly from Kubernetes, thus minimizing the information the proxy needs to know about itself.

title: Remove references to `cli` images
body:
CI builds on master have been failing to publish `cli-bin` images because the
`bin/docker-push` script still refers to the `cli` image, though it was removed in
e7c4a9d4b91fda34446fbe3e74b63643a6665c03.

This change removes references to the `cli` image from all scripts.

Note that `bin/docker-pull` now fails when an image doesn't exist.
author: olix0r

title: Improve CLI docker caching
body:
Currently, the CLI docker image copies the entire `controller`
directory, though the CLI only requires a few of its subdirectories.
This causes the CLI's docker cache to be needlessly invalidated when,
for instance, a service implementation changes.

By restricting the copied directories to `controller/{api,public,util}`,
build caching is improved.
author: olix0r

title: Skip flaky tests for #613
body:
The metrics endpoint tests are flaky because there are no guarantees
that the metrics pipeline has processed events before the metrics
endpoint is read. This can cause CI to fail spuriously.

Disable these tests from running in CI until #613 is resolved.

title: Add process_start_time_seconds Prometheus metric
body:
As described in #619. `process_start_time_seconds` is the idiomatic way of reporting to Prometheus the uptime of a process. It should contain the time in seconds since the beginning of the Unix epoch.

The proxy now exports this metric:
```
➜ http get localhost:4191/metrics
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Length: 902
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Date: Mon, 26 Mar 2018 22:09:55 GMT

# HELP request_total A counter of the number of requests the proxy has received.
# TYPE request_total counter

# HELP request_duration_ms A histogram of the duration of a request. This is measured from when the request headers are received to when the request stream has completed.
# TYPE request_duration_ms histogram

# HELP response_total A counter of the number of responses the proxy has received.
# TYPE response_total counter

# HELP response_duration_ms A histogram of the duration of a response. This is measured from when theresponse headers are received to when the response stream has completed.
# TYPE response_duration_ms histogram

# HELP response_latency_ms A histogram of the total latency of a response. This is measured from whenthe request headers are received to when the response stream has completed.
# TYPE response_latency_ms histogram

process_start_time_seconds 1522102089

```

Closes #619

passed already
but outbound_destinations_reset_on_reconnect_followed_by_add_none
and outbound_destinations_reset_on_reconnect_followed_by_remove_none
failed. Now all these tests pass.

title: Add response classification to proxy metrics
body:
This PR adds a `classification` label to proxy response metrics, as @olix0r described in https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/issues/634#issuecomment-376964083. The label is either "success" or "failure", depending on the following rules:
+ **if** the response had a gRPC status code, *then*
   - gRPC status code 0 is considered a success
   - all others are considered failures
+ **else if** the response had an HTTP status code, *then*
  - status codes < 500 are considered success,
  - status codes >= 500 are considered failures
+ **else if** the response stream failed **then**
  - the response is a failure.

I've also added end-to-end tests for the classification of HTTP responses (with some work towards classifying gRPC responses as well). Additionally, I've updated `doc/proxy_metrics.md` to reflect the added `classification` label.

proxy-init has these arguments:

title: Add labels from service discovery to proxy metrics reports
body:
PR #654 adds pod-based metric labels to the Destination API responses for cluster-local services. 

This PR modifies the proxy to actually add these labels to reported Prometheus metrics for outbound requests to local services. 

It enhances the proxy's `control::discovery` module to track these labels and add a `LabelRequest` middleware to the service stack built in `Bind` for labeled services. Requests transiting `LabelRequest` are given an `Extension` which contains these labels, which are then added to events produced by the `Sensors` for these requests. When these events are aggregated to Prometheus metrics, the labels are added.

I've also added some tests in `test/telemetry.rs` ensuring that these metrics are added correctly when the Destination service provides labels.

I don't quite understand how this works...

- We have a `Self`-typed cache holding `T`-typed values.
- We have an `I`-typed iterator of `Q`-typed values.
- `T`-typed values are dereferenced to `Q`-typed values.
- We iterate over `Q`-typed values, and lookup each `Q`-typed value--by reference--into the cache.

How can we do Q-typed lookups for T-typed values? Are we relying on the fact that inserts take a reference before computing the hash or something? I'm confused.

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body:
> `T`-typed values are dereferenced to `Q`-typed values.

This is not quite correct; the `T: Borrow<Q>` bound means that `Q`-typed values _are a borrowed form_ of `T`-typed values: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/borrow/trait.Borrow.HTML

`HashSet` lookups for a `HashSet<T>` don't take arguments of type `T`, they [take arguments of a type `Q` bounded with `T: Borrow<Q>`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/collections/struct.HashSet.html#method.take). This is just applying the same bound placed on the `HashSet` lookup functions to the type of the items in the iterator.

title: Define a new telemetry Stat API
body:
Proposal definition for a new `Stat` api, for the purposes of satisfying the queries proposed in #627.
StatV2 will replace Stat once implemented and the original Stat deleted.

I wasn't sure what I should do with the resource not found error. I could make it an optional field on the top level StatSummaryResponse, or we could just return an `ApiError` from the controller if the resource isn't found. (This is if a user requests a resource like `conduit stat deploy/foo` but `deploy/foo` doesn't exist (i.e. different from where that deployment exists but we don't have stats for it).
author: rmars

review_threads.author: olix0r
review_threads.body: Is it possible for the service to respond with multiple errors (i.e. if multiple specified resources do not exist)?

review_threads.author: rmars
review_threads.body:
The way I was thinking about it is that if we send requests for multiple resources, we'd  first parse a request like `conduit stat namespaces, deploys` into one `StatSummaryRequest` per resource.  So the response would only have one requested resource pertaining to it (though you can do thinks like, stats for deploys by pod, etc) but since we'd be getting things like pods per deployment from the k8s api, we wouldn't encounter non-existing resources at that point.

If we were thinking of moving the parsing of the resource string further back, and 
 the `ResourceSpec`'s `resource` could be a string like "namespaces,deployments", then I agree, the service could respond with multiple selected resources being missing

review_threads.body:
Based on my reading of the spec in #627, these two fields correspond to the `--out-from` and `--out-to` command line flags. In that case the naming makes sense, but I'm not sure I understand exactly what those flags do.

I'm guessing that, by default, the stat command returns inbound stats, but if either `--out-from` or `--out-to` is set, then the command instead returns outbound stats, filtered by either the source resource (`--out-from`) or the target resource (`--out-to`)? Whether or not we return inbound or outbound stats feels like a binary flag to me, whereas I would expect for us to be able to add filtering regardless of whether or not we're returning inbound or outbound stats. But it's also possible I'm not fully understanding the design.

On a related note, do we need this request message to also pass the values that are passed via the `--out-from-namespace` / `--out-from-selector` / `--out-to-namespace` / `--out-to-selector` flags?

I can post this feedback directly on #627 if that's more appropriate. Just figured I'd mention it while I was looking at the definition here.

title: Add optional GZIP compression to proxy /metrics endpoint
body:
Closes #598.

According to the Prometheus documentation, metrics export endpoints should support serving metrics compressed using GZIP. I wrote [a quick library](https://github.com/hawkw/hyper-compress) for gluing together `flate2` and `hyper`, and used it to add support for serving GZIP-encoded metrics to the proxy.

I've also added a new unit test that attempts to get the proxy's metrics endpoint as GZIP, and asserts that the metrics are decompressed successfully.

comments.body: I didn't review the code in detail. The main concern I have with this is the memory allocation. Are we allocating a buffer that holds the huge uncompressed data and then allocating new buffers for the smaller-but-hard-to-reason-about compressed variants, causing quite a lot of memory allocation? It would be bad to be potentially using our entire memory allocation budget just to serve the metrics.

I'd still like to be able to do this without buffering at all but that doesn't seem possible with the currently available APIs in `hyper` and `deflate-rs`, so hopefully the current approach will at least cut down on allocations. It's certainly much simpler!

review_threads.author: hawkw

However, it's only listed as a `dev-dependency` in Cargo.toml. I'd like to remove the dependency on `flate2` entirely, but that would require `deflate-rs` adding support for decompression.

review_threads.author: seanmonstar
review_threads.body: Spawning another task by itself doesn't help the server. It can juggle several different futures at once (though HTTP/1 means 1 per connection at a time). It'd only matter if compression were CPU intensive, in which case, a separate task by itself isn't enough. It'd need to compress on a separate thread.
