review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body:
Please add some comments about how this works in terms of memory usage and Content-Length. In particular, document whether this buffers the entire output in memory instead of streaming it, or is it intended to stream it?

If we're buffering the entire output in memory then let's document the rationale; i.e. that we expect the output will always be small, i.e. less than 100K, and some justification for that. Maybe we should have a TODO comment to switch to a streaming implementation in this case.

If we're streaming the response body then let's document that we're streaming the response body because we don't want to allocate a potentially large amount of memory.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: Isn't there any way to avoid this `Vec::from()` allocation? It seems like we're potentially allocating a lot of memory?

review_threads.author: seanmonstar

The `writer` header it the `mpsc::Sender` side of `WriteBody`, right? And `text` is the `Vec<u8>` taken out of the `GzEncoder`? I think the extra write can just be skipped, and the `Vec` can be used directly as `hyper::Chunk`.

title: Add `eventually!` macro to help de-flake telemetry tests
body:
Closes #615.

Based on @olix0r's suggestion in https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/issues/613#issuecomment-376024744, this PR adds an `eventually!` macro to retry an assertion a set number of times, waiting for 15 ms between retries. This is loosely based on ScalaTest's [eventually](http://doc.scalatest.org/1.8/org/scalatest/concurrent/Eventually.html).

I've rewritten the flaky telemetry tests to use the `eventually!` macro, to compensate for delays in the served metrics being updated between client requests and metrics scrapes.
author: hawkw

comments.author: hawkw
comments.body: @olix0r I've re-enabled all the flaky tests in `telemetry` except for the ones that rely on the timer for latency measurements as well (which this won't fix)

comments.author: hawkw
comments.body: @carllerche with regards to the name, it's called `eventually!` because a similar function in ScalaTest is called that, and @olix0r initially suggested "we should have something like ScalaTest's `eventually`". I'm definitely open to changing it, though I agree `assert_eventually!` is a bit lengthy --- how about just `assert_eventual` or `eventual_assert`? I'm not sure if I like that better.

comments.author: hawkw
comments.body: Okay, I've changed the name to `assert_eventually!` as per @carllerche. Will merge when CI passes.

review_threads.author: carllerche
review_threads.body: Probably... but not super important.

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body:
The main reason I didn't just go ahead and use `lazy_static` is because it's a macro, and `extern crate` statements with `#[macro_use]` have to go in the crate root. Since `tests/support` is a module that's included separately in each test module, that means that each test file would have to `#[macro_use] extern crate lazy_static;` or else it won't compile, even if it doesn't actually make use of the `assert_eventually!` macro. I thought this behaviour would be confusing and might pose a minor barrier to entry for writing new tests.

WDYT?

review_threads.author: seanmonstar
review_threads.body: Yea, re-checking the environment is fine, it's just a test, and that way we don't need the lazy_static dependency.

title: Add CA certificate bundle distributor to conduit install
body:
This branch adds another controller command that runs a kubernetes controller that distributes the `conduit-ca-bundle` configmap from the conduit namespace to all namespaces where a conduit proxy is running. The controller implementation is loosely based on @jbeda's [tgik-controller](https://github.com/jbeda/tgik-controller) project.

I've updated the `conduit install` output to run the distributor as a separate deployment in the conduit namespace. As it is currently implemented, all pod specs in the install output are injected with a conduit-proxy sidecar, including this one. Since the distributor pod does not accept inbound traffic, it probably doesn't need to be injected. But it does make outbound calls to the kubernetes api, in which case it might be useful to route those calls through the proxy. We can remove it in the future if we feel like that's unnecessary.

Fixes #309.

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
I can't seem to find it written out explicitly anywhere, but the add and update funcs always receive an object, so it's safe to cast them without checking to make sure the cast succeeded. The delete func can receive a tombstone, in which case you have to have the check. From the cache docs:

```
* OnAdd is called when an object is added.
* OnUpdate is called when an object is modified. Note that oldObj is the
    last known state of the object-- it is possible that several changes
    were combined together, so you can't use this to see every single
    change. OnUpdate is also called when a re-list happens, and it will
    get called even if nothing changed. This is useful for periodically
    evaluating or syncing something.
* OnDelete will get the final state of the item if it is known, otherwise
    it will get an object of type DeletedFinalStateUnknown. This can
    happen if the watch is closed and misses the delete event and we don't
    notice the deletion until the subsequent re-list.
```

This convention also appears to be prevalent in the kubernetes code base. For instance, in the controller that I previously linked to, I see:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/certificates/certificate_controller.go#L74

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body:
curious at the interaction between `wait.Until` and `processNextWorkItem`. 

from https://godoc.org/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/wait#Until:
`Until loops until stop channel is closed, running f every period.`

the implementation of `worker()` calls `c.queue.Get()` in a for loop. from https://godoc.org/k8s.io/client-go/util/workqueue#Type.Get:
`Get blocks until it can return an item to be processed.`

wouldn't `worker()` run forever on its own, without the need for `wait.Until` wrapping it?

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
Hmm, yeah, this is a great question! I assumed that the main benefit of using `wait.Until` here was to be able to stop the worker by closing `stopCh`, but I think you're right that if the worker loops forever without returning, then closing the channel won't actually stop it.

I guess another possibility is that the worker process could exit in some other way (a panic, I suppose), and `wait.Until` would restart it. At least, this comment from tgik-controller seems to indicate that that's a possibility:

```
// runWorker will loop until "something bad" happens. wait.Until will
// then rekick the worker after one second.
```

But, looking at the implementation of `wait.Until`, it doesn't actually recover from panic, so ¯\\_(ツ)_/¯

FWIW, this pattern seems to be all over the kubernetes codebase. For instance:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/certificates/certificate_controller.go#L121

So I'm inclined to use it here as well, even though we can't figure out what it's actually doing for us :-/

title: Pretty-print durations in log messages
body:
This branch adds simple pretty-printing to duration in log timeout messages. If the duration is >= 1 second, it's printed in seconds with a fractional part. If the duration is less than 1 second, it is printed in milliseconds. This simple formatting may not be sufficient as a formatting rule for all cases, but should be sufficient for printing our relatively small timeouts.

Log messages now look something like this:
```
ERROR 2018-04-04T20:05:49Z: conduit_proxy: turning operation timed out after 100 ms into 500
```

Previously, they looked like this:
```
ERROR 2018-04-04T20:07:26Z: conduit_proxy: turning operation timed out after Duration { secs: 0, nanos: 100000000 } into 500
```

I made this change partially because I wanted to make the panics from the `eventually!` macro added in #669 more readable.

title: proxy: improve graceful shutdown process
body:
- The listener is immediately closed on receipt of a shutdown signal.
- All in-progress server connections are now counted, and the process will
  not shutdown until the connection count has dropped to zero.
- In the case of HTTP1, idle connections are closed. In the case of HTTP2,
  the HTTP2 graceful shutdown steps are followed of sending various
  GOAWAYs.

Closes #430 

-----

The amount of test coverage here is fairly sparse. It would be ideal to have a gamut of tests where shutdown is received with various request types in-progress.

Still, here's what the tests *do* cover:

- HTTP2 connection is sent a GOAWAY and closed.
- HTTP1 idle connection is closed.
- TCP connection is not abruptly closed, but shutdown process waits for it to complete.

title: Make `control::Cache` key-value in order to store discovery metadata
body:
This PR changes the proxy's `control::Cache` module from a set to a key-value map. 

This change is made in order to use the values in the map to store metadata from the Destination API, but allow evictions and insertions to be based only on the `SocketAddr` of the destination entry. This will make code in PR #661 much simpler, by removing the need to wrap `SocketAddr`s in the cache in a `Labeled` struct for storing metadata, and the need for custom `Borrow` implementations on that type.

Furthermore, I've changed from using a standard library `HashSet`/`HashMap` as the underlying collection to using `IndexMap`, as we suspect that this will result in performance improvements. 

Currently, as `master` has no additional metadata to associate with cache entries, the type of the values in the map is `()`. When #661 merges, the values will actually contain metadata.

If we suspect that there are many other use-cases for `control::Cache` where it will be treated as a set rather than a map, we may want to provide a separate set of impls for `Cache<T, ()>` (like `std::HashSet`) to make the API more ergonomic in this case.

@briansmith 
> Is this really supposed to be `Change::Insert` when this is an update and not an insertion? If so, why?

This is `Change::Insert` because `tower-discover` lacks a concept of a metadata update. We do have to re-bind the service, as `self.bind.bind()` is responsible for adding the `Labeled` middleware to the bound service. A metadata change (currently) implies a change in labels, so we need to change the `Labeled` middleware wrapping the bound service, and to my knowledge there's no way to do that besides binding a new service for the address.

 > Otherwise, isn't this case and the `Update::Insert()` case exactly the same? It seems like they should be in the same match arm if they're doing the same thing.

I thought these _were_ collapsed into one match arm in this branch, but it looks like I actually only made that change in #661: https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/pull/661/files#diff-3d7563188396c0392342b192778deb15L186

A metadata change (currently) implies a change in labels, so we need to change the Labeled middleware wrapping the bound service, and to my knowledge there's no way to do that besides binding a new service for the address.

OK, but does everything tolerate a "duplicate insert"? That is, is Tower's semantics for `Change::Insert` really an "upsert" i.e. "Insert or Update"? Is there any test that things work correctly on a duplicate insert?

It would be good to confirm with @carllerche that this is the best way of handling this.

Does it make sense to have a single `Query<T>`  type that holds both the `DestinationServiceQuery<T>` and `Option<IpAddrListFuture>`? tioli... just asking questions as i read.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body:
> It's the case that when we have a dns_query, we're guaranteed to also have a query?

No. When we first create the `DestinationSet`, we check if the query is `None` and then automatically create the `dns_query` if it is None. So all combinations are possible.

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body: Hmm. Are there specific states in which we would expect a given combination of `None` and `Some`? If so we might want to consider an `enum` that encodes those states and the allowable transitions between them...

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: `(None, None)` is not a valid state but intermittently we do have `(None, None)` sometimes because of the uses of `take` in `poll_destinations()`.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body:
As far as the transitions go:

`(Some, None)` is a valid initial state, when the name is of a form for which we'd query the Destination service.
`(None, Some)` is a valid initial state, when that's not the case.

`(Some, None) => (Some, Some)` when the destination service indicates that the service doesn't exist.
`(Some, Some) => (Some, None)` when the destination service indicates the service exists after previously telling us it didn't.

`(None, None)` is a frequent intermediate state but it isn't a valid state in general.

We could try to encode this into a typed state machine, but I think that would impede immediately-upcoming work to generalize service discovery beyond the Destination service and DNS. I suggest we add that 3rd type of service discovery and do that refactoring before we fossilize the current design too much more. In particular, in the future it would be nice to not have `control::discovery` aware of the Destination service or DNS at all. But not yet, and not in this PR. :)

title: CLI: change conduit namespace shorthand flag to -c
body:
All of the conduit CLI subcommands accept a `--conduit-namespace` flag, indicating the namespace where conduit is running. Some of the subcommands also provide a `--namespace flag`, indicating the kubernetes namespace where a user's application code is running. title: Refactor control::Cache and add tests
body:
Closes #713. This is a follow-up from #688.

This PR makes a number of refactorings to the proxy's `control::Cache` module and removes all but one of the `clone` calls. 

The `CacheChange` enum now contains the changed key and a reference to the changed value when applicable. This simplifies `on_change` functions, which no longer have to take both a tuple of `(K, V)` and a `CacheChange` and can now simply destructure the `CacheChange`, and since the changed value is passed as a reference, the `on_change` function can now decide whether or not it should be cloned. This means that we can remove a majority of the clones previously present here.

I've also rewritten `Cache::update_union` so that it no longer clones values (twice if the cache was invalidated). There's still one `clone` call in `Cache::update_intersection`, but it seems like it will be fairly tricky to remove. However, I've moved the `V: Clone` bound to that function specifically. `Cache::clear` and `Cache::update_union` so that they no longer call `Cache::update_intersection` internally, so they don't need a `V: Clone` bound.

In addition, I've added some unit tests that test that `on_change` is called with the correct `CacheChange`s when key/value pairs are modified.
author: hawkw

comments.author: briansmith
comments.body: My understanding is that this is something that should be done after 0.4.0. Is that right?

comments.author: hawkw
comments.body: @briansmith yeah, that's correct, this refactor isn't necessary for 0.4.0.

comments.author: hawkw
comments.body: @olix0r should this merge now or wait 'til after the release?

comments.author: olix0r
comments.body: @hawkw let's wait on this, please.

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body:
The main impact of this change is that changed values are now passed as borrowed references, so it's left up to the `on_change` function that receives the `CacheChange` notification to decide whether or not the value should be cloned. 

If, for example, we wanted an `on_change` function that only logs changes to the cache and only needs a reference to log an added or modified value, we wouldn't have to clone the value. If the value ends up being inserted into some other structure as well, then the `on_change` function would be free to clone it if necessary.

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body: There was previously a call to `update_intersection` here. I've replaced it with this code, because `update_intersection` takes an `IndexMap<K, V>`, which would require us to clone the inserted values. However, all we care about here is removing any stale keys, regardless of what their values are, since any changed values were already updated by `update_inner`, so we only need to filter out keys that weren't in the inserted key-value pairss.

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body: This function previously just called `update_intersection`. I've removed that call because `update_intersection` still requires the `V: Clone` bound, and I didn't want `clear` to require that `V: Clone`. This also means we no longer have to  construct a new empty `IndexMap` just to clear the cache.

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body: This is the one remaining `clone` call in this module. I couldn't figure out how to remove it easily. @briansmith, if you have any insight it would be greatly appreciated.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: Isn't `update_intersection()` dead code now? It seems like it was only used in this module and now its uses have been removed, so I think we can just delete it.

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body:
Oh, I think you're right --- I mistakenly assumed it was part of the cache's API surface but now I realise it was only used internally. 

In that case, how do you feel about renaming `update_union` to just `update`, since we no longer have to distinguish the two operations?

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: I think `update_union` is really the better name. The `update` part is there to indicate that existing entries will be replaced with the new values, and the `union` part is there to indicate that any new entries will be added to the set.

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body: That's fair. I'll just remove the unused function, then.

review_threads.author: briansmith
hawkw
review_threads.body:
@briansmith that does, in fact, solve this problem, thanks for the suggestion.

As a side note, you'll notice that I used pattern matching on the entry rather than `.and_modify(...).or_insert(...)` as you suggested. This is actually because `IndexMap`'s entry API lacks an `and_modify` method --- only `std::collections`'s maps have that method.

title: Move request open timestamp to the top of the stack
body:
Currently, the request open timestamp, which is used for calculating latency, is captured in the `sensor::http::Http` middleware. However, the sensor middleware is placed fairly low in the stack, below some of the proxy's components that can add measurable latency (e.g. the router).

This PR moves the request_open timestamp out of the `Http` middleware and into a new `TimestampRequestOpen` middleware, which is installed at the top of the stack (before the router). The `TimestampRequestOpen` middleware adds the timestamp as a request extension, so that it can later be consumed by the `Http` sensor to generate the request stats.

By moving the timestamping to the top of the stack, the timestamp should more accurately cover the overhead of the proxy, but a majority of the telemetry work can still be done where it was previously.

I'd like to have included unit tests for this change, but since the expected improvement is in the accuracy of latency measurements, there's no easy way to test this programmatically. 

Fixes #479.
author: hawkw

comments.author: olix0r
comments.body:
to test this i might do something like the following:

- off of master -- add a significant delay into the call stack (probably within the router), confirm that the proxy doesn't report that added latency.
- off of this branch -- add the same delay and confirm that the proxy _does_ report the added latency.

i'd do this for at least http/1 (i tend to use curl/twistd, but anything is fine) and http/2 requests (i tend to use nghttp/nghttpd).

comments.author: briansmith
comments.body: It seems like at least @hawkw and @olix0r agree that the proposed implementation is OK. It at least improves the amount of the stack that we measure. I think that, in the future, we can improve the accounting further, and/or with greater confidence that we're measuring as much as we can, and I don't think we should consider the issue of accounting for all the overhead of the proxy that we can account for to be resolved. But, also, I think it is fine to merge this PR as-is.

review_threads.author: olix0r
review_threads.body: let's put this around `router` instead of around `map_err`, so that we still uniformly handle errors. Basically, i think that MapErr should wrap _everything_ unless there's a good reason not to.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body:
If the intent is that we really capture the earliest instant that we have the request, then why not just add this extension at the time we constructed `req`, instead of here? In particular, it's really unclear to me what happens between the time we constructed `req` and the time `call()` is called here, and it's unclear how we know that there are no non-trivial delays between those two things.

In other words, while it seems clean to implement this as middleware, I'm not convinced that implementing it as middleware most accurately captures the data.

review_threads.author: hawkw
briansmith
review_threads.body: OK. Thinking in terms of middleware, then, wouldn't the ideal be for the layer that adds the request extension to be the later directly wrapping the hyper/h2 layers?

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body: I'm not sure if I entirely understand what you mean --- by placing this middleware at the top of the stack (modulo https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/pull/744#discussion_r180920549), it should be among the first layers to see the request object once its' been constructed.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body:
> I'm not sure if I entirely understand what you mean --- by placing this middleware at the top of the stack (modulo #744 (comment)), it should be among the first layers to see the request object once its' been constructed.

How could we ensure that it is definitely the first layer to see the request object?

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body:
1. We wrap the rest of the `NewService` stack with the `TimestampRequestOpen` `NewService`, so it's at the top of the stack:
https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/blob/be9be0ccab97680df90f814884634c5479f02f56/proxy/src/lib.rs#L374
2. that stack of `NewService`s is passed to `Server::new`, and goes in the constructed `Server`'s `new_service` field 
3. when the `Server` serves an HTTP/1 request, it calls `new_service` on that stack, constructing a new `Service` where the `TimestampRequestOpen` middleware is the outermost service (the first to see the request object). It's wrapped in an adapter that turns a `tower::Service` into a `hyper::Service`, but we can't put it before that because  the version of `hyper` we depend on uses the `hyper::Request` type rather than `http::Request`, and we can't add extensions to a `hyper::Request`:
https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/blob/be9be0ccab97680df90f814884634c5479f02f56/proxy/src/transparency/server.rs#L155-L169
4. When the server is constructed, it constructs a `tower_h2::Server` with the `stack`
https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/blob/be9be0ccab97680df90f814884634c5479f02f56/proxy/src/transparency/server.rs#L73-L81
which is used to serve HTTP/2 connections:
https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/blob/be9be0ccab97680df90f814884634c5479f02f56/proxy/src/transparency/server.rs#L178

---

In both cases, there are protocol-specific adapter middlewares around the rest of the middleware stack (`HttpBodyService` and `HyperServerService`),. In the case of the `HyperServerService` for HTTP/1, we can't add the timestamp before that service, for the reason discussed above. The H2  `HttpBodyService` just does a type conversion on the request body. We could place the middleware before that service, although I don't think it has a significant impact on latency, and this would complicate the implementation. What do you think?

review_threads.author: olix0r
review_threads.body:
> How could we ensure that it is definitely the first layer to see the request object?

I don't think it should be the _first_ layer. I think the error-handling/logging layer should be the first layer, so it can capture any errors emitted by middlewares like this; though it's true that the timestamping middleware can't fail on its own, so this is all semantics.

For now, I think the best we can do to _ensure_ that this is early in the stack is to document it well.

In the future, I hope that we can have better stacking primitives so these assurances can be made more explicitly (as in finagle stacks).

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body:
> I don't think it should be the first layer. I think the error-handling/logging layer should be the first layer, so it can capture any errors emitted by middlewares like this; though it's true that the timestamping middleware can't fail on its own, so this is all semantics.

In past work, I've found that logging had added significant overhead, so I think that we should start the measurement before logging. And, I think it's not unreasonably to expect "error handling" could likely do the same, as "error handling" evolves over time.

review_threads.author: olix0r
review_threads.body: i meant "error logging." I don't feel super strongly about this -- it makes some sense to just put this at the top of the stack. I don't think we have to spend too much time trying to build solid assurances that this is always at the top (yet) -- though I agree that we should at least begin to document the stack ordering.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body:
What does "Open" mean? Is there another term that would better capture this? E.g. "Parsed"?

What is this measuring and what *isn't* it measuring? I think it's important to document that this does not and cannot measure the time the request spend in the TCP receive window and any time spend parsing and/or otherwise pre-processing the request header. Simlarly, we should have some note about what our expectations are on the response end regarding unmeasured overhead. It would be also good to note any other overhead that isn't accounted for.

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body:
The name "RequestOpen" was chosen because it was previously used here
https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/blob/e9b209829d8b5514b89850bb0b7a64a28b3348b1/proxy/src/telemetry/sensor/http.rs#L215

and elsewhere in the module. I'll improve the documentation.

review_threads.author: olix0r
review_threads.body: Can we be more defensive than panicking?  Above, we are graceful to missing Server context, for instance... it seems better to fail silently (possibly logging) than to fail hard here.

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body: @olix0r what do you think of 55ee99876a0dc77017e884aed87cccf9fe7a1a1b?

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body: Note that we log only the request URI here, because logging the entire request struct would require a `A: Debug` bound on the request's body type, which I didn't want to add.

review_threads.author: olix0r
review_threads.body: alternatively, just match on the `(Some(), Some())` case first and fall back to `(ctx, request_open)`

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body: Yeah, that's much clearer, changed in 0b6014fcaae38aa8f2e53626f75ac0c72d20d458

title: Add --all-namespaces flag to CLI statsummary command
body:
In this branch I'm updating the statsummary command to support the `--all-namespaces` flag, which will override the `--namespace` flag and return stats for all namespaces when set to `--all-namespaces=true`.

It looks like this:

```
$ ./bin/go-run cli --api-addr 127.0.0.1:8085 --all-namespaces=true statsummary deployments

emojivoto     voting                    1/1    83.1rps   1.08%           1ms           1ms           1ms
emojivoto     web                       1/1    90.3rps   2.07%           3ms           5ms           5ms
kltest        controller                1/1   100.0rps   1.80%           2ms           5ms           9ms
kltest        grafana                   1/1   100.0rps   0.10%           1ms           1ms           1ms
```

title: rfc: Make DestinationServiceQuery generic
body:
The goals of this change are:
1. Reduce the size/complexity of `control::discovery` in order to ease code reviews.
2. Extract a reusable grpc streaming utility.

There are no intended functional changes.

`control::discovery::DestinationServiceQuery` is used to track the state of a request (and streaming response) to the destination service. Very little of this logic is specific to the destination service.

The `DestinationServiceQuery` and associated `UpdateRx` type have been moved to a new module, `control::remote_stream`, as `Remote` and `Receiver`, respectively. Both of these types are generic over the gRPC message type, so it will be possible to use this utility with additional API endpoints.

The `Receiver::poll` implementation has been simplified to be more idiomatic with the rest of our code (namely, using `try_ready!`).

Additionally, the enum states are now hidden behind an API. `Remote` now exposes constructors, a `needs_reconnect()` method that indicates whether the remote is disconnected, and a `into_receiver_maybe()` that consumes the remote, producing a receiver if one exists.

---

Note: It may help to review the individual commits in order.
author: olix0r

comments.author: briansmith
comments.body:
I understand that the goal here is to enable other implementations of service discovery with equivalent functionality to the Destination service.

I think a good way to validate this design would be to refactor the DNS-based service discovery to implement this interface. Or, if that's practical and we think DNS is special in some way, then we should document why we didn't redo DNS in this mold.

comments.author: hawkw
olix0r
comments.body:
> I understand that the goal here is to enable other implementations of service discovery with equivalent functionality to the Destination service.

Not exactly. The goal is to enable interacting with arbitrary gRPC streaming endpoints. `remote_stream` models the state of such an endpoint (note that its `M` type must be `prost::Message + Default` and its `F` type is `Future<Item = http::Response<Body>>`, for example).

comments.author: olix0r
comments.body:
@briansmith per your feedback, I've minimized the API change so that there's lesser impact to discovery.

The Remote type is now generic over the HttpService instead of its Future and body types -- this simplifies type signature complexity.

comments.author: olix0r
comments.body: @briansmith feedback addressed

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: Why is it necessary to have separate `Remote` and `Inner` types? Usually we would have an `Inner` type if if we have an `Option<Inner>` that we sometimes `take()`, but that's not the case here. If we can combine this into `Remote`, let's do so, to make the code easier to read. Otherwise, let's add a comment here about why it is split out.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: This shouldn't be `pub`, AFAICT.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: We should rename this function to `connect_to_destination_service_maybe()` since it is now in a more general context than before.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: I think we should have a type alias `type DestinationServiceQuery<T> = Remote<PbUpdate, T::Future, T::ResponseBody>` and use it in this module instead of `Remote` directly. Otherwise IMO the code would be harder to understand than it is now.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: It would be much clearer to just make the `Remote` enum public with public variants so that we can match on it directly. This code here only makes sense if `Remote::new()` is equivalent to what `query` was originally, which means we're not gaining anything by hiding the structure of `Remote` since, if there was a third variant of that enum, or if the enum had any different structure, this code would almost definitely be wrong.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: Again, here we're creating a big API with a bunch of boilerplate for, AFAICT, no reason, since there's no way to implement or use this API correctly unless `Remote` is an enum isomorphic to `Some<Receiver<M, F, B>>`. It would be better to lose all this boilerplate and make the code a lot easier to understand.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: `valid_auth` seems like a poor name to me. Really the distinction isn't "valid" vs "invalid" but rather "may be an internal service" vs "is definitely not an internal service". I suggest `query_destination_service_if_relevant` or similar. In particular I would like to avoid implying anything about the validity of the authority in the name.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: TIL we can't refer to this as `DestinationServiceQuery` because of https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/26264. (No change necessary.)

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: `connected()` is too misleading since the connection might not be connected yet. I suggest we just use `ConnectedOrConnecting` directly to make it clearer.

review_threads.author: briansmith
olix0r
review_threads.body:
The underlying issue here is the following:

* `grpc::Error<T>` is generic over `T`: the underlying future's failure (for `grpc::Error::Inner`)
* `stream.poll` can't actually fail with an Inner error, so it returns an `grpc::Error<()>`
* here, we want to coerce the stream's error response to the general grpc error, so we need to drop the () type and convert to a T type.
* This is why `e => e` doesn't work here -- the types are actually different.

i'll comment this a bit at least.

title: v0.4.0
body:
Conduit 0.4.0 overhauls Conduit's telemetry system and improves service discovery
reliability.

* Web UI
  * **New** automatically-configured Grafana dashboards for all Deployments.
* Command-line interface
  * `conduit stat` has been completely rewritten to accept arguments like `kubectl get`.
    The `--to` and `--from` filters can be used to filter traffic by destination and
    source, respectively.  `conduit stat` currently can operate on `Namespace` and
    `Deployment` Kubernetes resources. More resource types will be added in the next
    release!
* Proxy (data plane)
  * **New** Prometheus-formatted metrics are now exposed on `:4191/metrics`, including
    rich destination labeling for outbound HTTP requests. The proxy no longer pushes
    metrics to the control plane.
  * The proxy now handles `SIGINT` or `SIGTERM`, gracefully draining requests until all
    are complete or `SIGQUIT` is received.
  * SMTP and MySQL (ports 25 and 3306) are now treated as opaque TCP by default. You
    should no longer have to specify `--skip-outbound-ports` to communicate with such
    services.
  * When the proxy reconnected to the controller, it could continue to send requests to
    old endpoints. Now, when the proxy reconnects to the controller, it properly removes
    invalid endpoints.
  * A bug impacting some HTTP/2 reset scenarios has been fixed.
* Service Discovery
  * Previously, the proxy failed to resolve some domain names that could be misinterpreted
    as a Kubernetes Service name. This has been fixed by extending the _Destination_ API
    with a negative acknowledgement response.
* Control Plane
  * The _Telemetry_ service and associated APIs have been removed.
* Documentation
  * Updated Roadmap
  * Added prometheus metrics guide
author: olix0r

title: Permit arbitrary time windows in public-api
body:
The public-api previously only permitted 4 hard-coded time windows:
10s, 1m, 10m, 1h. This was primarily a relic of the recently removed
telemetry system.

Modify the public-api to validate the time string, but allow for any
window size, which is then passed through to Prometheus.

Fixes #686

Signed-off-by: Andrew Seigner <siggy@buoyant.io>
author: siggy

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
Now that we're switching to an actual duration, you can use a duration flag here, and that will handle validation of the duration automatically.

```
	statCmd.PersistentFlags().DurationVarP(&timeWindow, "time-window", "t", time.Minute, "Stat window (for example: \"10s\", \"1m\", \"10m\", \"1h\")")
```

And in the event that the flag isn't a valid duration, that returns:

```
$ bin/go-run cli stat -t asdf
Error: invalid argument "asdf" for "-t, --time-window" flag: time: invalid duration asdf
```

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body:
I did consider this approach. The drawback here is that we lose information about the original string when it's parsed into a `time.Duration`. This issue compounds because Prometheus accepts a subset of valid time strings, specifically `[integer][h|m|s]`. Passing in `1m` would yield `1m0s` which fails in Prometheus.

We could go a step further and try to guess at the best representation:
https://play.golang.org/p/5N4bjnEucoA
... this would still yield queries that don't exactly match the user's input. Another option would be to convert everything to seconds.

The approach I took in this PR is to use `time.Parse` to validate the input is a valid time string, but then to still pass the user's original string through to Prometheus. This also ensures the `timeWindow` string in the API response matches what the user typed. Let me know what you think.

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body: Ah yep, that all makes sense to me. Thanks for the explanation.

title: rfc: A Kubernetes-aware Tap API
body:
This changes the public api to have a new rpc type, `K8sTap`. This api
supercedes the `Tap` api. `K8sTap` is richer, more closely reflecting
the proxy's capabilities.

The proxy's `Tap` api is extended to select over destination labels,
corresponding with those returned by the `Destination` api.

Now both `Tap` and `K8sTap`'s responses may include destination labels.

This change avoids breaking backwards compatability by:
- introducing the new `K8sTap` rpc type, opting not to change `Tap`

title: proxy: Add transport-level metrics
body:
This branch adds all the transport-level Prometheus metrics as described in #742, with the exception of the `tcp_connections_open` gauge (to be added in a subsequent branch). 

A brief description of the metrics added in this branch:
* `tcp_accept_open_total`: counter of the number of connections accepted by the proxy
* `tcp_accept_close_total`: counter of the number of accepted connections that have closed
* `tcp_connect_open_total`: counter of the number of connections opened by the proxy
* `tcp_connect_close_total`: counter of the number of connections opened by the proxy that have been closed.
* `tcp_connection_duration_ms`: histogram of the total duration of each TCP connection (incremented on connection close)
* `sent_bytes`: counter of the total number of bytes sent on TCP connections (incremented on connection close)
* `received_bytes`: counter of the total number of bytes received on TCP connections (incremented on connection close)

 These metrics are labeled with the direction (inbound or outbound) and whether the connection was proxied as raw TCP or corresponds to an HTTP request. 

Additionally, I've added several proxy tests for these metrics. Note that there are some cases which are currently untested; in particular, while there are tests for the `tcp_accept_close_total` counter, it's more difficult to test the `tcp_connect_close_total` counter, due to connection pooling. I'd like to improve the tests for this code in additional branches.
author: hawkw

review_threads.author: seanmonstar
review_threads.body:
So, here's something that I was thinking: perhaps we don't show the "protocol" yet, since I think the current design of labeling a transport is deficient. These are the problems that I know of:

- Since the `protocol` is required to create a context, we actually delay triggering the `accept` event until after protocol detection. While we still capture the correct `Instant`, it does mean that if there is a socket error during protocol detection, we just never record anything about that socket.
- It's not clear to me how we would migrate to a different protocol. For example, a connection could start as HTTP/1, but be used for a websockets upgrade. During the upgrade, it's HTTP, but afterwards, we'd downgrade to just a TCP proxy (and maybe someday we could add in WS-specific telemetry, does that mean we'd need to then transition to a 3rd protocol label?).

Since we no longer need to send these events over gRPC to the controller, I've been thinking that we just rip the `protocol` field out completely. If that seems like the right idea, then it'd probably be better if this PR didn't include that label, ya?

title: Introduce tapByResource cli command
body:
The existing `tap` command is being deprecated.

Introduce a `tapByResource` cli command. It supports tapping a Kubernetes
resource or collection of resources, optionally filtered by outbound resources.
This command will eventually replace `tap`.

Part of #778

Signed-off-by: Andrew Seigner <siggy@buoyant.io>

```bash
$ bin/go-run cli tapByResource -h
Listen to a traffic stream.

  The RESOURCE argument specifies the resource to tap, for example:

  * deploy
  * deploy/my-deploy
  * deploy my-deploy
  * ns/my-ns

  Valid resource types include:

  * deployments
  * namespaces
  * pods
  * replicationcontrollers

Usage:
  conduit tapByResource [flags] (RESOURCE)

Examples:
  # tap the web deployment in the default namespace
  conduit tapByResource deploy/web

  # tap the web-dlbvj pod in the default namespace
  conduit tapByResource pod/web-dlbvj

  # tap the test namespace, filter by request to prod namespace
  conduit tapByResource ns/test --to ns/prod

Flags:
      --authority string      Display requests with this :authority
  -h, --help                  help for tapByResource
      --max-rps float32       Maximum requests per second to tap. (default 1)
      --method string         Display requests with this HTTP method
  -n, --namespace string      Namespace of the specified resource (default "default")
      --path string           Display requests with paths that start with this prefix
      --scheme string         Display requests with this scheme
      --to string             Display requests to this resource
      --to-namespace string   Sets the namespace used to lookup the "--to" resource; by default the current "--namespace" is used

Global Flags:
      --api-addr string            Override kubeconfig and communicate directly with the control plane at host:port (mostly for testing)
  -c, --conduit-namespace string   Namespace in which Conduit is installed (default "conduit")
      --kubeconfig string          Path to the kubeconfig file to use for CLI requests
      --verbose                    Turn on debug logging
```

title: proxy: Rewrite mock controller to accept a stream of dst updates
body:
Currently, the mock controller, which is used in tests, takes all of its
updates a priori, which makes it hard to control when an update occurs within a
test.

Now, the controller exposes a `DstSender`, which wraps an unbounded channel of
destination updates. This allows tests to trigger updates at a specific point
in the test.

In order to accomplish this, the controller's hand-rolled gRPC server
implementation has been discarded in favor of a real gRPC destination service.
This requires that the `controller-grpc` project now builds both clients
and servers for the destination service. Additionally, we now build a tap
client as well (assuming that we'll want to write tests against our tap
server).

---
This change is necessary in order to test an upcoming change to telemetry labeling.

title: proxy: Remove the `Labeled` middleware in favor of client context labels
body:
The `Labeled` middleware is used to add `DstLabels` to each request. Now that
each client context maintains a watch on its endpoint's `DstLabels`, the
`Labeled` middleware can safely be removed.

This has one subtle behavior change: labels are associated with requests
_lazily_, whereas before they were determined _eagerly_. This means that if an
endpoint's labels are updated before the telemetry system captures the labels
for the request, it may use the newer labels. Previously, it would only use the
labels at the time that the request originated.

title: proxy: Add destination labels to TapEvents
body:
The Tap API supports key-value labels on endpoint metadata. The proxy was not
setting these labels previously.

In order to add these labels onto tap events, we store the original set of
labels in an `Arc<HashMap>` on `DstLabels`. When tap events are emitted, the
destination' labels are copied from the DstLabels into each event.

review_threads.author: olix0r
review_threads.body: Yes, as @hawkw mentioned, this is an optimization so that we can amortize the cost of serialization. Note that this pattern isn't all that onerous in Rust, since `formatted` and `original` are explicitly _immutable_ -- it's literally impossible to change the contents of that map once DstLabels is created.  And, furthermore, because DstLabels does not provide mutable access to these fields, we have reasonable constraints/guarantees that they can't get out of sync at runtime!

title: Make simulate-proxy match proxy output
body:
This PR makes two changes to the `simulate-proxy` script: 

1.  Removed the `protocol={"http", "tcp"}` label from TCP metrics. The proxy no longer adds this label (see https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/pull/785#discussion_r182563499).

2. Fixed failed responses being labeled with `classification="fail"` rather than `classification="failure"` (the label the proxy sets). I noticed that while I was here and decided to fix it as well.

Note that the first change required some minor changes to the `proxyMetricCollectors` struct in `simulate-proxy`; since the label cardinality for TCP open stats decreased by one due to removing the `protocol` label, it's no longer necessary for that struct to `haveCounterVec`/`GaugeVec` pointers for these stats. It now owns the actual `Counter`/`Gauge` instead. This means that the metric vecs that are created to be labeled for `inbound` and `outbound` are now stored as variables in the `newSimulatedProxy` function rather than going in a `proxyMetricCollectors` struct first. This shouldn't impact behaviour at all.

title: Introduce the `peer` label to transport metrics
body:
Previously, the proxy exposed separate _accept_ and _connect_ metrics
for some metric types, but not for all. This leads to confusing
aggregations, particularly for read and write totals.

This change primarily introduces the `peer` prometheus label (with
possible values _src_ or _dst_) to indicate which side of the proxy the
metric reflects.

Additionally, the `received_bytes` and `sent_bytes` metrics have been
renamed as `tcp_read_bytes_total` and `tcp_write_bytes_total`,
resectively. This more naturally fits into existing idioms.  Stream
classification is not applied to these metrics, as we plan to increment
them throughout stream lifetime and not only on close.

The `tcp_connections_open` metric has also been renamed to
`tcp_open_connections` to reflect Prometheus idioms.

Finally, `msg1` and `msg2` have been constified in telemetry test
fixtures so that tests are somewhat easier to read.

title: proxy: Make `Histogram` generic over its value
body:
In order to support histograms measured in, for instance, microseconds,
Histogram should blind store integers without being aware of the unit.
In order to accomplish this, we make `Histogram` generic over a `V:
Into<u64>`, such that all values added to the histogram must be of type
`V`.

In doing this, we also make the histogram buckets configurable, though
we maintain the same defaults used for latency values.

The `Histogram` type has been moved to a new module, and the `Bucket`
and `Bounds` helper types have been introduced to help make histogram
logic clearer and latency-agnostic.
author: olix0r

comments.author: hawkw
comments.body: I also added a number of unit tests in PR #775 which I think should be fairly easy to adapt to work with your changes as well --- I'm happy to open a follow-up PR to add them?

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body:
When I made a similar change to `Histogram`s in #775, I implemented this by having the `Histogram` own an array of counts and a reference to an array of bounds (rather than storing the bounds in every instance of `Histogram`):
https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/blob/30dd1a3b8bee68fe18af20d79195b422f84c9df9/proxy/src/telemetry/metrics/histogram.rs#L7-L16

 Including the bounds in each instance effectively doubles the size of the histogram. Since I'd expect we'll create a great deal of `Histogram` instances that all share the same set of bounds, I think having a reference to the bounds will likely lead to a significant difference in memory usage.

This introduces a lifetime parameter, but if the array of bounds is a static array, that's not really a problem.

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body:
Also, TIOLI, since we don't expect either the bounds or counts to grow over the lifetime of the histogram, con sider `Box<[...]>` rather than `Vec<...>`.

I don't believe there's any real performance difference between these types (someone correct me if I'm wrong), but a boxed array better reflects that we need the storage to be heap-allocated (because it's dynamically sized) but that we don't expect it to grow. When I see a `Vec`, I take that to mean "this will contain a variable number of elements".

and using `Bucket<V>` in `Histogram` so you can remove the `PhantomData<V>`.

title: proxy: Remove Arcs from metric labels
body:
This PR removes the `Arc`s from the various label types in the proxy's 
`metrics` modules. This should make the write side of the metrics code
much more efficient (and makes the code much simpler! :D).

This change was particularly easy to implement for the TCP `TransportLabels`
and `TransportCloseLabels`, which consisted of only `struct`s and `enum`s,
and could easily be changed to derive `Copy`. 

For protocol-level `RequestLabels`, the request's authority was a `String`,
which still needs to be reference-counted, as the overhead of cloning `String`s
is almost certainly worse than that added by ref-counting. However, rather than
adding an additional `Arc<str>`, I changed `RequestLabels` to store the 
authority as a `http::uri::Authority`, which is backed by a `ByteStr` and thus
already ref-counted. Now, when constructing `RequestLabels`, we just take 
another reference to the `Authority` already stored in the request context.
Since `Authority` implements `fmt::Display` already, formatting the labels 
still works.

`ResponseLabels` already store the `DstLabels` string in an `Arc`, so no
additional changes there were necessary. By removing the outer `Arc` around
`ResponseLabels`, we now only have to ref-count the portion of the label type
that would actually be inefficient to clone.

@olix0r ran the benchmarks from #874 against this branch, and it seems to be 
a small but noticeable improvement:
```
test record_many_dsts        ... bench:     151,076 ns/iter (+/- 182,151)
test record_one_conn_request ... bench:       1,599 ns/iter (+/- 209)
test record_response_end     ... bench:         676 ns/iter (+/- 144)
```

before:
```
test record_many_dsts        ... bench:     158,403 ns/iter (+/- 130,241)
test record_one_conn_request ... bench:       1,823 ns/iter (+/- 1,408)
test record_response_end     ... bench:         547 ns/iter (+/- 70)
```

Signed-off-by: Eliza Weisman <eliza@buoyant.io>

title: Group metrics by label
body:
Previously, we maintained a map of labels for each metric. Because the same keys are used in multiple scopes, this causes redundant hashing & map lookup when updating metrics.

With this change, there is now only one map per unique label scope and all of the metrics for each scope are stored in the value. This makes metrics inserting faster and prepares for eviction of idle metrics.

The `Metric` type has been split into `Metric`, which now only holds metric metadata and is responsible for printing a given metric, and `Scopes` which holds groupings of metrics by label.

The `metrics!` macro is provided to make it easy to define `Metric` instances statically.

This change moves the Tap ID to be stored in a shared atomic integer.

In a followup, we might consider removing tap IDs entirely.

The proxy's Dockerfile is split into stages: build and runtime.
The build stage includes all of the intermdiate build information, and

image.

This reduces the docker build of the proxy in CI from 15 minutes to
about 7.5 minutes (when the proxy is not changed).

title: proxy: Limit Router cache size
body:
The proxy can currently store an unbounded number of routes, which can potentially lead
memory exhaustion panics for applications that expose or connect to an unbounded number of
endpoints. Note that applications like monitoring systems (like Prometheus) can exhibit
these sorts of behaviors in dynamically scheduled environments.

This change adds a hard upper limit to the number of HTTP endpoints a proxy (i.e. either
_inbound_ or _outbound_ directions) may route to.

In followup changes:
- An eviction policy should be put in place so that unused routes can be reaped to make
  space for new routes.
- Telemetry events should be added for router table modifications so diagnostics can be
  instrumented.
- Single-use routes should consume router capacity.

title: Fix bug where GetPodsFor(pod) was returning all pods in a namespace
body:
*Problem*
In `lister.GetPodsFor`, when the input object was a pod, we would return all the pods in the namespace. I would expect `GetPodsFor(pod)` to return only one pod - the pod itself.

*Cause*
The cause of this is that when the object type was `pod` we were setting the selector to `selector = labels.Everything()` which gets all the pods in the namespace. 

*Fix*
I changed the selector when the input object is a pod to be the pod's labels. Now we don't return all pods in a namespace when `GetPodsFor` is called on a pod.

Fixes #860

title: proxy: change peek to use reads for eventual support of TLS
body: Closes #417
author: seanmonstar

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: The issue isn't exactly that the TLS stream will need to decrypt the bytes before being able to "peek", as far as I understand it. I suggest we just delete the second half of the sentence, rather than get into the specifics.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body:
In the case of TLS 1024 is going to be more than sufficient in the vast majority of cases, however theoretically we might need to peek further than even 8192 bytes. If we're going to cap peeking at 8192 bytes, that's reasonable to do, but we should note that this limits, in theory but probably not in practice, our ability to do protocol detection.

In particular, if we cap the peeking at an arbitrary number like this then we'll need to have a way for the protocol detection logic to say "we didn't peek enough so we can't detect the protocol."

review_threads.author: seanmonstar
review_threads.body: I chose 8192 as its a commonish max size of a packet, while not being too big. I figured we'd need to adjust a little when TLS is put in place, since I don't know exactly what that'd look. I could also just drop this down to 1kb or smaller too, but I don't have great reasons for doing so that are better than just trying to fit the first read into a single buffer/syscall.

title: proxy: Track SingleUse services against router capacity
body:
PR #898 introduces capacity limits to the balancer. However, because the
router supports "single-use" routes--routes that are bound only for the
life of a single HTTP1 request--it is easy for a router to exceed its
configured capacity.

In order to fix this, the `Reuse` type is removed from the router
library so that _all_ routes are considered cacheable. It's now the
responsibility of the bound service to enforce policies with regards to
client retention.

Routes were not added to the cache when the service could not be used to
process more than a single request. Now, `Bind` wraps its returned
services (via the `Binding` type), that dictate whether a single client
is reused or if one is bound for each request.

This enables all routes to be cached without changing behavior with
regards to connection reuse.
author: olix0r

review_threads.author: seanmonstar
review_threads.body: Does this mean that a `LazyOneoff` would actually be reusable, just as long as it binds a new stack for each request?

review_threads.author: olix0r
review_threads.body:
Yeah, perhaps the naming isn't as clear as it could be...

the two variants are:
1. we have bound a service early and can reuse it indefinitely.
2. we have to bind a new service for each request.

`LazyOneoff` refers to the second case.  Because we want to honor the `poll_ready` API, we may still bind a service before `call` is invoked, and we need to take care to consume it here.

review_threads.author: olix0r
review_threads.body: Maybe the variants should be `Bound` and `BindsPerRequest`

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body: +1 for `Bound` and `BindsPerRequest` (or `BindOnRequest`?)

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body: Nit: since we always want to initialize `next` to `None`, consider a constructor `Binding::per_request(&Endpoint, &Protocol, &Bind)` or something. Not important, but just expresses the intention slightly more clearly, IMO.

title: proxy: Use Duration types for config defaults
body:
It's easy to misconfigure default durations, since they're recorded as
integers and converted to Durations separately.

Now, all default constants that represent durations use const `Duration`
instances (enabled by a recent Rust release).

This fixes #905 which was caused by using the wrong time unit for the
metrics retain time.

Relates to #880.

title: proxy: Parse units with duration configurations
body:
Configuration values that take durations are currently specified as
time values with no units.  So `600` may mean 600ms in some contexts and
10 minutes in others.

In order to avoid this problem, this change now requires that
configurations provide explicit units for time values such as '600ms' or
'10 minutes'.

After this, users may set environment vars like `CONDUIT_PROXY_METRICS_RETAIN_IDLE="1h"`.

comments.body: Note that this fixes #27.

title: router: Store `recognize` outside of lock
body:
The router stores its cache and `Recognize` implementation within a `Mutex`,
but there is no need for the recognizer to be locked.

This change creates a new `Cache` type that is locked independently of
`Recognize`. In order to accomplish this, `Recognize::bind_service` has
been changed to take an immutable reference to its `self`.

The (unused) `Single` type has been removed because it relied on
`bind_service` being mutable.

title: docker: Cache versionless builds before building versioned go binaries
body:
The way that git-related version information is linked into Go binaries
busts Docker's cache such that every commit causes all binaries to be
rebuilt.

In order to ameliorate this, we can build each binary once without
version information first so that its artifacts are cached. When Go
sources are not changed and only the version information changes
builds are are now <90s, compared to 5+ minutes.

### On `master`

Branch off of master and build (mostly cached):

```
:; time DOCKER_TRACE=1 bin/docker-build
...
DOCKER_TRACE=1 bin/docker-build  9.10s user 6.30s system 5% cpu 4:26.47 total
```

Rebuild without changing anything (highly cached):

```
:; time DOCKER_TRACE=1 bin/docker-build
...
DOCKER_TRACE=1 bin/docker-build  9.23s user 6.04s system 47% cpu 32.017 total
```

Update only the git sha and rebuild:

```
:; git ci -am 'bump it' --allow-empty
```

title: proxy/router: Implement LRU cache eviction
body:
The router's cache has no means to evict unused entries when capacity is
reached.

This change does the following:

- Wraps cache values in a smart pointer that tracks the last time of
  access for each entry. The smart pointer updates the access time when
  the reference to entry is dropped.
- When capacity is not available, all nodes that have not been accessed
  within some minimal idle age are dropped.

Accesses and updates to the map are O(1) when capacity is available.
Reclaiming capacity is O(n), so it's expected that the router is
configured with enough capacity such that capacity need not be reclaimed
usually.
author: olix0r

review_threads.author: carllerche
review_threads.body:
This has a bad worse case of a linear scan per request.

The slack discussion conclusion was to not using a doubly linked list to keep entries ordered by access to avoid additional overhead during access.

Another option would be to have a time granularity (like, 1 second), so that many requests within a single second would not result in repeated linear scans that don't do much.

title: Fix compile errors in `reserve()`
body:
This fixes the compile errors in `reserve()` relating to `std::time::Instant` being an opaque type that can't be converted to a duration. 

Rather than calculating an `epoch` from the current time minus the maximum idle age and then testing that the `last_access` timestamp for each value is within the `epoch`, I've modified the code to simply test whether the time _elapsed_ since each timestamp (a `Duration`, which we _can_ round to whole seconds) is less than or equal to the max age. This should have the same behaviour as the original implementation intended, but with the advantage of actually compiling :)

title: proxy: Add a lazy version of ThreadRng
body:
This is in preparation for landing the Tokio upgrade. 

In order to be generic over Tokio's current thread and threadpool executors,
a number of types in Conduit which were not previously `Send` are now required
to be `Send`. A majority of this work will be done in the main Tokio upgrade
PR, as it is in many cases not possible to make these types `Send` _without_
using the new Tokio API (in order to remove `Handle`s, etc.); however, I'm
factoring out everything possible and trying to land it in separate PRs.

The p2c load balancer constructed in `Outbound` is currently parameterized
over a random number generator. We currently construct it by getting the 
thread-local RNG, and passing it to the load balancer constructor. However,
the thread-local RNG is not `Send`. I've fixed this issue by creating a new
zero-sized empty struct type which implements `rand::Rng` simply by calling
`thread_rng()` every time its' called, and passing that to 
`choose::power_of_two_choices` instead. Since this is an empty type which 
contains no data, and the correct thread-local RNG is accessed whenever
the methods are called, this new type can trivially be `Send`. According to
the `rand` crate's documentation, this is the correct way to use `ThreadRng`
anyway:
> Retrieve the lazily-initialized thread-local random number generator, seeded
> by the system. Intended to be used in method chaining style, e.g. 
> `thread_rng().gen::<i32>()`.
> (from https://docs.rs/rand/0.4.2/rand/fn.thread_rng.html)

This shouldn't lead to any functional changes.

Signed-off-by: Eliza Weisman <eliza@buoyant.io>
author: hawkw

comments.body: @olix0r probably in the long term that would be a good call, yeah...it was quite simple to write, though, so I'm not sure if it deserves its' own crate.

title: proxy: Move absolute URI detection to `bind::Protocol`
body:
This is in preparation for landing the Tokio upgrade. 

In the upcoming Hyper release, the handling of absolute form request URIs
moved from `hyper::Request` to the `hyper::client::connect::Connect` trait.
Once we upgrade to the new Tokio, we will have to upgrade our Hyper 
dependency as well.

Currently, Conduit detects whether the request URI is in absolute form in
`h1::normalize_our_view_of_uri` and adds an extension to the request if it is.
This will no longer work with the new Hyper, as that function is called from
the `bind::NormalizeUri` service, which is not constructed until after the 
client connection is established. Therefore, it is necessary to move this
information to `bind::Protocol`, so that it can be passed to 
`transparency::client::HyperConnect` (our implementation of Hyper's `Connect`
trait) when we are using the newest Hyper. 

For now, however, I've left in the `UriIsAbsoluteForm` extension and continued
to set it in  `h1::normalize_our_view_of_uri`, since we currently still use it
on the current Hyper version. I thought it was good to minimize the changes to
this existing code, as it will be removed when we migrate to the new Hyper.

This PR shouldn't cause any functional changes.

Signed-off-by: Eliza Weisman <eliza@buoyant.io>
author: hawkw

review_threads.author: olix0r
review_threads.body:
If I understand correctly, this change moves this information into the router's `Key`. Is that correct?  Why?

Can you update the comment to indicate what this field means?

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body:
I believe it's correct for absolute-form and non-absolute-form requests to bind to different services in the router. This is because Hyper handles absolute URIs at the connection level in the upcoming release, so a service stack can no longer set whether the request URI was absolute per-request; we'll now need to construct separate service stacks for absolute-form and non-absolute-form URIs. Also, this configures the behaviour of `NormalizeUri` when the service stack is bound, so we won't want to share that stack between absolute-form and non-absolute-form requests.

I can add a comment documenting this.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: The change to hyper doesn't sound good to me, if it results in us needing to make changes like this.

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body: @briansmith I'm also curious to know what motivated this change in Hyper. I suspect @seanmonstar might be able to offer some insight?

review_threads.author: seanmonstar
review_threads.body:
In hyper 0.11, it used its own `Request` type, which allowed setting a boolean that the request should be written in absolute-form. In 0.12, using `http::Request`, there is no simple property to be set to indicate this. So, a new mechanism was needed. These were the choices I considered:

Have users put that desire in the `extensions`, such as `req.extensions_mut().insert(UriAbsoluteForm)`. This would be most similar to how 0.11 works. That would require looking for that extension before performing each request, which would be a hashmap lookup instead of an explicit field check. Still, it probably wouldn't be that bad. However, there was actually a papercut in 0.11 with having to set that property at all.

The only reason to set that property is when talking to a proxy over HTTP (not HTTPS). Usually, users would have already set up that information when configuring a connector. So, having to remember to set the field on the request as well was duplicate information, and easy to forget.

It was more painful if the connector knew to proxy only *some* requests, such as to specific hosts. Then users again needed to duplicate that information both for the connector and when creating a request.

In 0.12, since the `Connect` API was able to be updated, it was changed to allow a connector to indicate to the hyper `Client` that an established connection was to a proxy or not. It's pretty rare to want to send requests with absolute-form and origin-form to the same connection, so it's easier for users all around to just put that information in once, with the `Connect` API.

What this change means for Conduit is that in HTTP1, we'd treat "proxy" connections as separate from direct connections. (I haven't yet published 0.12, specifically so that this integration could have a chance to prove that I'm crazy and something can be changed.)

title: proxy: Make `outbound_updates_newer_services` test forward-compatible
body:
This is in preparation for landing the Tokio upgrade.

The test `discovery::outbound_updates_newer_services` currently contains an
assertion that an HTTP/2 request to an HTTP/1 service will return a response
with status code 500. This is because the current version of Hyper on which
Conduit depends does not support protocol upgrades.

However, commit hyperium/hyper@bc6af88a32e29e5a4f3719d8abc664f9ab10dddd, which
adds support for this kind of protocol upgrade, was recently merged to Hyper's
master branch. Therefore, this assertion will no longer be correct once we 
depend on the upcoming Hyper release. When we migrate to the new Tokio, it will
be necessary to upgrade our Hyper dependency as well, and this test will fail.

I've modified the test to no longer make assertions about the response's status
code, so that it's compatible with both the current and future Hyper versions.
If the response is not `Ok`, the test will still fail, since 
`tests::support::Client::request()` `expect`s that the response is successful,
but the status code is ignored. I've added a comment in the test explaining 
this.

Eventually, when the master version of Conduit depends on the latest Hyper, we
may want to change this test to assert that the status code is 200 instead. We
may also want to add more tests for Hyper's protocol upgrade functionality, but
that seems out of scope for this PR.

Signed-off-by: Eliza Weisman <eliza@buoyant.io>

title: proxy: rebind services on connect errors
body:
Instead of having connect errors destroy all buffered requests,
this changes Bind to return a service that can rebind itself when
there is a connect error.

It won't try to establish the new connection itself, but waits for
the buffer to poll again. Combing this with changes in tower-buffer
to remove canceled requests from the buffer should mean that we
won't loop on connect errors for forever.

Closes #899

(Currently, this yields to the executor, so any other work should be polled again first, and then this will get polled again...)

title: rfc: proxy: Split `control::discovery` into submodules
body:
While preparing #946, I was again struck by the `discovery` module being very weighty (nearly 800 dense lines). The intent of this change is only to improve readability. There are no functional changes. The following aesthetic changes have been made:

* `control::discovery` has been renamed to `control::destination` to be more consistent with the rest of conduit's terminology (destinations aren't the only thing that need to be discovered).
* In that vein, the `Discovery` type has been renamed `Resolver` (since it exposes one function, `resolve`).
* The `Watch` type has been renamed `Resolution`. This disambiguates the type form `futures_watch::Watch`(which is used in the same code) and makes it more clearly the product of a `Resolver`.
* The `Background` and `DiscoveryWork` names were very opaque.  `Background` is now `background::Config` to indicate that it can't actually _do_ anything; and `DiscoveryWork` is now `background::Process` to indicate that it's responsible for processing destination updates.
* `DestinationSet` is now a private implementation detail in the `background` module.
* An internal `ResolveRequest` type replaces an unnamed tuple (now that it's used across files).
* `rustfmt` has been run on `background.rs` and `endpoint.rs`

title: proxy: Drop destination resolutions when unused
body:
A proxy dispatches requests over a constrained number of routes. When
the router's upper bound is reached---and potentially in other future
scenarios---router capacity is created by removing unused routes, their
load balancers, and all related endpoint stacks.

However, in the current regime, the controller subsystem will continue
to monitor discovery observations. As the number of active observations
expands over time, the controller task ends up with more and more work
to do.

This change introduces a shared atomic boolean between the resolution
returned to the load balancer and the state maintained when
communicating with the service. Before the controller polls its active
resolutions, it first ensures that all unused resolutions are dropped.
author: olix0r

I want to make sure I understand the design here: The destination module doesn't try to bound its resource usage at all. Instead, it is the application's responsibility to ensure that it bounds its usage of the destination service. Conduit does this by enforcing bounds on the resource usage of load balancers, which are the consumers of the destination module. We plan to improve the destination module to ensure that its internals are well-bounded, e.g. by configuring the DNS resolver and the destination service gRPC client to limit their resource usage (the number of IP addresses they parse out of a response, raw maximum response size, etc.).

Either an explanation like that, or a correct one if that's incorrect, should be included in the module-level docs for the destination module.

comments.body: My understanding is that `mpsc::UnboundedSender::unbounded_send` returns [`SendError`](https://docs.rs/futures/0.1/futures/sync/mpsc/struct.SendError.html) if and only if the receiver has been dropped.  Is there any reason we can't simply use that to indicate that the receiver is gone, rather than adding the additional complexity of the `active` field?

comments.body:
> My understanding is that mpsc::UnboundedSender::unbounded_send returns SendError if (and only if) the receiver has been dropped. Is there any reason we can't simply use that to indicate that the receiver is gone, rather than adding the additional complexity of the active field?

Because we're trying to detect the opposite situation -- the receiver needs to be able to know whether there are senders.

Also, on the send-side, we might be able to check this using sender::poll_ready, but we need to be able to detect deactivation without actually sending an event.

comments.author: briansmith
comments.body: https://docs.rs/futures/0.1/futures/sync/mpsc/index.html provides some guidance on shutting things down.  It does seem like we're duplicating functionality provided by mpsc but I admit I haven't worked out how exactly to take advantage of the dropping logic that mpsc has.

comments.author: olix0r
comments.body:
OK, to summarize:

- We _do_ care about a _sender_ discovering when a _receiver_ has been dropped. But this shouldn't require an update to trigger this discovery. (i.e. we may not have something to send on that channel).
- `mpsc::sync::Sender` exposes `poll_ready` to ensure that the receiver has capacity, and will error if the receiver is gone.
- `mpsc::sync::UnboundedSender` does **not** expose `poll_ready`, but implements `Sink`.
- `Sink` exposes `poll_complete`, but this fn is not guaranteed to error unless there are pending items being sent.

Ideally, I think `UnboundedSender` needs to add a `poll_ready` that just calls the underlying sender's poll_ready, which ensures the receiver is still held.  In the short term, we can work around that. with our `Arc<()>` hack.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body:
This seems backwards? I expected this to work like so:

We want to know when an object has been dropped. That object should have an `Arc<()>` that it doesn't do anything with except drop when it itself is dropped.

Then the other side will hold a `Weak<()>`. Every time it tries to use the `Weak<()>` it has to upgrade it to an `Arc<>`. That upgrade will succeed if the object(s) on the other side haven't all been dropped yet. But, as soon as the other side is dropped, there will be no more `Arc<>`s and then upgrading the `Weak<()>` to an `Arc<()>` will return `None`. When that happens we know we can drop the destination.

title: proxy: Fix end events not firing when a stream is ended by a DATA frame
body:
A recent upstream change in `tower-h2` (tower-rs/tower-h2@d9b3140) caused some
HTTP/2 streams that were previously terminated by TRAILERS frames to be 
terminated by empty DATA frames with the end of stream bit set, instead.

This broke some tests in my dev branch for #944, as our test server also uses
`tower-h2`, and some of the metrics tests were no longer seeing the expected
`StreamResponseEnd` events due to this change. This issue may also occur in
other cases, resulting in incorrect metrics.

This PR changes `MeasuredBody::poll_data` to trigger the Stream End event if
it sees a DATA frame that ends the stream.

Fixes #954 

Signed-off-by: Eliza Weisman <eliza@buoyant.io>
author: hawkw

title: proxy: Remove configure-and-bind-to-executor pattern
body:
Requires #944.

A common pattern when using the old Tokio API was separating the configuration
of a task from binding it to an executor to run on. This was often necessary
when we wanted to construct a type corresponding to some task before the
reactor on which it would execute was initialized. Typically, this was 
accomplished with two separate types, one of which represented the 
configuration and exposed only a method to take a reactor `Handle` and
transform it to the other type, representing the actual task.

After we migrate to the new Tokio API in #944, executors no longer need to be
passed explictly, as we can use `DefaultExecutor::current` or 
`current_thread::TaskExecutor::current` to spawn a task on the current 
executor. Therefore, a lot of this complexity can be refactored away.

This PR refactors the `Config` and `Process` structs in
i`control::destination::background` into a single `Background` struct, and 
removes the `dns::Config` and `telemetry::MakeControl` structs (`dns::Resolver`
and `telemetry::Control` are now constructed directly). It should not cause
any functional changes.

Closes #966
