title: proxy: Honor TTLs for DNS responses
body:
Closes #711. Depends on #967.

This PR changes the proxy's `destination` module to honor the TTLs associated
with DNS lookups, now that bluejekyll/trust-dns#444 has been merged and we can
access this information from the Trust-DNS Resolver API. 

The `destination::background::DestinationSet` type has been modified so that, 
when a successful result is received for a DNS query, the DNS server will be 
polled again after the deadline associated with that query, rather than after
a fixed deadline. The fixed deadline is still used to determine when to poll
again for negative DNS responses or for errors.

Furthermore, Conduit now accepts an optional CONDUIT_PROXY_DNS_MIN_TTL 
environment variable that will configure a minimum TTL for DNS results. If the
deadline of a DNS response gives it a TTL shorter than the configured minimum,
Conduit will not poll DNS again until after that minimum TTL is elapsed. By
default, there is no minimum value set, as this feature is intended primarily
for when Conduit is run locally for development purposes.

Signed-off-by: Eliza Weisman <eliza@buoyant.io>
author: hawkw

comments.body:

programmatically seems rather difficult --- we'd either have to mock Conduit's

by mocking an entire DNS server. This also seems like a significant amount of
work to test a fairly straightforward change (and I noticed that very little of
the DNS code in Conduit has unit or e2e tests currently). Any input on easier 
ways of testing this change would be highly appreciated.

title: proxy: Alter telemetry to use discrete instants
body:
Proxy tasks emit events to the telemetry system. These events are used
aggregate counts and latencies, as well as to inform Tap requests.
Initially, these events included durations, describing the relevant time
that elapsed between this event and another.

This approach is somewhat inflexible -- it unnecessarily constrains the
set of measurements that can computed in the telemetry system.

To remedy this, the `Event` types can be changed to report discrete
`Instant`s (rather than `Duration`s). Then, when latencies are computed
in the telemetry system, these discrete instants can be compared to
produce durations.

There are no functional changes in this PR.

title: proxy: Record HTTP latency at first data frame
body:
Currently, the proxy records a request's latency as the time between
when a request is opened and when its response stream completes. This is
not what we intend to record, especially when a response is long-lived.

In order to more accurate record latency, we want to track the time at
which the first response body frame is received (which is a close
approximation of time-to-first-byte).

Telemetry aggregation has been changed to use the first-frame time to
compute latencies; tests have been updated to exercise this behavior; and
the metrics documentation has been updated to reflect this change.

Addresses #818 
Depends on #980

review_threads.body:

I *do* think that we should add `total_request_time_ns` back in at some point in the future though.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body:
I think it would be helpful to users to indicate that this is basically "time to first byte" except in the case where the server has sent an empty frame, and except for the fact that we're measuring from the time the request was *received* instead of from the time the request was *forwarded*, so this includes internal overhead of the proxy.

I suggest that we explain explicitly what this means for each of (1) HTTP/1 non-chunked transfer encoding, (2) HTTP/1 chunked transfer encoding, and (3) HTTP/2, and avoid using "frame" in the part that isn't specific to HTTP/2.

title: Add queries to prometheus to determine number of fully meshed requests
body:
In order to have an indication of what percentage of traffic is meshed, I've added another query to prometheus that determines how much of the traffic to/from the specified resource started and ended in the mesh.

At first I did this as a separate query from the client-side, but if this number is something we'll want to know for every stat query and for every combination of --to/--from flags, I decided it was better to put it alongside the existing `response_total` query. 

The stat query basically issues an additional `response_total` query that groups by `dst_` on the original resource being queried. Since we have the source and dst conduit namespace labels on these metrics, we can use those labels to determine how many requests start and end within the mesh. The tricky thing is wrangling what the behaviour of this additional query is when `--to` or `--from` is specified.

Conduit stat output:
```
$ go run cli/main.go stat deploy --api-addr localhost:8085 --kubeconfig ~/.kube/config --all-namespaces --from deploy/web
NAMESPACE   NAME     MESHED   SUCCESS      RPS   LATENCY_P50   LATENCY_P95   LATENCY_P99   SECURED
emojivoto   emoji       2/2   100.00%   1.8rps           5ms          11ms          18ms   100.00%
emojivoto   voting      2/2    89.09%   0.9rps           6ms          26ms          29ms   100.00%
```

This PR also modifies the web dashboard to display a column of `Secured` traffic (assumes all mesh traffic is TLS-ed by default; if that is not the case, we'll need to change that title).

Sometimes, the percent meshed shows up at >100% because the prometheus querys have occurred at slightly different instants. I believe we can fix this by adding a timestamp to the prometheus query so that the queries measure the same time.

![secured](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/549258/40389052-2a46d358-5dc6-11e8-8b7d-8e3051f47215.png)
author: rmars

comments.author: rmars
comments.body:
It's true that those requests don't differ a lot for the ones were we request *outbound* metrics, but for a 'normal' request (i.e. inbound stats, which is what we display for the web currently, e.g., `http://localhost:8084/api/stat?resource_type=deploy`), the original prometheus query is 

```
sum(increase(response_total{direction="inbound"}[1m])) by (namespace, deployment, classification)
```

But to get the percentage of traffic that started/ended in the mesh we would need the information from this query too:
```
sum(increase(response_total{direction="outbound"}[1m])) by (dst_namespace, dst_deployment, conduit_io_control_plane_ns, dst_conduit_io_control_plane_ns)
```
(because we need dst_ to determine whether the request started and ended in the mesh)

Of course, we could special case only making that one extra request for the inbound case, and save the extra query the other times. (Originally I'd thought that all the extra queries would have to be modified, and so added the query for all the cases).

comments.author: rmars
comments.body:
@siggy brought up a great point, which is that if we're using 'inbound' collected from one pod (e.g. `foo`) to report requests total, and 'outbound' collected from a bunch of other pods that send traffic to `foo`, that Prometheus will have different collection times for all of these metrics, making it impossible to actually make those numbers line up in a reasonable way.

I'm going to change the approach to assume a 'secured' flag will be set by the proxy for inbound and outbound requests, and work off that instead. That should simplify much of the code in `stat_summary.go`

title: proxy: Fix h1 body implementation
body:
In the h1-h2 glue code, we incorrectly called `is_empty()` to determine
if an H1 stream had ended. `is_empty` only returns true if there was no
body at all (rather than if the body has been fully consumed). This
causes H1 streams with bodies to be recorded incorrectly for telemetry.

By changing this to call `hyper::body::Payload::is_end_stream`, h1
bodies now behave the same as h2 bodies.

Relates to #994

title: proxy: Remove dynamic label updating on bound services
body:
Depends on tower-rs/tower#75. Required for #386

In order for the proxy to use the TLS support metadata from the Destination 
service correctly, we determined that the code for dynamically changing the
labels on an already-bound service should be removed, and any change in
metadata should cause an endpoint to be rebound.

I've modified the proxy so that we no longer update the labels using 
`futures-watch` (as a sidenote, we no longer depend on that crate). Metadata
update events now cause the `tower-discover::Discover` implementation for 
`DestinationSet` to re-insert the changed endpoint into the load balancer.
Upstream PR tower-rs/tower#75 in tower-balance changes the load balancer 
to honor duplicate insertions by replacing the old endpoint rather than 
ignoring them; that change is necessary for the tests to pass on this branch.
author: hawkw

comments.author: briansmith
comments.body:
First, let me make sure I'm remembering history correctly: Previously, we couldn't change tower to do the re-insertion thing, probably because of schedule pressure. The alternative we had was to either remove + add the endpoint from/to the load balancer, or not change anything. We were concerned that remove + add was the wrong thing to do because between the remove and the add, there might be a hole where we'd null-route the traffic. That's why `Cache` spends effort to translate `Add+Remove` sequences into `Change`s in the first place. However, we were still doing a wrong thing because we weren't rebinding on a `Change` event.

Now, we've fixed the load balancer to do re-insertion when the address is already bound. We still need to translate an "Add + Remove" from the destination service into a change that then gets translated into a re-insertion.

Is this all correct?

comments.author: olix0r
comments.body:
> Previously, we couldn't change tower to do the re-insertion thing, probably because of schedule pressure.

Not quite: previously, we thought this would be incorrect behavior for the balancer. After some usage, it seems clearer that `Discover` needs to handle deduping if it doesn't want the balancer to replace an entry.

title: Abstract I/O interface into a trait.
body:
Instead of pattern matching over an `Io` variant, use a `Box<Io>` to
abstract the I/O interface. This will make it easier to add a TLS
transport.
author: briansmith

comments.author: hawkw
comments.body:
@briansmith In order to review this change, I'd love some more context on why it's not sufficient to add more variants to the `Io` enum. 

Additionally, although I don't intend to base my review of this change on performance without actual measurements, I am _curious_ to hear about your intuitions are regarding the performance implications of using dynamic dispatch here.

comments.author: briansmith
comments.body:
> I am curious to hear about your intuitions are regarding the performance implications of using dynamic dispatch here.

I don't think there are any notable performance implications.

comments.author: briansmith
comments.body:
> why it's not sufficient to add more variants to the Io enum.

It would be sufficient.

comments.author: hawkw
comments.body:
@briansmith 
> > why it's not sufficient to add more variants to the Io enum.
>
> It would be sufficient.

That's fair, I suppose I should have asked why the trait object was _preferable_ to adding more variants. :)

comments.author: briansmith
comments.body:
> That's fair, I suppose I should have asked why the trait object was preferable to adding more variants. :)

I've written the TLS code both ways; I actually just wrote this PR this morning to clean up the Variant-based approach before submitting the TLS PRs themselves.

It's hard to answer these the question "How are TLS connections different and how are they treated differently than non-TLS connections?" with the Variant-based approach. I introduced the `Io` trait to show that what they have in common.

Once I added the `Io` trait I tried adding an `AddRef<Io>` function to the `Io` struct to replace all the `match` statements, to show that TLS and non-TLS connections are (currently) treated the exact same way, by changing every `match self.io { Io::Plain(ref x) => x.something() } ` to `self.io.as_ref().something()`. I think that makes the code clearer. That step itself added the dynamic dispatch. The benefit is that you don't have to review every single function call to see that TLS and non-TLS are treated exactly the same.

Then I just decided to replace the `AddRef` implementation with `Box` to avoid using *both* dynamic dispatch and a `match` for every method call, which was the worst of both words, at the cost of one heap allocation per connection, which won't matter in practice.

comments.author: hawkw
comments.body: Okay, thanks for explaining the rationale behind this, @briansmith! Given that, I agree that this seems like the right approach.

title: proto: Add TLS verification strategy to WeightedAddr message
body:
Required for #1008.

This PR adds the `TlsVerification` message to the Destination service proto,
to describe what strategy the proxy should use for verifying an endpoint's TLS
certificates. It also adds a `TlsVerification` field to the `WeightedAddr`
message.

Currently, there is one possible variant for `TlsVerification`, 
`KubernetesPodName`, which consists of the Kubernetes pod name of the endpoint
and the namespace of that pod's Conduit control plane. The proxy should attempt
to connect over TLS if the control plane namespace matches its own control
plane namespace. The pod name is used to verify the endpoint's TLS certificate.

See https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/issues/386#issuecomment-392948046.

This change was initially part of #1008, but I factored it out to make the diff
smaller.

Signed-off-by: Eliza Weisman <eliza@buoyant.io>
author: hawkw

comments.author: hawkw
comments.body:
@olix0r 
> Specfically, I'd want to ensure that a client that does not know how to read this field can continue to connect to destinations without honoring the tls validation

That's what I intended by using a `None` value for `TlsVerification` to indicate that TLS should not be used, rather than adding a `NoTls` or similar variant. 

That way, if the field can't be parsed or the client has an older version of the proto, it will default to not trying to use TLS.

title: Add initial infrastructure for optionally accepting TLS connections
body:
If the environment gives us the paths to the certificate chain and private key
then use TLS for all accepted TCP connections. Otherwise, continue on using
plaintext for all accepted TCP connections. The default behavior--no TLS--isn't
changed.

Later we'll make this smarter by adding protocol detection so that when the TLS
configuration is available, we'll accept both TLS and non-TLS connections.

Signed-off-by: Brian Smith <brian@briansmith.org>

title: proxy: Reload TLS config on changes
body:
This PR modifies the proxy's TLS code so that the TLS config files are reloaded
when any of them has changed (including if they did not previously exist).

If reloading the configs returns an error, we log an error and continue using
the old config.

Currently, this is implemented by polling the file system for the time they
were last modified at a fixed interval. However, I've implemented this so 
that the changes are passed around as a `Stream`, and that reloading and
updating the config is in a separate function the one that detects changes.
Therefore, it should be fairly easy to plug in support for `inotify` (and 
other FS watch APIs) later, as long as we can use them to generate a 
`Stream` of changes.

Closes #369

title: Stop cloning & hashing HTTP requests & related types.
body:
During code review of another change I noticed that a lot of types seem
to derive `Hash` (and `Eq`, `PartialEq`) even though the types should
never (for performance reasons) be used as keys of a hash table, and
where it is kind of questionable what equality should mean for those
types. Then I noticed that similarly many types implement `Clone` even
though I expect we should never be cloning them, again because of our
performance goals.

Because these types derive these traits, then whenever we add a field
to them, that field also has to implement these traits. That means we
then have to expand the problem, deriving implementations of these
traits for types that don't otherwise want/need to implement these
traits. This makes review complicated, because, for example, we have
to decide whether something should be compared case-insensitively or
case-sensitively when really we don't want to compare those things at
all.

To prove that we can get by by doing less, to speed up code review
(particularly related to some stuff related to TLS), stop deriving
`Clone`, `Eq`, `PartialEq`, and `Hash` for these types.

I believe that, in particular, the change to key the Tap hash table
based on request ID, instead of the whole request, should speed up
the tap feature since we don't hash and/or compare every field,
recursively, of requests.

Later, more such cleanup of this sort should be done.

Signed-off-by: Brian Smith <brian@briansmith.org>
author: briansmith

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: I think it might be more efficient to avoid storing the request ID twice, once as the key, and once as a field inside the value. I thought about creating a `RequestById(ctx::http::RequestId)` type that manually forwards `Hash`, `Eq`, `PartialEq`, to `self.0`, but it seems like that's a lot of boilerplate and there must be some way to avoid that boilerplate. Suggestions?

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: Note that I think we can/should eventually abstract this pattern out into a reusable trait, something like `trait IdentifiedByField<T: Hash + Eq + PartialEq + Clone> { id(&'a self) -> 'a T }`, but I didn't want to bog this down.

title: Implement `dns::Name` using webpki's `DNSName`.
body:
webpki's DNSName type does full validation and normalization (lowercasing) of
DNS names, which is exactly what `dns::Name` does. webpki's DNSName type
considers a DNS name to be valid according to the rules for TLS certificates,
which is slightly stricter than what a DNS library might otherwise allow. In
anticipation of possible compatibility issues, introduce separate tls::DnsName
and dns::Name names for this type. In the future, if we find that tls::DnsName
is too strict for non-TLS cases, we can have these types diverge without
affecting TLS validation.

title: Rename Lister to API and expose both listers and informers
body:
All of our controller services except the destination service use [Lister](https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/blob/master/controller/k8s/lister.go) to do cached reads against the Kubernetes API, leveraging shared informers from the [k8s.io/client-go/informers](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/tree/master/informers) package. The [GenericInformer](https://godoc.org/k8s.io/client-go/informers#GenericInformer) interface provides both an `Informer()` func for accessing the [SharedIndexInformer](https://godoc.org/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache#SharedIndexInformer) interface and a `Lister()` func for accessing the [GenericLister](https://godoc.org/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache#GenericLister) interface. To date, however, our `Lister` implementation has only provided access to the `GenericLister` interface for each resource type.

In order to move the destination service over to using shared informers, it's going to require access to the `SharedIndexInformer` interface for the endpoint and pod resources. In this branch, I'm renaming `Lister` to `API` and refactoring it to provide access to the `GenericInformer` interface instead of the `GenericLister` interface for each resource, which will allow us to use `API` for both listers and informers.

As part of this change I've added some test helpers to remove some of the redundancy that we had using shared informers in our tests.
author: klingerf

comments.author: klingerf
comments.body: #1073 has a concrete example of how we'll use this change when refactoring the destination service.

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body: curious about moving `sharedInformers.Start()` from `NewAPI()` to `Sync()`. since `Sync()` is called asynchronously in our servers, i'm wondering if there could be a timing issue where our server processes could start trying to interact with the `k8s.API` object prior to `Sync()` (and thus `sharedInformers.Start()`) getting called.

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
Good question -- what you describe is exactly the intent of this change. We can't call `sharedInformers.Start()` until all indexers and event handlers have been added. So for instance in #1073, the destination server adds an indexer by calling:

```
	k8sAPI.Pod.Informer().AddIndexers(cache.Indexers{"ip": indexPodByIp})
```

That call to `AddIndexers` has to happen before calling `sharedInformers.Start()`. This configuration wouldn't work if `sharedInformers.Start()` happened when the k8sAPI object was created.

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body: since the clients of `k8s.API` are now calling `Lister()` themselves, was there any issue with this happening after calls to `sharedInformers.Start(nil)` ?

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body: As far as I can tell, all of the clients of `k8s.API` only call `Lister()` in the request path, so the behavior should be unchanged, assuming the process calls `Sync()` before serving requests. This totally relates to #1013, however. It's definitely the case that some or our controller components can serve requests before the caches are fully synced, and we should fix this with readiness probes that fail until caches are synced.

title: proxy: Canonicalize TLS config paths before polling filesystem metadata
body:
This branch changes the polling-based implementation of TLS config file watches
to fully canonicalize the path to each config file prior to polling for its
metadata. Doing so fixes the issues detecting changes when the watched path is
a symbolic link to another symbolic link (see #1061), which is how Kubernetes
implements ConfigMaps mounted as volumes.

I've manually tested this with Conduit running in Docker for Mac Kubernetes,
by volume-mounting a ConfigMap containing the TLS config files, and 
regenerating, deleting, and adding the certificates. Watching the Conduit logs
confirms that the changes are now successfully detected.

Note that we have to re-canonicalize the path every time we poll the filesystem
for metadata. Otherwise, if the file is a symlink and the link target changes,
we will continue polling the _old_ link target's path, and fail to detect any
changes to the _new_ link target.

Signed-off-by: Eliza Weisman <eliza@buoyant.io>
author: hawkw

If the file changed, we log the last modified time [on line 105](https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/pull/1076/files/c8e74574baf42e7f1770f18b6dd3bcdd077e2ad6#diff-a4b5d277de7db26e1d308626fdad076aR105) still.

title: proxy: detect TLS configuration changes using inotify on Linux
body:
This branch adds an inotify-based implementation of filesystem watches
for the TLS config files. On Linux, where inotify is available, this is
used instead of the polling-based code I added in #1056 and #1076.

In order to avoid the issues detecting changes to files in Kubernetes 
ConfigMaps described in #1061, we watch the directory _containing_ the
files we care about rather than the files themselves. I've tested this 
manually in Docker for Mac Kubernetes and can confirm that ConfigMap
changes are detected successfully.

Note that this currently depends on code added to the `inotify` crate in 
my upstream pull request inotify-rs/inotify#103, rather than the version
on crates.io.

Closes #1061. Closes #369.

title: Fix conduit health grafana dashboard
body:
*Problem*
In the conduit health dashboard, we were making queries such as:
```
sum(irate(request_total{deployment=\"$deployment\", direction=\"inbound\"}[30s])) by (deployment, pod)
```
for every `$deployment` associated with conduit. Unfortunately, if another deployment in another namespace was present with the same name as a conduit controller deployment, its stats would get included as well.

*Fix*
Scope the prometheus queries to a conduit controller namespace by adding `namespace=\"$namespace\"` to the queries.

Adds a `Conduit Namespace` grafana variable on this page, so that we can use a prometheus query to determine the conduit namespace(s) available to get data from. (If there is more than one conduit install, you can switch between conduit namespaces)

![screen shot 2018-06-07 at 4 31 25 pm](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/549258/41131853-70219a6c-6a72-11e8-9927-e810d9403411.png)

title: Add a script for running proxy tests in Docker
body:
When developing features in the proxy, that rely on Linux-only OS features,
developers using other operating systems may find it inconvenient to test
their changes. While we run CI builds on Linux, and may have access to Linux
testing environments, this is not as tightly integrated into the proxy 
development workflow as running a quick `cargo test` on the host OS.

For example, I found it inconvenient to test the `inotify` based filesystem
watch code I've been adding in recent commits, and had to do things like
opening a WIP PR for a branch to get CI to run the tests. This workflow is not
ideal.

This PR adds an (admittedly somewhat hacky) script and Dockerfile for running
the proxy's tests in Docker. This accomplishes approximately the same goal as 
the `PROXY_SKIP_TESTS` flag that we used to have, but with the advantage that 
we no longer include the test dependencies in release builds. 

Of course, this also means that we no longer share any of the dependencies 
between the test docker build and the release docker build, which is a shame. 
It might be worthwhile to re-introduce a dependencies image so that cached
builds of the proxy's dependencies can be shared between the test and release
Dockerfiles. However, I thought that deserved to be discussed separately from
the changes I made in this branch.

Signed-off-by: Eliza Weisman <eliza@buoyant.io>

title: Move controller/util and web/util packages to pkg
body:
In the process of refactoring the destination service (#1073 and #1079), I realized that we have multiple different utility packages throughout the project, as follows:

* `controller/util`
* `controller/api/util`
* `web/util`
* `pkg/...`

Since these packages aren't very well scoped, we have a few unexpected dependencies. For instance, the `web` process depends on both the `web/util` and `controller/util` packages, which doesn't seem right.

In this branch I'm removing the `web/util` and `controller/util` packages, in favor of more narrowly-scoped packages in the the top-level `pkg` directory: `addr`, `filesonly`, and `prometheus`.

---

For reference, prior to the destination service refactor, our package dependency graph looked like this:

![old](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/9226/41309555-e9a159c6-6e33-11e8-85c1-4d7279d475df.png)

Now it looks like this:

![new](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/9226/41309564-f2380f62-6e33-11e8-8920-9094cad450a5.png)

There's still some additional room for improvement that we should pursue in follow-up branches.

What are we trying to accomplish with this? I agree that it is kind of silly to have a separate crate for this but it also seems bad to duplicate it.

I don't believe having it as a separate trait is really conferring any benefit to us now. Instead, I suggest we just don't use the `TryFrom` trait in the GRPC bindings module; instead we can just implement `try_from` as a regular method on the types that implement it.

title: Propagate errors in conduit containers to the api
body:
- It would be nice to display container errors in the UI. This PR gets the pod's container statuses and passes them through.
- Also add a `terminationMessagePolicy` so that we can capture the proxy's
error messages. 

From [the docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/debug-application-cluster/determine-reason-pod-failure/):
> users can set the terminationMessagePolicy field of a Container for further customization. This field defaults to “File” which means the termination messages are retrieved only from the termination message file. By setting the terminationMessagePolicy to “FallbackToLogsOnError”, you can tell Kubernetes to use the last chunk of container log output if the termination message file is empty and the container exited with an error. The log output is limited to 2048 bytes or 80 lines, whichever is smaller

There are several places we could put this check; it doesn't have to be a part of the `Stat` api. However, if we want to display errors per row of the various tables in the UI, I think we'll want the error information to come back with the same API call as the stats.

title: Allow k8s API clients to watch a subset of resources
body:
In this branch I'm updating `k8s.NewAPI` to accept a list of resource types to watch when configuring a new API client. This will allow clients to only watch the resource types that they require, resulting in fewer API calls overall. It will also allow us to more tightly scope RBAC configurations for these components when they're running under different service accounts.

As part of this change, I'm also adding a config map resource type, which is required for #675.

Fixes #1114.

title: proxy: Fix Inotify falling back to polling when files don't exist yet
body:
This PR changes the proxy's Inotify watch code to avoid always falling back to
polling the filesystem when the watched files don't exist yet. It also contains
some additional cleanup and refactoring of the inotify code, including moving
the non-TLS-specific filesystem watching code out of the `tls::config` module
and into a new `fs_watch` module.

In addition, it adds tests for both the polling-based and inotify-based watch
implementations, and changes the polling-based watches to hash the files rather
than using timestamps from the file's metadata to detect changes. These changes
are originally from #1094 and #1091, respectively, but they're included here
because @briansmith asked that all the changes be made in one PR.

Closes #1094. Closes #1091. Fixes #1090. Fixes #1097. Fixes #1061.

Signed-off-by: Eliza Weisman <eliza@buoyant.io>
author: hawkw

title: proto: Use explicit `go_package` option
body:
protobuf has a `go_package` option that can be used to explicitly name
Go packages such that they can be imported without additional rewrites.

This allows us to store proto files without additional, redundant
directories (which were used for packaging hints, previously).

This change adds an explicit `go_package` to all .proto files and
updates `bin/protoc-go.sh` to ensure these packages are output into
$GOPATH (so that the go_package can be absolute). This removes the need
to manually rewrite imports in bin/protoc-go.sh.

title: proxy: add HTTP/1.1 Upgrade support automatically
body:
Any HTTP/1.1 requests seen by the proxy will automatically set up
to prepare such that if the proxied responses agree to an upgrade,
the two connections will converted into a standard TCP proxy duplex.

## Implementation

This adds a new type, `transparency::Http11Upgrade`, which is a sort of rendezvous type for triggering HTTP/1.1 upgrades. In the h1 server service, if a request looks like an upgrade (`h1::wants_upgrade`), the request body is decorated with this new `Http11Upgrade` type. It is actually a pair, and so the second half is put into the request extensions, so that the h1 client service may look for it right before serialization. If it finds the half in the extensions, it decorates the *response* body with that half (if it looks like a response upgrade (`h1::is_upgrade`)).

The `HttpBody` type now has a `Drop` impl, which will look to see if its been decorated with an `Http11Upgrade` half. If so, it will check for hyper's new `Body::on_upgrade()` future, and insert that into the half. 

When both `Http11Upgrade` halves are dropped, its internal `Drop` will look to if both halves have supplied an upgrade. If so, the two `OnUpgrade` futures from hyper are joined on, and when they succeed, a `transparency::tcp::duplex()` future is created. This chain is spawned into the default executor.

The `drain::Watch` signal is carried along, to ensure upgraded connections still count towards active connections when the proxy wants to shutdown.

Closes #195
author: seanmonstar

comments.author: briansmith
comments.body: I didn't look at the code in the PR, just the description. What happens for HTTP/1.0 when upgrades are attempted?

comments.author: seanmonstar
comments.body:
@briansmith HTTP/1.0 does not specify upgrades (neither the `Upgrade` header, nor 1xx response codes). The `h1::wants_upgrade` check in this PR checks for `HTTP/1.1`, and if not found, it does our current default of stripping "connection" headers (which should include a refer to `Upgrade`).

[RFC 7231](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7231#section-6.2) claims:

> Since HTTP/1.0 did not define any 1xx status codes, a server MUST NOT send a 1xx response to an HTTP/1.0 client.

However, we don't currently intercept status codes and cancel responses in that way.

comments.author: briansmith
comments.body:
> The h1::wants_upgrade check in this PR checks for HTTP/1.1, and if not found, it does our current default of stripping "connection" headers (which should include a refer to Upgrade).

That seems like the right thing to me.

What about the case where the request includes `Upgrade` but it isn't in the `Connection` header, both for HTTP/1.0 and for HTTP/1.1?

comments.author: seanmonstar
comments.body:
> What about the case where the request includes Upgrade but it isn't in the Connection header, both for HTTP/1.0 and for HTTP/1.1?

So far, we only look at the `Connection` header and remove headers that it references. Technically upgrades require a `Connection: upgrade` header. For example, from the [Websocket RFC 6455](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6455#section-4.1):

> 5. The request MUST contain an |Upgrade| header field whose value MUST include the "websocket" keyword.
>
> 6. The request MUST contain a |Connection| header field whose value MUST include the "Upgrade" token.


However, it definitely does seem possible that clients in the real world could forget it. We could add an extra check when stripping connection headers, to make sure `Upgrade` is always removed also. 

Currently in this PR, if seeing a request like this:

```
GET /chat HTTP/1.X
Upgrade: websocket
```

- if `HTTP/1.1`, the proxy would pass along the header, and if the server responded with a 101 anyways, then we'd just assume an upgrade.
- If `HTTP/1.0`, the header would still be passed along, but the proxy would not have prepared for an upgrade, and so the connection could end up closed after writing back a 101 response (this is because hyper knows that if a 101 is written, but nothing handles an upgrade, there's nothing more to be done in HTTP).

comments.author: briansmith
comments.body:
I think that if the Upgrade header, or any hop-by-hop header that is required to be in `Connection`, is present, and it isn't in Connection, then we should reject the request with 400 Bad Request or similar.

Note that it isn't just the case where somebody might have forgotten to send the Upgrade header. It might be the case that another proxy accidentally forwarded the Upgrade header after stripping Connection, and doesn't actually expect an upgrade to happen. Or, a malicious client might be trying to trick us in some way.

comments.author: seanmonstar
comments.body: I agree with the sentiment. At the same time, it conflicts with the transparency goal we've often cited, which is that if it worked when the proxy wasn't in the way, it should still work after injecting. Granted, there are always going to be cases where that's not going to be true, but deciding how best to enforce that goal can be tricky.

comments.author: briansmith
comments.body: That's a good point. We should at least document somewhere these decision points so that we can consider them later. No need to hold this PR up to figure out a final answer about how to resolve such conflicts.

comments.author: seanmonstar
comments.body:
It seems like we would encounter `Upgrade` requests more often at ingress positions, as then the proxy would be talking to browsers (and ~~evil doers~~ outsiders) more. Also, HTTP Upgrades seem to be almost always Websockets (could be h2c), which is very strict about acceptance. There *could* be custom formats that companies are using internally that might be more lenient, and it'd be unfortunate to break them...

So I looked at a couple of other proxies to see what they do:

- nginx seems to only look at the `Upgrade` header, from what I can see, and only if configured to pass it along. Otherwise, it's stripped before forwarding.
- Envoy requires explicit configuration of a Websocket route. If configured so, it will look for exactly a `Connection` header with `upgrade` in it, and `Upgrade: websocket`. If both are found, it converts to Websockets. If both are not found, or Websocket hasn't been configured, both the `Connection` header and `Upgrade` are always stripped before forwarding.

comments.author: seanmonstar
comments.body: OK, I think it makes sense to consider and enable `CONNECT` support in a separate PR, and otherwise, this patch has been cleaned up. The release of hyper 0.12.2 should happen shortly, but besides this, this could use a review.

title: proxy: Add process stats to proxy metrics (on Linux)
body:
This branch adds process stats to the proxy's metrics, as described in
https://prometheus.io/docs/instrumenting/writing_clientlibs/#process-metrics.

In particular, it adds metrics for the process's total CPU time, number of 
open file descriptors and max file descriptors, virtual memory size, and 
resident set size.

This branch adds a dependency on the `procinfo` crate. Since this crate and the
syscalls it wraps are Linux-specific, these stats are only reported on Linux.
On other operating systems, they aren't reported.

Signed-off-by: Eliza Weisman <eliza@buoyant.io>

## Manual testing

Metrics scrape:
```
eliza@ares:~$ curl http://localhost:4191/metrics
# HELP process_cpu_seconds_total Total user and system CPU time spent in seconds.
# TYPE process_cpu_seconds_total counter
process_cpu_seconds_total 0
# HELP process_open_fds Number of open file descriptors.
# TYPE process_open_fds gauge
process_open_fds 19
# HELP process_max_fds Maximum number of open file descriptors.
# TYPE process_max_fds gauge
process_max_fds 1024
# HELP process_virtual_memory_bytes Virtual memory size in bytes.
# TYPE process_virtual_memory_bytes gauge
process_virtual_memory_bytes 45252608
# HELP process_resident_memory_bytes Resident memory size in bytes.
# TYPE process_resident_memory_bytes gauge
process_resident_memory_bytes 12132352
# HELP process_start_time_seconds Time that the process started (in seconds since the UNIX epoch)
# TYPE process_start_time_seconds gauge
process_start_time_seconds 1529017536
```
Note that the `process_cpu_seconds_total` stat is 0 because I just launched this conduit instance and it's not seeing any load; it does go up after i sent a few requests to it.

Confirm RSS & virtual memory stats w/ `ps`, and get Conduit's pid so we can check the fd stats
(note that `ps` reports virt/rss in kb while Conduit's metrics reports them in bytes):
```
eliza@ares:~$ ps aux | grep conduit | grep -v grep
eliza    16766  0.0  0.0  44192 12956 pts/2    Sl+  16:05   0:00 target/debug/conduit-proxy
```

Count conduit process's open fds:
```
eliza@ares:~$ cd /proc/16766/fd
eliza@ares:/proc/16766/fd$ ls -l | wc -l
18
```
author: hawkw

comments.author: hawkw
comments.body: The reason that the proxy reports 1 more open fd than `ls` sees in `/proc/../fd` is because in order to count the number of fds, the proxy opens `/proc/self/fd`to count them. comments.author: hawkw
comments.body:
@olix0r
>what's the semantic difference between trust anchors and a cert store? 

It seems like the `RootCertStore` is a container of multiple trust anchors. The `rustls` documentation says it's
> A container for root certificates able to provide a root-of-trust for connection authentication.

I'm sure @briansmith can explain in much greater detail!

comments.author: briansmith
comments.body:
> for my own edification, what's the semantic difference between trust anchors and a cert store? I take it that a cert store is a superset? What else might it contain?

"Trust anchor" refers to the CAs that are inherently trusted, i.e. root CAs. Most software we're familiar with represents trust anchors as self-signed X.509 certificates, usually in a file of concatenated PEM encodings of them.

Much (usually most) of the information in an X.509 certificate is irrelevant for a trust anchor (a.k.a. root CA). For example, tie signature is irrelevant because the certificate is signed with its own key.

In `webpki` the `TrustAnchor` type models precisely what is useful to know about a trust anchor. If one is so inclined, one could extract the useful information out of a self-signed root CA certificate and throw away the unuseful information. This is what the `webpki-roots` crate does, which is why it is less than half the size of Mozilla root CA store (which stores the entire self-signed certificate for each trust anchor).

The webpki crate and *ring* were originally written and optimized for applications running on small embedded devices where such things mattered. (That's why they spend the effort to minimize the size of the trust anchors, why they allow for the trust anchors to be embedded statically in the application, and why they they're designed, overall, to minimize code bloat.)

title: proxy: Fix false positives in polling-based fs watches
body:
There are currently two issues which can lead to false positives (changes being
reported when files have not actually changed) in the polling-based filesystem
watch implementation. 

The first issue is that when checking each watched file for changes, the loop
iterating over each path currently short-circuits as soon as it detects a 
change. This means that if two or more files have changed, the first time we
poll the fs, we will see the first change, then if we poll again, we will see
the next change, and so on. 

This branch fixes that issue by always hashing all the watched files, even if a
change has already been detected. This way, if all the files change between one
poll and the next, we no longer generate additional change events until a file
actually changes again.

The other issue is that the old implementation would treat any instance of a 
"file not found" error as indicating that the file had been deleted, and 
generate a change event. This leads to changes repeatedly being detected as
long as a file does not exist, rather than a single time when the file's 
existence state actually changes.

This branch fixes that issue as well, by only generating change events on
"file not found" errors if the file existed the last time it was polled. 
Otherwise, if a file did not previously exist, we no longer generate a new 
event.

I've verified both of these fixes through manual testing, as well as a new
test for the second issue. The new test fails on master but passes on this
branch.

Signed-off-by: Eliza Weisman <eliza@buoyant.io>

title: Don't panic on stats that aren't included in StatAllResourceTypes
body:
*Problem*
When we run `conduit stat ...`, the `writeStatsToBuffer` function would go through `StatAllResourceTypes` and print all the resources that were there. `namespaces` is not in `StatAllResourceTypes` however, so no stats are written to the buffer. This causes the buffer length to be 0, which causes a panic when we try to do `out := string(buffer.Bytes()[padding:])`

This bug was introduced by https://github.com/runconduit/conduit/pull/1088/files

*Solution*
Fix `writeStatsToBuffer` to not depend on what resources are in `StatAllResourceTypes`.
Also add a `stat` test that would fail on current master. We do already have an integration test for stat, but no unit tests.

Fixes #1151

title: proxy: re-enabled vectored writes through our dynamic Io trait object.
body:
This adds `Io::write_buf_erased` that doesn't required `Self: Sized`, so
it can be called on trait objects. By using this method, specialized
methods of `TcpStream` (and others) can use their `write_buf` to do
vectored writes.

Since it can be easy to forget to call `Io::write_buf_erased` instead of
`Io::write_buf`, the concept of making a `Box<Io>` has been made
private. A new type, `BoxedIo`, implements all the super traits of `Io`,
while making the `Io` trait private to the `transport` module. Anything
hoping to use a `Box<Io>` can use a `BoxedIo` instead, and know that
the write buf erase dance is taken care of.

Adds a test to `transport::io` checking that the dance we've done does
indeed call the underlying specialized `write_buf` method.

Closes #1162

title: Add controller admin servers and readiness probes
body:
This branch introduces a new package, `pkg/admin`, which our go processes can use to run an admin server. The admin server has the following three endpoints:

* `/metrics` -- prometheus metrics
* `/ping` -- liveliness check
* `/ready` -- readiness check

The `/ping` endpoint is a no-op at this point, but we might want to make that more sophisticated as part of #1116.

For controller components that sync with Kubernetes, the `/ready` endpoint doesn't return ready until the caches are fully synced.

I've also updated our install configs to configure the checks accordingly.

Fixes #1013.

title: proxy: Fall back to plaintext communication when a TLS handshake fails
body:
This branch modifies the proxy's logic for opening a connection so
that when an attempted TLS handshake fails, the proxy will retry that
connection without TLS.

This is implemented by changing the `UpgradeToTls` case in the `Future`
implementation for `Connecting`, so that rather than simply wrapping
a poll to the TLS upgrade future with `try_ready!` (and thus failing
the future if the upgrade future fails), we reset the state of the
future to the `Plaintext` state and continue looping. The `tls_status`
field of the future is changed to `ReasonForNoTls::HandshakeFailed`,
and the `Plaintext` state is changed so that if its `tls_status` is
`HandshakeFailed`, it will no longer attempt to upgrade to TLS when the
laintext connection is successfully established. This also ensures that
any subsequent telemetry events generated by that connection are labeled
with `tls="handshake_failed"`.

Closes #1084 

Signed-off-by: Eliza Weisman <eliza@buoyant.io>
author: hawkw

comments.author: olix0r
comments.body: This looks fine to me. I'd like to test it before merging

title: proxy: Rebind endpoint stacks on TLS config changes using WatchService
body:
This branch changes the proxy's `Bind` module to add a middleware layer 
which watches for TLS cliend configuration changes and rebinds the 
endpoint stacks of any endpoints with which it is able to communicate with over 
TLS (i.e. those with `TlsIdentity` metadata) when the client config changes. The 
rebinding is done at the level of individual endpoint stacks, rather than for the
entire service stack for the destination.

This obsoletes my previous PRs #1169 and #1175.

Closes #1161

title: Proxy: Add parser to distinguish proxy TLS traffic from other traffic.
body:
Distinguish incoming TLS traffic intended for the proxy to terminate
from TLS traffic intended for the proxied service to terminate and from
non-TLS traffic.

The new version of `untrusted` is required for this to work.

Signed-off-by: Brian Smith <brian@briansmith.org>
author: briansmith

review_threads.author: olix0r
review_threads.body:
While `Async` does model your states nicely, it seems incorrect to use it here. When I see `Async`, I automatically assume that we are beholden to the constraints of operating within a future: that this must be called from the context of a task, and that the caller will receive a notification when the function should be called again.  Granted, it's hard to assume the latter from this API; but I think it would be less confusing to use a one-off enum:


```rust
pub enum ClientHelloMatch {
  Incomplete,
  Matched,
  NotMatched,
}
```

Or something to this effect

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: OK, I also had similar misgivings. I changed it to be as you suggested, though I shorted the name to `Match`.

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body: NIT: I'm not very familiar with `untrusted`, so I don't know how _much_ less safe `as_slice_less_safe` is, but, generally I'd like to see a comment explaining why a function with "less safe" in its name is being used...

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: Fair. It is explained in the `untrusted` documentation at https://briansmith.org/rustdoc/untrusted/: "untrusted.rs goes beyond Rust's normal safety guarantees by also guaranteeing that parsing will be panic-free, as long as untrusted::Input::as_slice_less_safe() is not used." Basically when using `untrusted` we try to expose the input only as `untrusted::Input` and `untrusted::Reader` to ensure there are no bounds checking panics. When we can't do that, e.g. because we need to interact with an API that doesn't take `untrusted::Input` as a parameter, then we have to give up the panic-safety, and that's what this name indicates.

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body: TIOLI: This parser is fairly understandable (and the comments make it more so!) but I wonder if giving some of these closures names by assigning them to `let` bindings (or just making them local functions) would make it even clearer? Just a thought; perhaps it would only complicate things.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: I think there's definitely stuff that could be done to make this clearer but I don't think reorganizing it like that is going to have a large enough benefit to justify any more delay. In the future we'll probably extend this parser to do more interesting things; I suggest we consider refactoring it at that point. WDYT?

We would need way less than 8192. I have a branch around somewhere to decrease this size, but  I kept it that size since I didn't know how it would impact the current (HTTP) protocol disambiguation.

title: proxy: Fix ConditionallyUpgradeServerToTls not being notified
body:
#1203 introduced a bug in the implementation of `Future` for 
`connection::ConditionallyUpgradeServerToTls`. If the attempt to match
the current peek buffer was incomplete, the `Future` implementation
would return `Ok(Async::NotReady)`. This results in the task yielding.
However, in this case the task would not be notified again, as the 
`NotReady` state wasn't from an underlying IO resource. Instead, the
would _never_ be ready.

This branch fixes this issue by simply continuing the loop, so that 
we instead try to read more bytes from the socket and try to match
again, until the match is successful or the _socket_ returns `NotReady`.

Signed-off-by: Eliza Weisman <eliza@buoyant.io>

body:
This branch adds a new `TlsIdentity` strategy to the destination service: `K8sPodIdentity`. The `K8sPodIdentity` strategy sends back a fully-qualified pod identity string in the following format:

```
{pod_name}.{pod_type}.{pod_ns}.conduit-managed.{controller_ns}.svc.cluster.local
```

review_threads.body: We could eventually remove `K8sPodNamespace`, once the proxy is updated to stop using that strategy.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: Yes, I already have a similar, but different, change queued up. I'll rebase it on top of this.

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
Note that this sends back the following labels for the owner segment of the identity string:

* deployment
* replication_controller
* replica_set
* k8s_job
* daemon_set
* stateful_set

That matches the `dst_*` labels that are exported to prometheus, but the underscores might be problematic. If we need those segments to be represented differently, I suggest we try to tackle #740 to fix it.

review_threads.author: briansmith
review_threads.body: Right now the DNS label validator in the proxy accepts underscores in DNS labels, even though various DNS specs say that they are not legal. I would like to use only 100% valid DNS labels, but that's really an aesthetic thing that's relatively unimportant, so we can/should address #740 asynchronously with this.

I'm worried that if we start introducing multiple different strings representing the same pod owner, we'll have trouble keeping track of which type of string representation we're expecting. I think we need a more holistic approach to addressing that, which is covered in #740 (and related to #741).

title: Proxy: Get identity of pod & controller from configuration.
body:
Instead of attempting to construct identities itself, have the proxy
accept fully-formed identities from whatever configures it. This allows
us to centralize the formatting of the identity strings in the Go code
that is shared between the `conduit inject`, `conduit install`, and CA
components.

One wrinkle: The pod namespace isn't necessarily available at
`conduit inject` time, so the proxy must implement a simple variable
substitution mechanism to insert the pod namespace into its identity.

This has the side-effect of enabling TLS to the controller since the
controller's identity is now available.

Signed-off-by: Brian Smith <brian@briansmith.org>

title: Fix issue with injected resource name, add test
body:
I noticed that the inject output with `--tls optional` appears to be missing the service name when formulating the TLS identity string. For instance:

```
$ bin/conduit inject --tls optional cli/cmd/testdata/inject_emojivoto_deployment.input.yml | grep -EA1 '(secretName|CONDUIT_PROXY_TLS_POD_IDENTITY)'
        - name: CONDUIT_PROXY_TLS_POD_IDENTITY

        - name: CONDUIT_PROXY_TLS_POD_IDENTITY

--

title: Fix bug in public-api stat_summary tests
body:
I realized that our stat summary expectation checker would only check the actual proto responses against the expectations if the expectations were non-empty. 

## Problem

The problem is this line:
```
if len(exp.expectedResponse.GetOk().StatTables) > 0 {
```
So if we expected empty results and the api returned actual results, we never actually check those results against the expectations.

The bug can be reproduced by replacing any nonzero metric we expect in `expectedResponse`  with 
`expectedResponse: genEmptyResponse(),`. The tests on master will still pass.

## Solution

Remove this line and ensure we get the expected number of stat tables.

title: proxy: Handle connection close during TLS detection
body:
During protocol detection, we buffer data to detect a TLS Client Hello
message. If the client disconnects while this detection occurs, we do
not properly handle the disconnect, and the proxy may busy loop.

To fix this, we must handle the case where `read(2)` returns 0 by
creating a `Connection` with the already-closed socket.

While doing this, I've moved some of the implementation of
`ConditionallyUpgradeServerToTls::poll` into helpers on
`ConditionallyUpgradeServerToTlsInner` so that the poll method is easier
to read, hiding the inner details from the polling logic.

title: proxy: Fix out-of-control inotify CPU use
body:
The `inotify-rs` library's `EventStream` implementation currently 
calls `task::current().notify()` in a hot loop when a poll returns
`WouldBlock`, causing the task to constantly burn CPU. 

This branch updates the `inotify-rs` dependency to point at a branch
of `inotify-rs` I had previously written. That branch  rewrites the 
`EventStream` to use `mio` to  register interest in the `inotify` file 
descriptor instead, fixing the out-of-control polling. 

When inotify-rs/inotify#105 is merged upstream, we can go back to 
depending on the master version of the library.

Fixes #1261

Signed-off-by: Eliza Weisman <eliza@buoyant.io>

title: Ensure destination service always sends pod metadata
body:
The destination service previously used an in-memory index of pods by IP to return pod metadata as part of address updates streamed back to the proxies. This meant that if we couldn't find a pod by IP, we'd end up sending back an address without any metadata, which is problematic for stats collection and TLS.

It turns out the pod IP index was extraneous, since the endpoints update event that the destination service receives from the Kubernetes API contains a pod owner reference in addition to the pod's IP. In this branch I'm removing the index by IP, and updating the endpoint watcher to also find the associated pods when an endpoints update is received. If a pod cannot be found, then it is skipped until the next endpoints update. Testing locally I haven't observed any instances where the pod cannot be found, which suggests to me that the primary pod index is more reliable than the secondary index by IP that we were previously using.

Fixes #783.
Fixes #1264.

comments.author: siggy
comments.body:
> Why are these ClusterRoles in the first place? Can't they be just normal roles in the namespace of the control plane?

Unfortunately we need `ClusterRole`'s because our `ServiceAccount`'s (`conduit-controller`, `conduit-prometheus`, `conduit-ca`)  need access to all k8s objects, cluster-wide. AFAICT the concepts of  cluster-wide `ClusterRole`/`ClusterRoleBinding` objects is conflated with access to the whole k8s cluster. There is no way to have a `Role`/`RoleBinding` in a namespace that can provide access to objects outside of that namespace.

> Also, I think every object we create should have the product name in it, so that we can minimize the likelihood that our objects will clash with users' objects if/when they install the conduit control plane into a namespace where they have other objects (e.g. because they are only able to create objects in one namespace).

Yeah, because we don't want objects conflicting between multiple control-plane namespaces, I ended up putting the namespace in the names, but you are right that this would create objects like `myns-controller` which may already be taken. I can format the names as `conduit-[ns]-controller`. This would make the default `conduit-conduit-controller`, which isn't the greatest naming but it's functional. Open to other ideas.

/cc @briansmith

comments.author: briansmith
comments.body:
@siggy Thanks for explaining that. I think that in the future we may be able to do something more fine-grained than `ClusterRoleBinding`s, and I think we more-or-less *have* to do something better than `ClusterRoleBinding` for the read/write roles (and role bindings) for the "CA distributor" component, but that would require some experimentation and that shouldn't block this PR.

I do think that `$productName-$controllerNamespaceName-$componentName` or any similar naming convention makes sense. In the near future (outside of this PR) we should agree and document what naming convention we're using. I know that the Conduit CA uses a different convention, a `-conduit-io` suffix, and we probably should be a bit more consistent. I don't have a strong opinion about which specific scheme we pick though.

My rationale is that we shouldn't require the latest available version of kubectl to delete a few namespaces; I would rather update the script so that it works regardless of kubectl version.

I think something like this would work:

```
if ! namespaces=$(kubectl get ns -oname | grep "/$linkerd_namespace"); then
  echo "no namespaces found for [$linkerd_namespace]" >&2
  exit 1
else
  kubectl delete $namespaces
fi
```

That will exit with an error if no namespaces exist, and otherwise it will delete all namespaces in parallel.

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
If you use `kubectl get ns -o name` here, there's no need to `cut` the output to extract the name field. Note that the `name` output format also includes a resource type, and the resource type changed from plural to singular in kubectl 1.10 (e.g. `namespace/linkerd` instead of `namespaces/linkerd`). But this should work:

```
if ! namespaces=$(kubectl get ns -oname | grep -E "/$linkerd_namespace(-|$)"); then
```

title: Increase outbound router capacity for Prometheus pod's proxy
body:
Currently, when a cluster has over 100 pods injected with the Linkerd2
proxy, Prometheus metrics are not collected correctly. This is because
Prometheus appears to be making more concurrent requests than its'
proxy's outbound router cache can handle See issue #1322 for further 
details.

This branch introduces a workaround for this issue, by increasing the
outbound router cache capacity to 10000 routes for the Prometheus pod's
proxy only. The router capacity limit of 100 active routes is primarily
due to the limitation of the number of active Destination service 
lookups, so increasing the capacity for the Prometheus pod specifically
is probably okay, as the scrape requests are made to IP addresses 
directly and therefore will not cause service discovery lookups. 

This change was originally implemented and tested in @siggy's PR #1228.
I've rebased his branch onto the current `master`, and updated the code
to reflect the project name change.

Signed-off-by: Eliza Weisman <eliza@buoyant.io>
Co-authored-by: Andrew Seigner <siggy@buoyant.io>
author: hawkw

title: Build version tags in CI
body:
This branch updates our travis CI config to start publishing docker images when new version tags are created in the linkerd2 repo, provided that the tags match the regex `/^v\d+\.\d+\.[\w-]+$/`. This change works because travis does not distinguish between a tag and a branch -- it treats all tags and branches as branches.

As part of this change I also had to add a CI-specific environment variable in order for integration tests to pass -- `CI_FORCE_CLEAN` -- since our integration tests don't run in a clean repo checkout and I've never been able to figure out why.

I tested this branch by naming the branch in a way that matches the version tag regex, and validating that docker images were published and integration tests passed: https://travis-ci.org/linkerd/linkerd2/builds/407820373

Fixes #1364.

title: Read all bytes of message length header
body:
The `reader.Read` method only reads as many bytes as are currently available from reader.  When reading the 4 byte message length header, if not all 4 of those bytes are available, `Read` will only read the available bytes and return.  This causes alignment issues when the message body is read and there are still unread header bytes in the reader.  These bytes will appear at the beginning of the message body and cause a crash when the message is unmarshalled.

Use `io.ReadFull` to ensure that we read all 4 of the message length header bytes.

Fixes #1287 

Signed-off-by: Alex Leong <alex@buoyant.io>
author: adleong

comments.body: This seems tricky to test reliably.  `ReadAll` effectively calls `Read` in a busy loop which means that to test this, we would need to give the reader more bytes from another goroutine.  But without a way to guarantee the ordering, this may not exercise the issue.

review_threads.author: rmars

`propTypes` is where we tell the component what types of props to expect for example:
`static propTypes = { message: PropTypes.string }`

`defaultProps` is where we tell the component what the prop's default value should be if the prop is not a required prop. so like: `static defaultProps = { message: "my default message" }`

So here in `defaultProps` you actually want to place your default value and not the `PropTypes` type. So this should be:

```
static defaultProps = {
+    message: null,
     error: null
```

title: Add client-side filters to the tap columns in the web UI
body:
Add client side filtering to the tap table, so that we can narrow down queries while still tapping a whole resource. There are two general kinds of filters here:
- filters where the number of possible values is bounded/small and we know them (e.g. inbound/outbound, grpc status)
  - here, I've tried to hardcode the list of possible options with explanations (see the GRPC status filters)
- filters where the number of possible values can be very large (e.g. paths)
  - here, I've generated the list of options as we process the incoming data. I also periodically delete the oldest filter option so the list of filters doesn't grow unbounded

When #1391 merges, I'll rebase this on top of master.

Things that will be added:
- alphabetical sorting of filter options
- custom numeric filtering e.g. > 5 B for response sizes
- a clear button for the table filters, so that if we set multiple filters, we can easily unset them all 
- a clear button for the tap query form

In this branch I'm re-adding the rule but scoping it to only operate on labels that are prefixed with "linkerd.io/", as follows:

      - action: labelmap
        regex: __meta_kubernetes_pod_label_linkerd_io_(.+)
```

This change also strips the "linkerd_io_" prefix from those labels, which is more consistent with how we're rewriting all of the linkerd.io/proxy* labels. Have verified that the Linkerd Health dashboard loads successfully with this change.

title: Add additional validation for stat command-line arguments
body:
Closes #776.

This branch adds the following validation to the `linkerd stat` command:

* The `--to` and `--from` flags are now mutually exclusive
* The `--to-namespace` and `--from-namespace` commands are also mutually
  exclusive.
* The `namespace` resource type conflicts with the `--namespace`, 
  `--to-namespace`, and `--from-namespace` flags.

Examples:

```
$ bin/go-run cli/main.go stat deploy --to deploy/foo --from deploy/bar
Error: --to and --from flags are mutually exclusive
Usage:
  linkerd stat [flags] (RESOURCE)
  ...
```

```
$ bin/go-run cli/main.go stat deploy --to-namespace foo --from-namespace bar
Error: --to-namespace and --from-namespace flags are mutually exclusive
Usage:
  linkerd stat [flags] (RESOURCE)
  ...
```

```
$ bin/go-run cli/main.go stat namespace foo --namespace bar
Error: --namespace flag is incompatible with namespace resource type
Usage:
  linkerd stat [flags] (RESOURCE)
  ...
```

```
$ bin/go-run cli/main.go stat ns --to-namespace bar
Error: --to-namespace flag is incompatible with namespace resource type
Usage:
  linkerd stat [flags] (RESOURCE)
  ...
```

```
$ bin/go-run cli/main.go stat namespace --from-namespace bar
Error: --from-namespace flag is incompatible with namespace resource type
Usage:
  linkerd stat [flags] (RESOURCE)
  ...
```

```
$ bin/go-run cli/main.go stat ns/foo --from-namespace bar
Error: --from-namespace flag is incompatible with namespace resource type
Usage:
  linkerd stat [flags] (RESOURCE)
  ...
```

Signed-off-by: Eliza Weisman <eliza@buoyant.io>
author: hawkw

review_threads.body: This is super trivial, but can you move all of these new validation methods to the bottom of the file? The (loosely held) convention for files in this directory is for the `newCmd...` funcs to come first.

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body: We already have this functionality for parsing resource types, so I'd rather not duplicate it. At other places in this file where we parse resources from the command line, we use [util.BuildResource](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/master/controller/api/util/api_utils.go#L208), which should work for this use case as well.

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body: I think initially, I wasn't sure if `util.BuildResource` would do what I wanted, but after taking a closer look at the code, I believe it does. Thanks!

review_threads.author: klingerf
klingerf
review_threads.body:
This is minor, but standard godoc convention is to start all function comments with the function name itself. From [golang.org](https://blog.golang.org/godoc-documenting-go-code):

> Notice this comment is a complete sentence that begins with the name of the element it describes. This important convention allows us to generate documentation in a variety of formats, from plain text to HTML to UNIX man pages, and makes it read better when tools truncate it for brevity, such as when they extract the first line or sentence.

Mind rewriting all of the function comments that you're adding in this diff to comply?

review_threads.body: Throughout the rest of this file we use `fmt.Errorf`, which is equivalent to `errors.New`, and my preference is to use the `fmt` package throughout, rather than adding an import for the `errors` package.

title: Fix Destination returning no endpoints for single unnamed container port
body:
Fixes #1405.

According to the Kubernetes Endpoints API documentation, the `name`
field in the `EndpointPort` response object is "Optional if only one
port is defined". (see
https://v1-9.docs.kubernetes.io/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/v1.9/#endpointport-v1-core)
However, when the Destination service an endpoints response for a
service with a named target port, it expects the ports in the endpoints
response to have the same name as the target port in the service. 

When a user creates a `NodePort` service with an unnamed port that
targets a named container port, this behaviour results in Linkerd
failing to route to that service by hostname. Without Linkerd injected,
the hostname is still reachable. 

This branch fixes this issue by changing the `endpointsToAddresses`
function in `endpoints_watcher.go` to handle the case when an endpoints
response contains only a single unnamed port.

I've manually verified that this fixes the issue described in #1405.

title: Better CLI error messages when control plane is unavailable
body:
The branch overhauls the way in which the CLI builds its public-api client in order to give the user better error messages when the CLI can't talk to the control plane.

#258 describes a bunch of scenarios in which the output of the `conduit dashboard` command is confusing. Here's a summary of how those scenarios are handled with this branch:

If the user is not configured to talk to Kubernetes, the CLI waits for 5 seconds trying to connect and then prints:

```
Cannot connect to Kubernetes: Error calling the Kubernetes API: Get https://192.168.99.100:8443/version: context deadline exceeded
```

If the linkerd namespace does not exist, then the CLI prints

```
Cannot connect to Linkerd: The "linkerd" namespace does not exist
Validate the install with: linkerd check
```

If the public API container is not up yet, or if the container had errors starting, then the CLI prints:

```
Cannot connect to Linkerd: Unexpected API response: 503 Service Unavailable
Validate the install with: linkerd check
```

If the public API container is receiving requests but it's unable to talk to prometheus, the CLI prints a message and then retries the check every 10 seconds. This behavior is designed to account for the fact that Prometheus takes ~30 seconds longer to pass its readiness checks. Eventually the check succeeds and the dashboard opens. The output looks like this

```
$ ./bin/go-run cli dashboard
Waiting for controller to connect to Prometheus
Linkerd dashboard available at:
http://127.0.0.1:52638/api/v1/namespaces/linkerd/services/web:http/proxy/
Grafana dashboard available at:
http://127.0.0.1:52638/api/v1/namespaces/linkerd/services/grafana:http/proxy/
Opening Linkerd dashboard in the default browser
```

The same error handling has been applied to all CLI subcommands that access the public API (not just the `dashboard` command), which also addresses #222.

Fixes #222.
Fixes #258.

title: Add source metadata to Tap server tap events
body:
The `TapEvent` protobuf contains two maps, `DestinationMeta` and
`SourceMeta`. The `DestinationMeta` contains all the metadata provided
by the proxy that originated the event (ultimately originating from the
Destination service), while the `SourceMeta` currently only contains the
source connection's TLS status.

This branch modifies the Tap server to hydrate the same set of metadata
from the source IP address, when the source was within the cluster. It
does this by adding an indexer of pod IPs to pods to its k8s API client,
and looking up IPs against this index. If a pod was found, the extra
metadata is added to the tap event sent to the client.

This branch also changes the client so that if a source pod name was
provided in the metadata, it prints the pod name rather than the IP
address for the `src` field in its output. This mimics what is currently
done for the `dst` field in tap output. Furthermore, the added source
metadata will be necessary for adding src resource types to tap output
(see issue #1170).

The implementation is slightly more complex than what you posted above, however, as I thought it was still worthwhile to handle pods in the `Pending` (and `Unknown`) phases correctly?

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body: Hmm, yeah, that's a good point about the other pod phases. I guess my overall thinking is that if we have only one pod, we should return that pod. We don't need to do any other introspection of the pod, since we were looking for exactly one pod and we found one. If there's more than one pod, then we should return whichever one is running, since it should never be the case that two running pods have the same IP. And if there are multiple pods but none of them are running, then I'm not super concerned about what we do at that point. I opted to return nil, but it would also be fine to return the pod at index 0 or something equally simple. I just don't think it's worth adding any more complexity than that to handle this edge case.

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body:
Hmm. I don't think this function should ever return a `Pending` pod --- it can't possibly have sent the request if it hasn't yet started. 

Consider the following cases:
+ `[Pending, Terminated]`: The pending pod can't possibly have sent the request, as it hasn't started _running_ yet --- it must have come from the terminated pod before it terminated.

+ `[Pending]` (and `[Pending, Pending, Pending...]`, which AFAIK should not actually happen): Again, the pending pod can't have sent the request. Presumably, the IP either belonged to a terminated pod that has since been garbage-collected, or something outside of the cluster --- either way, we can't provide correct metadata for it, so we should return `nil`.

+ `[Terminated, Terminated...]` This is the case where we would previously try to select the most recently terminated pod. Since that is overly complex, I'm okay with removing that logic and returning `nil` in this case.

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body:
> I opted to return nil, but it would also be fine to return the pod at index 0 or something equally simple. 

Personally, I think returning nil is more correct in this case --- I'd rather say "we can't positively identify the pod that sent the request" rather than claiming that the request was sent from a pod that we can't definitively identify.

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
That breakdown of various potential pod states makes sense to me, but it's complicated enough to warrant tests for each of the cases that you enumerated.

And that said, I feel like this discussion is a bit moot. It's true that if a pod is pending, then it will not have sent any requests. Or is it? What if some of the containers came up and started making requests, but others have not, leaving the pod in a pending state? It feels like there could be dozens of confusing states for any given group of pods, but at the end of the day, if the group size is 1, we should just return it.

title: Add resource metadata to Tap CLI output
body:
Closes #1170.

This branch adds a `-o wide` (or `--output wide`) flag to the Tap CLI.
Passing this flag adds `src_res` and `dst_res` elements to the Tap
output, as described in #1170. These use the metadata labels in the tap
event to describe what Kubernetes resource the source and destination
peers belong to, based on what resource type is being tapped, and fall
back to pods if either peer is not a member of the specified resource
type.

In addition, when the resource type is not `namespace`, `src_ns` and
`dst_ns` elements are added, which show what namespaces the the source
and destination peers are in. For peers which are not in the Kubernetes
cluster, none of these labels are displayed.

The source metadata added in #1434 is used to populate the `src_res` and
`src_ns` fields.

Also, this branch includes some refactoring to how tap output is
formatted.

Signed-off-by: Eliza Weisman <eliza@buoyant.io>
