title: Add inbound destination label hydration to Tap server
body:
Based on @adleong's suggestion in
https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/pull/1434#pullrequestreview-145428857,
this branch adds label hydration from destination IPs to the Tap server.
This works the same as the label hydration for destination IPs added in
#1434. However, it is only applied to the destination fields of events
recorded by proxies in the inbound direction, since outbound
destinations are already labeled with metadata provided by the
Destination service.

This means that when a user taps inbound traffic, the CLI will show k8s
metadata labels for the destination peer (if it's available). This can
be useful especially when tapping several pods at once, as it makes it
easier to distinguish what pod received a request.

This branch also refactors how the label hydration is performed,
primarily to make adding it to the destination field less repetitive.
Also, the `hydrateIPLabels` function now mutates the label map in the
`TapEvent`, rather than returning a new map of labels, so that the case
where no pod was found doesn't require an additional allocation of an
empty map.

Signed-off-by: Eliza Weisman <eliza@buoyant.io>
author: hawkw

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body: @rmars I guess this is just "beginner's mind", I just looked up "switch" in Go by Example: https://gobyexample.com/switch :)

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
Sorry for the late review on this branch. I just wanted to add one style comment, but it's super minor, so no need to submit a follow-up branch. We tend to use go's [CodeReviewComments](https://github.com/golang/go/wiki/CodeReviewComments) as our default style guide in this code base. And using the default case of the switch statement here to handle the normal code path goes against their recommendation regarding [indent error flow](https://github.com/golang/go/wiki/CodeReviewComments#indent-error-flow). Specifically:

> Try to keep the normal code path at a minimal indentation

Since your first two cases have early returns, then you could exit the switch statement before resuming the normal code path. E.g.:

```
	pod, err := s.podForIP(ip)
	switch {
	case err != nil:
		return err
	case pod == nil:
		log.Debugf("no pod for IP %s", addr.PublicIPToString(ip))
		return nil
	}

	ownerKind, ownerName := s.k8sAPI.GetOwnerKindAndName(pod)
	podLabels := pkgK8s.GetPodLabels(ownerKind, ownerName, pod)
	for key, value := range podLabels {
		labels[key] = value
	}
	return nil
```

But at that point I'd probably remove the switch statement altogether and write this as:

```
	pod, err := s.podForIP(ip)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if pod == nil {
		log.Debugf("no pod for IP %s", addr.PublicIPToString(ip))
		return nil
	}

	ownerKind, ownerName := s.k8sAPI.GetOwnerKindAndName(pod)
	podLabels := pkgK8s.GetPodLabels(ownerKind, ownerName, pod)
	for key, value := range podLabels {
		labels[key] = value
	}
	return nil
```

I find that method of error handling to be easier to follow.

review_threads.author: hawkw
review_threads.body: Okay, thanks for the feedback --- I'll keep that in mind as a refactor if I make additional changes to this branch.

body:
Add a `Top` page to the linkerd web UI. This is the web equivalent of #1435.

I've used the same fields as in the current implementation.

This branch also includes some slight refactors to the Tap code to enable code reuse.

The request processing logic is pretty similar to that in Tap, except that we can immediately discard the result once we receive the response end and aggregate that result into the top results. So the index of tap results will tend to be smaller (unless they're long running requests like streaming). But we also add a similar index of aggregated Top results, and discard oldest results if top has been running for a long time.

![screen shot 2018-08-14 at 3 09 44 pm](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/549258/44121338-6ac8d1d8-9fd4-11e8-9487-70fd8ebf981d.png)

If I'm reading this correctly, this actually does mirror what I had in the CLI.  There are two different aggregation steps.  First, we receive tap events and aggregate them by id until we've collected the reqInit, rspInit, and rspEnd.  Once we have all 3 parts of the request, we send it over to the table where whole requests are aggregated by (src, dst, path).

In order to avoid relying on event id, I've now changed the CLI implementation to do that first aggregation step by (src, dst, stream).  That same change should probably made here as well for the same reason.

title: Add resource detail skeleton page
body:
Add a barebones resource detail page. The page can be accessed via a URL like `http://localhost:8084/namespaces/emojivoto/pods/emoji-7578f4f846-m6872`. 

We'll follow the kubernetes style URL conventions for namespaces and resources:
`http://localhost:8084/namespaces/emojivoto/deployments/voting`

![screen shot 2018-08-16 at 12 53 20 pm](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/549258/44231721-ed46d580-a153-11e8-9565-20e92c68200b.png)



Fixes #1457
author: rmars

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
How would you feel about making this route `"/resource/:type/:name"`? We should be able to do something like that pretty easily with httprouter, and it would make for somewhat nicer URLs.

Alternatively, if we wanted the resource detail page to be analogous to how we're already handling namespaces, then it might make sense to hardcode all of the resource types:

```
server.router.GET("/pods/:pod", handler.handleIndex)
server.router.GET("/deployments/:deployment", handler.handleIndex)
server.router.GET("/replicationcontrollers/:replicationcontroller", handler.handleIndex)
...
```

That would be more REST-y, too.

review_threads.author: rmars
review_threads.body:
Yeah! I have been trying to make a decision on that too.
I did alternate between those choices as well. I'd settled on /resource because I realized that we'd need to pass in namespace as well, and it would allow us to handle arbitrary resource types without making any additional changes to the web server, but I think making it REST-y is appealing.

Yeah, it probably would make the most sense to do the hardcoding of the resource type routes so that we can be analogous to how we handle namespaces. For the other resource types, namespace can be a URL parameter, so we can do something like:
`/deployments/voting?namespace=emojivoto`

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body: Agreed! I like `/deployments/voting?namespace=emojivoto`, as I feel like that's most consistent with `/namespaces/emojivoto`. Plus it means that the URL paths are valid k8s resources. Or if we wanted to get super REST-y with this, we could do something like `/namespaces/emojivoto/deployments/voting`, but I'm ambivalent about that.

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
Peering just a bit more deeply into this rabbit hole... the Kubernetes API uses scoped resource routes, e.g.:

```
GET /api/v1/namespaces/{namespace}/pods/{name}
GET /apis/apps/v1/namespaces/{namespace}/deployments/{name}
...
```

So it could make sense for us to follow that convention here.

review_threads.author: dadjeibaah
review_threads.body: I am definitely in favor of having this be more REST-y. I can definitely see this being extended further so that we could also have tap and top-like resources associated for each resource endpoint, for example, if we wanted to get the top results for a deployment, the URL may look something like `/deployments/:deployment/top?top_filters=...` I am not sure if that is worthwhile to do, but it definitely provides for shareable and user-friendly URLs.

review_threads.author: rmars
review_threads.body: Yeah! Agreed. Let's follow the k8s API convention for now, and see how we feel.

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
One downside of using the kubernetes url structure is that it's the same structure we use for proxying requests to the dashboard. So when I run this via `linkerd dashboard`, I see:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/9226/44232775-e7062880-a156-11e8-82f1-898e1077c249.png)

I think we'll need the regex to be more restrictive in order to match this. Maybe we can leverage the `pathPrefix` from context? Something like:

```
`${pathPrefix}/namespaces/${match.params.namespace}/([^/]+)/([^/]+)`)
```

Or similar. Note also that I think we should also restrict the path matches to not match "/", so that they only match a single segment. Otherwise we'll run into problems for paths like `/namespaces/ns/deployments/dep/tap`.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/9226/44366304-1b445680-a481-11e8-8854-0e1d9a28b9fe.png)

In this screenshot, the deployment is "prometheus", but the pods listed in the pods table belong to the "controller" and "grafana" deployments, not the "prometheus" deployment.

sum(increase(response_total{direction="outbound", dst_deployment="prometheus", dst_namespace="linkerd", namespace="linkerd"}[1m])) by (namespace, pod, classification, tls)

```
sum(increase(response_total{direction="outbound", dst_deployment="prometheus", dst_namespace="linkerd", namespace="linkerd"}[1m])) by (dst_namespace, dst_pod, classification, tls) 
```

So I think we'll have to try one of the other approaches outline in #1467 to get this data.

title: Move all healthcheck-related code to pkg/healthcheck
body:
This branch is a substantial refactor to the way our health check code was setup:

* All checks are now defined in `pkg/healthcheck/healthcheck.go`
* Check definitions use the `healthcheck.checkers` struct instead of protobuf
* Checks can now be marked as fatal, which will skip all remaining checks on failure
* Checks are now binary (passing/failing); we no longer distinguish between failing and errored
* The `MockKubeApi` struct has been removed, since it was no longer used
* The `KubernetesApi` interface has been removed, since it only had one implementation after removing the mock

This refactor is in support of #1470, #1471, #1473, #1477, and #1478.

title: Fix missing ns/svc labels in metadata hydrated by Tap server
body:
Fixes #1493.

When the tap server hydrates metadata for the source or destination peer
of a Tap event from the peer's IP address, it doesn't currently add a
namespace label. However, destinations labeled by the proxy do have such
a label.

This is because the tap server currently gets the hydrated labels from
the `GetPodLabels` function, which is also used by the Destination
service for labeling the individual endpoints in a `WeightedAddrSet`
response. However, the Destination service also adds some labels to all
the endpoints in the set, including the namespace and service, so
`GetPodLabels` doesn't return these labels. However, when the tap server
uses that function, it does not add the service or namespace labels.

This branch fixes this issue by adding those labels to the Tap event 
after calling `GetPodLabels`. In addition, it fixes a missing space 
between the `src/dst_res` and `src/dst_ns` labels in Tap CLI output
with the `-o wide` flag set. This issue was introduced during the 
review of #1437, but was missed at the time because the namespace label
wasn't being set correctly.

Signed-off-by: Eliza Weisman <eliza@buoyant.io>
author: hawkw

In the process of working on #1477, I decided to streamline the way in which the `HealthChecker` is configured as follows:

* `NewHealthChecks` now takes a list of checks to execute and a struct with check options

title: Add --wait flag for CLI check and dashboard commands
body:
This branch updates the check and dashboard commands to support a `--wait` flag. This flag can be used to control the behavior of the pod ready check that was added in #1498.

When `--wait` is specified, check will retry on failed pod ready check up to 10 times / 50 seconds, which looks like this:

```
$ bin/linkerd check --wait --expected-version=$(bin/root-tag)
kubernetes-api: can initialize the client..................................[ok]
kubernetes-api: can query the Kubernetes API...............................[ok]
kubernetes-api: is running the minimum Kubernetes API version..............[ok]
linkerd-api: control plane namespace exists................................[ok]
linkerd-api: control plane pods are ready..................................[retry] -- No running pods for controller
linkerd-api: control plane pods are ready..................................[retry] -- The grafana pod's grafana container is not ready
linkerd-api: control plane pods are ready..................................[retry] -- The grafana pod's grafana container is not ready
linkerd-api: control plane pods are ready..................................[retry] -- The grafana pod's grafana container is not ready
linkerd-api: control plane pods are ready..................................[retry] -- The prometheus pod's prometheus container is not ready

title: Increase default max-rps for tap and top
body:
The default value for the max-rps argument to the tap and top commands is an overly conservative 1rps.  This causes the data to come in very slowly and much data to be discarded.  Furthermore, because tap requests are windowed to 10 seconds, this causes long pauses between updates.

We fix this in two ways.  Firstly we reduce the window size to 1s so that updates will come in at least once per second, even when the actual RPS of the data path is extremely high.  Secondly, we increase the default max-rps parameter from 1 to 100.  This allows tap to paint an accurate picture of the data much more quickly and sidesteps some sampling bias that happens when the max-rps is low.

In general, tap events tend to happen in bursts.  For example, one request in may trigger one or more requests out.  Likewise, a single upstream event may trigger several requests to the tapped pod in quick succession.  Sampling bias will occur when the max-rps is less than the actual rps and when the tap event limit subdivides these event bursts (biasing towards the first few events in the burst).  The greater the max-rps, the less the effects of this bias.

Fixes #1525 

Signed-off-by: Alex Leong <alex@buoyant.io>
author: adleong

comments.author: olix0r
comments.body: Do i understand correctly that this will cause the tap server to issue new requests to all proxies once per second? This seems potentially... costly, especially if the user intends to view results for more than 1s. I suspect we'll need to push down sampling deeper into the proxy

comments.author: adleong
comments.body: Yes, that's correct.  This will cause the tap server to issue a new tap request to the proxy/proxies it is tapping once per second.  I don't have a good sense for how costly this really is.

comments.author: adleong
comments.body:
Actually, let me clarify.  The tap server will wait a *minimum* of 1 second between sending tap requests.  If the limit (now defaulting to 100) has not been reached after 1 second, the tap request will remain open and a new tap request will not be made until 100 events have been received.  

It's only in the case where the limit is reached in less than 1 second that the tap server will make a new request after the 1 second window.

comments.author: adleong
comments.body: Tested this at 200rps and it behaved as I expected: each second we get 100 requests and then pause until the next second.

title: Only tap pods that are meshed
body:
Previously, we would tap any resource's pods, regardless of whether the pods were meshed or not.
We can't actually tap non-meshed pods, so I'm adding a check that will filter out non-meshed pods from the pods that tap watches.

*Previous behaviour*
when attempting to hang a non meshed pod, it would establish a watch on the pods, but then never return any results. In the CLI you could just cancel it with Ctrl-C. In the web, clicking Stop would send a `WebSocket.close(1000)` but wouldn't actually close the connection... (I think that part is web not handling the close properly, but I discovered this while trying to address that).

*Behaviour after change*
If no pods under the specified resource are meshed, it'll go on to this line, which will return an error of no pods being found to tap:
```
	if len(pods) == 0 {
		return status.Errorf(codes.NotFound, "no pods found for ResourceSelection: %+v", *req.Target)
	}
```

title: Modify inject to warn when file is un-injectable
body:
If an input file is un-injectable, existing inject behavior is to simply
output a copy of the input.

Introduce a report, printed to stderr, that communicates the end state
of the inject command. Currently this includes checking for hostNetwork
and unsupported resources.

Malformed YAML documents will continue to cause no YAML output, and return
error code 1.

example outputs...

some pods injected, none with host networking:

```
hostNetwork: pods do not use host networking...............................[ok]
supported: at least one resource injected..................................[ok]

Summary: 4 of 8 YAML document(s) injected
  deploy/emoji
  deploy/voting
  deploy/web
  deploy/vote-bot
```

some pods injected, one host networking:

```
hostNetwork: pods do not use host networking...............................[warn] -- deploy/vote-bot uses "hostNetwork: true"
supported: at least one resource injected..................................[ok]

Summary: 3 of 8 YAML document(s) injected
  deploy/emoji
  deploy/voting
  deploy/web
```

no pods injected:

```
hostNetwork: pods do not use host networking...............................[warn] -- deploy/emoji, deploy/voting, deploy/web, deploy/vote-bot use "hostNetwork: true"
supported: at least one resource injected..................................[warn] -- no supported objects found

Summary: 0 of 8 YAML document(s) injected
```

TODO: check for UDP and other init containers

Part of #1516

Signed-off-by: Andrew Seigner <siggy@buoyant.io>
author: siggy

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body: if everything went fine, should we print this at all? another way to put it: do we want to communicate to the user the number of documents that were injected?

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
`ShortNameFromCanonicalResourceName` only works for a subset of all Kubernetes object types, so if the inject yaml includes an object type that's not covered by that function, then we won't properly format the name. For instance, if we were trying to inject a Secret named "super", `report.name` would be "/super".

I don't think this is an issue in the current implementation, however, since we only print the names of objects that include pod specs in the report, and all objects that include pod specs are covered in `ShortNameFromCanonicalResourceName`. But I'm inclined to switch to using full names so that down the road we know that the name field is printable for all object types.

```
	report.name = fmt.Sprintf("%s/%s", strings.ToLower(meta.Kind), om.Name)
```

title: Improve performance of Top tables
body:
*Problem*
We receive a lot of websocket events from the tap server. Previously, we were processing each event as we received it, then calling setState after processing to update the tables. Each call to setState triggered a re-render of the whole table. We were rerendering multiplie times a second, causing the whole page to become unresponsive.

*Solution*
`throttle` setState for receiving websocket tap events to prevent continuous rerendering.
Store the tap events in an index outside of state, and only update the state once every specified interval (currently 500ms).

We can now view entire namespaces with Top and the page won't crash! 
To verify: Go to `/top` and try topping a namespace

For more reading: 
https://css-tricks.com/debouncing-throttling-explained-examples/
https://nolanlawson.com/2018/09/01/a-tour-of-javascript-timers-on-the-web/

Part of #1601

title: Cleanly shutdown tap stream to data plane proxies
body:
This work is part of a #1504. Sometimes, the tap server causes the controller pod to restart after it receives this error:
```bash
time="2018-08-22T05:57:00Z" level=error msg="rpc error: code = Canceled desc = context canceled"
panic: send on closed channel

goroutine 139 [running]:
github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/controller/tap.(*server).tapProxy(0xc420442c20, 0x14843a0, 0xc420966fc0, 0x3f800000, 0xc420981510, 0xc4205fe740, 0xa, 0xc420a0c180)
	/go/src/github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/controller/tap/server.go:278 +0x3b6
created by github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/controller/tap.(*server).TapByResource
	/go/src/github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/controller/tap/server.go:94 +0x50b
```

This error arises when the Tap server does not close gRPC tap streams to proxies before the tap server terminates its streams to its upstream clients and causes the controller pod to restart.

This PR uses the request context from the initial `TapByReource` to help shutdown tap streams to the data plane proxies gracefully.

fixes #1504 

Signed-off-by: Dennis Adjei-Baah <dennis@buoyant.io>
author: dadjeibaah

comments.author: dadjeibaah
comments.body: @adleong, from the debugging session I had with @klingerf, it looks like there aren't related. I have created the issue #1630 to track that issue.

review_threads.author: adleong
review_threads.body: Without propagating the context from the client request, how do the proxy tap requests ever get cancelled?

review_threads.author: dadjeibaah
review_threads.body: From my reading of the [gRPC GoDocs](https://godoc.org/google.golang.org/grpc#DialContext) DialContext uses`ctx` the set up of the connection and the `ctx` struct doesn't manage the lifetime of the connection. IIUC, that means there is no need for the proxy tap requests to use the parent `ctx` provided by the `TapByResource`. The thought process is that each connection to a data plane tap should have its own context and when the connection is closed the context is canceled with it.

review_threads.author: dadjeibaah
review_threads.body: I am not sure what the difference is between `Dial` and `DialContext` but we could probably get away with just using `Dial` when creating a connection since it provides its own context.

review_threads.author: adleong
review_threads.body: I'm wondering if a better solution would be to get rid of this goroutine altogether and instead add a switch when reading from the events channel so that we read from both the events channel and the context's Done channel and return when Done becomes closed.  I think this has the intended behavior without needing to worry about closing the events channel.

title: Improve top table to better cope with high RPS traffic
body:
There are two variables we use to control the volume of Top output, maxRowsToDisplay, which controls how many rows are in the table, and maxRowsToStore, which controls the size of the event index we keep in memory for aggregating results.

Previously, we were only keeping in index maxRowsToDisplay rows, which for the Resource Detail page was 10 (which is really small for high traffic rest-y resource traffic - it causes rows to be deleted from the index too soon, and then causes the data in the table to change a lot). Change this to store maxRowsToStore rows, and also bump this to 50. This allows us to store results for longer, and also ensures more consistent data over time.

Another fix for the appearance of the Top columns is to add fixed widths to the metrics. This will prevent the table from wobbling from side to side. Some widths were added in #1620 and #1628 though, so it'd be helpful to look at widths again once these three branches have merged.

Fixes #1601

title: Add data plane check for metrics Prometheus
body:
The `linkerd check` command was not validating whether data plane
proxies were successfully reporting metrics to Prometheus.

Introduce a new check that validates data plane proxies are found in
Prometheus. This is made possible via the existing `ListPods` endpoint
in the public API, which includes an `Added` field, indicating a pod's
metrics were found in Prometheus.

Fixes #1517

Signed-off-by: Andrew Seigner <siggy@buoyant.io>
author: siggy

comments.author: dadjeibaah
comments.body: Changes LGTM! thanks for adding this to the check command :package:

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body: Mind switching this to `fmt.Errorf`? That's more consistent with how we produce errors throughout the rest of this file.

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body: I don't think this check needs to be fatal. A fatal check cancels all remaining checks, but if metrics aren't present in prometheus, I think it's still ok to continue with the remaining checks. I tend to categorize a check as fatal only if subsequent checks depend some side effect of the current check.

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body: Innnnteresting. I'm not sure this error will ever fire, since the ListPods endpoint builds its list of pods from the Kubernetes API, so if a host is not found in the Kubernetes, it also won't exist in the response from the ListPods endpoint. But it certainly doesn't hurt to leave this in here just in case something is really wonky.

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body: Agreed! I put this here primarily as a guard in case the behavior of ListPods ever changes.

review_threads.author: dadjeibaah
review_threads.body: I was thinking maybe we could have used the prometheus endpoint `api/v1/targets`'s results and compare that with the data plane pods to verify that data plane pods are in fact reporting stats. But, considering that we would have to deal with unmarshalling JSON and other things to make the endpoint's result consumable, this is probably a better way to do this.

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body: @dadjeibaah Yup I definitely thought about that approach. I think if ListPods at some point changes in behavior, we could revisit which Prometheus endpoint we use.

title: Key rows of top table on the resource type being requested
body:
*Problem*
Previously, we'd display one row in top per sourcePod -> dstPod. When viewing resources at a higher level though (e.g. deployments with multiple pods) the src/dst column displays the resource at that level, and displaying multiple rows with `deploy/foo` is confusing. 

*Solution*
Key the top table off of the resource currently being requested, so that all the rows are rolled up appropriately.
In the popover for that column, display a list of pods/ips that are rolled up.

This branch also adds a generic list of resources to the tap/top dropdown (you were always able to tap them, but when I switched from autocomplete to select for this dropdown, you lost the ability to type in arbitrary resources).

comments.body:
Yessssssssssssssss!

Does this work when the source and destination resources are different types?  e.g. when a pod that's part of a replication controller sends a request to a pod that's part of a deployment?

comments.author: rmars
comments.body:
Great question!
Currently, the key function is set up to fall back to pod, then to ip if there's no resourceType that matches.
So for example if we were on a replicationcontroller page, and we were displaying a row that has a pod being part of an rc sending traffic to a pod that's part of a deployment, it would try to key both src and dst under replication controller, but dst wouldn't have an rc label, so it'd fall back to keying on dst pod. So the key would be [rc/source-rc, pod/dst-pod, path].... so we would still experience the current problem, where it would look like there were duplicate rows.

title: Ignore websockets error code 1006

When a websocket connection is closed between Chrome and a server, we get a `1006` error code signifying abnormal closure of the websocket connection. It seems as if we only get this error on Chrome web clients. Firefox and Safari do not encounter this issue.

The solution is to suppress `1006` errors that occur in the web browser since the connection is closed anyway. There is no negative side effect that occurs when the connection is closed abnormally and so the error message is benign. 

![tap-output](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2197104/45576718-38c0d200-b82d-11e8-8ed9-19ff46f9f78f.gif)


fixes #1630 

Signed-off-by: Dennis Adjei-Baah <dennis@buoyant.io>

title: Fix unresponsive tap button when no data is available.
body:
When a resource has no tap events being streamed to the Tap UI, and a user hits the "Stop" button in the Tap page, the tap stream is left open due to the WebSocket connection not being closed.

It looks like the web server's tap client that is created to stream events from the tap server blocks the main request thread in the web server. This causes the web server to stop receiving any subsequent close frames from the UI i.e. when the "Stop" button is clicked. 

This PR moves the tapClient initialization code to a separate goroutine, specifically, the goroutine that reads tap events from the incoming grpc tap stream. This allows the main thread to continue reading messages from the WebSocket connection and allow it to receive close frames.

fixes #1665

Signed-off-by: Dennis Adjei-Baah <dennis@buoyant.io>

title: Stop trying to call setState on unmounted Tap and Top components
body:
We were getting react errors because we were calling setState in Tap and Top after the component unmounted (surprise!). 

In Top, when we unmount the component, we close the websocket. The websocket close handler calls updateTapClosingState which.. updates the state. But we shouldn't update the state on closing components. Fix this by changing updateTapClosingState to a `_.noop` if the component is unmounting.

In Tap, similarly, `stopTapStreaming` calls `setState`, so we shouldn't call `stopTapStreaming` when the component is unmounting. Instead, add an `_isMounted` variable so we can avoid setting state when the component is unmounting.

Fixes #1664

title: cli: add support for LINKERD_NAMESPACE environment variable
body:
This PR adds support to set the control plane namespace with the environment variable `LINKERD_NAMESPACE` (following the cli flag). It will give preference to the cli flag in case it is present, e.g. `LINKERD_NAMESPACE=nope linkerd --linkerd-namespace this-is-the-one` will use `this-is-the-one` as the control plane namespace).

The reason for this PR is because I've all my cluster core components on namespaces with a standard prefix, which makes the default namespace for the control plane a no go for my production environment.
This is solved with the `--linkerd-namespace` flag, however having to specify this on every command and every CI script is a bit annoying. For local use I've configured an alias (`alias linkerd="linkerd --linkerd-namespace my-mesh"`) however I would like to set this globally for our CI environment to ease developer adoption, thus the use of an environment variable is pretty handy here.

title: Proxy init and sidecar containers auto-injection
body:
Per discussion with @grampelberg, here's a PR that contains a proposed implementation for the proxy init and side containers auto-injection feature. 

Example usage can be found in this [gist](https://gist.github.com/ihcsim/cc58769cd84e746f89e123b94a2f3fb2).

The following is a summary of the changes in this PR:

### Control Plane

1. Add the `proxy-injector` pod to the control plane.
1. The `proxy-injector` creates the webhook's mutating webhook configuration by using the CA controller's trust anchor as its CA bundle.
1. The mutating webhook configuration ignores namespaces that are labelled with `linkerd.io/auto-inject: disabled` or `linkerd.io/auto-inject: completed`.
1. The webhook is triggered by `CREATE` events of `Deployment`s.
1. The webhook ignores `Deployment` with pods that are labelled with `linkerd.io/auto-inject: disabled` or `linkerd.io/auto-inject: completed`.
1. A TLS secret named `proxy-injector-service-tls-linkerd-io` is created by the CA controller to enable TLS communication between the API server and the webhook.
1. Declare a new config map to store the proxy init and sidecar container specs used for the auto-injection.

### CLI

1. Update `cli/install/template.go` with new `Deployment`, `Service`, RBAC etc. specs.
1. Make some of the `inject` proxy options available to the `install` command because `cli/install/template.go` now contains proxy container specs.
1. New `install` option to enable or disable proxy auto-injection.
    * Auto-injection only works when the `--tls=optional` and `proxy-auto-inject` options are set.

### CA Controller

1. Add a new handler to create a new TLS secret when a new mutating webhook configuration is created. The `Service` name defined in the webhook configuration will be used as the TLS identity.

### RBAC

1. CA cluster role is updated with permissions to `get`, `list` and `watch` mutating webhook configuration.
1. Add a new cluster role with permission for the controller to `create`, `get`, `list` and `watch` mutating webhook configuration. This cluster role also has permission to `get`, `list` and `watch` config maps. (I tried to limit the config map permissions to namespace-scoped, but I *think* the usage of `informers.Lister().Get()` requires global scope?)
 
(I can submit a PR for usage documentation once this PR is reviewed.)

comments.author: ihcsim
comments.body:
@klingerf Thanks for the feedback.

> From an architectural perspective, how would you feel about running the proxy-injector service in a separate proxy-injector pod? 

No objections. That was my initial plan. I actually misread a [comment](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/pull/1423#pullrequestreview-145349316) in the other older PR, thinking that the intent was to run the injector as a container in the controller pod.

>  Is is the case that we'll receive a new MutatingWebhookConfiguration event for each new deployment that's created..

The MutatingWebhookConfiguration is created just once when the injector starts up. It contains information used by the k8s API server to communicate with the admission webhook (which conceptually, is made up of a TLS server and the actual webhook that does the spec mutation). The configuration has nothing to do with any other new "application" deployments.

(Tangent: The only other times the MutatingWebhookConfiguration needs to be re-created is when the CA controller's trust-anchors.pem changed because it uses the trust-anchors.pem as its CA bundle. This is how the k8s API server knows it can trust the cert presented by the webhook TLS server. Currently, I am doing re-creating the MutatingWebhookConfiguration manually.)

> and we need to watch those events in order to propagate certs to those deployments? And that replaces the Pod watch events, since the pods no longer have injected YAML that tells us they're part of the data plane?

Nothing about how LD2 is currently doing automatic certs propagation has changed. If it does, it's unintentional and I screwed up!

My changes to the CA controller is simply my way of telling the CA controller, _"hey, I need a CA cert for my webhook's TLS server. btw, the API server will be talking to my TLS server as https://`proxy-injector-service-name`.`controller-namespace`:443. You can find the values of `proxy-injector-service-name` and `controller-namespace` in the MutatingWebhookConfiguration"_. 

Open to more feedback and suggestions...

title: Add --single-namespace install flag for restricted permissions
body:
This branch updates the `linkerd install` and `linkerd check` commands to accept a `--single-namespace` boolean flag, which if provided will modify the linkerd install YAML to use Roles instead of ClusterRoles, and it will adjust the pre-install check accordingly.

The bulk of the code changes required for conditionally switching to Roles happens in `controller/k8s/api.go`, where we configure the shared informers used by all of our controller components for reading from the Kubernetes API. If the `--single-namespace` flag is specified, all watches established in this file are scoped to an individual namespace.

Fixes #1705.
author: klingerf

comments.author: klingerf
comments.body: @olix0r I updated the `install` command to prefix all of the deployments and configmaps with "linkerd-" when the `--single-namespace` flag is present. Note that I haven't renamed the services as part of this change, since all of our other CLI subcommands use hardcoded service names for the control plane, and I didn't want to require users to add the `--single-namespace` flag to every command that they run. I think a better fix would be to rename all of the services to always include the "linkerd-" prefix, even in cluster-wide mode, but that would be a breaking change for upgrading the control plane, so I've punted on it for now.

comments.author: klingerf

@siggy Thanks for the feedback on this PR. I agree that renaming things as part of a single namespace install will be more of a burden going forward. I spoke to @olix0r about this, and I'm going to back out that change. Instead, we're going to signal that this feature "experimental", likely by changing the flag to indicate that explicitly.

But all of that said, I'm also going to wait to update and merge this branch until #1714 is ready, since that change has implications for this one as well.

To support reading and writing of the ServiceProfile custom resource, we add a codegen'd Kubernetes client for this resource.

* Adding the ServiceProfile type and related boilerplate to /controller/gen/apis/serviceprofile. This boilerplate also contains directives that control how codegen works.
* A script in /hack which invokes codegen that generates Kubernetes client machinery for interacting with ServiceProfile resources. The majority of the generated code lives in /controller/gen/client.
* The above-mentioned generated code.

comments.body: Note to reviewers: this is a subset of the already reviewed https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/pull/1608

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
I realize this is the convention in other repos, but I'm not super thrilled about a new top-level directory called "hack", especially when we already have a "bin" dir. There's nothing in this script that requires it live in a "hack" directory, so my preference is to move it to "bin" and make it a bit more stylistically consistent with the rest of the scripts in that directory. Something like:

```diff
diff --git a/hack/update-codegen.sh b/bin/update-codegen.sh
similarity index 56%
rename from hack/update-codegen.sh
rename to bin/update-codegen.sh
index d6252851..5e1e6507 100755
--- a/hack/update-codegen.sh
+++ b/bin/update-codegen.sh
@@ -1,8 +1,9 @@
-#!/usr/bin/env bash
+#!/bin/bash
 
-set -o errexit
-set -o nounset
-set -o pipefail
+set -eu
+
+bindir="$( cd "$( dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}" )" && pwd )"
+rootdir="$( cd $bindir/.. && pwd )"
 
 # ROOT_PACKAGE :: the package (relative to $GOPATH/src) that is the target for code generation
 ROOT_PACKAGE="github.com/linkerd/linkerd2"
@@ -11,9 +12,5 @@ CUSTOM_RESOURCE_NAME="serviceprofile"
 # CUSTOM_RESOURCE_VERSION :: the version of the resource
 CUSTOM_RESOURCE_VERSION="v1alpha1"
 
-HACK_DIR=$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE}")
-REPO_ROOT=${HACK_DIR}/..
-
 # run the code-generator entrypoint script
-
-${REPO_ROOT}/vendor/k8s.io/code-generator/generate-groups.sh all "$ROOT_PACKAGE/controller/gen/client" "$ROOT_PACKAGE/controller/gen/apis" "$CUSTOM_RESOURCE_NAME:$CUSTOM_RESOURCE_VERSION"
+$rootdir/vendor/k8s.io/code-generator/generate-groups.sh all "$ROOT_PACKAGE/controller/gen/client" "$ROOT_PACKAGE/controller/gen/apis" "$CUSTOM_RESOURCE_NAME:$CUSTOM_RESOURCE_VERSION"
```

title: Improve docker layer caching for web image
body:
Our web Dockerfile was previously setup to reinstall all yarn dependencies and rebuild the go binary any time any of our css or js files changed.

In this branch I've tweaked the layers in the Dockerfile so that yarn dependencies are only rebuilt when package.json or yarn.lock changes, and the go binary is only rebuilt when go source files change.

I also realized that our production web image included all of our unbundled javascript and css files, which aren't used when running the app in production, so I've removed them.

And in the process I change the file layout of the web image to match the defaults expected by the web server, which means we can remove the `-static-dir` and `-template-dir` flags from our install configs.

Testing locally, prior to make this change, making a modification to `web/app/js/index.js` would cause the docker build to take about 3m15s. After making this change, it rebuilds in about 1m5s.

This branch doesn't modify webpack, which accounts for the bulk of the remaining time required to build the web image (relates to #1662).

title: Implement getProfiles method in destination service
body:
We implement the getProfiles method in the destination service. This method returns a stream of destination profiles for a given authority. It does this by looking up the ServiceProfile resource in the controller namespace named `<svc>.<ns>` where `<svc>` is the name of the service and `<ns>` is the namespace of the service.

This PR includes:
* Adding a ServiceProfile Custom Resource Definition to linkerd install
* A watch based implementation of the getProfiles method in the destination service, similar to the implementation of get.
* An update to the destination client script that allows querying the getProfiles method.

Thank you very much @klingerf for your detailed review :-)
Your suggestions indeed made much more sense. I've implemented them in my latest push.

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
Authorities are a bit of a special case for our stats, since there's no notion of a `dst_authority` label -- the `authority` label is both the source and the destination, in some sense.

That said, in this row, I think we want to display stats for all deployments that are sending traffic to the authority that's stored in the `$authority` variable. The only way to query for that information is to use outbound stats, rather than inbound stats, and group by "deployment" instead of authority. Something like:

```
sum(irate(request_total{namespace="$namespace", authority="$authority", direction="outbound", tls!="true"}[30s])) by (deployment)
```

That will produce a list of deployments that are sending traffic to the authority that is being displayed in this dashboard. We'd want to make the same modification for all charts in this row.

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body: Related to my comment above, once we start grouping by outbound deployment, we should modify this label to display the deployment instead of the authority: "deploy/{{deployment}}".

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
Likewise for pods, we'd also need to use outbound stats to find all pods that are sending traffic to this authority:

```
sum(irate(request_total{namespace="$namespace", authority="$authority", direction="outbound", tls!="true"}[30s])) by (pod)
```

And we'd want to make the same modification for all charts in this row.

title: Add linkerd profile --template command
body:
Add a new CLI command: `linkerd profile --template` which outputs a sample service profile yaml.  Users can edit this sample and then `kubectl apply` it to add a service profile.  The sample serves as "documentation by example" of what service profiles may contain.

Example usage:
```bash
linkerd profile --template web-svc.emojivoto > web-svc-profile.yaml
# edit web-svc-profile.yaml in your favorite editor
kubectl apply -f web-svc-profile.yaml
```

Signed-off-by: Alex Leong <alex@buoyant.io>
author: adleong

comments.author: adleong
comments.body:
@grampelberg totally.  This all started while I was writing docs for service profiles and it started to feel like having an editable template to point to would be helpful.  The main tricky bit that the template helps with is getting the name and namespace just right.  The service profile resource needs to be in the controller namespace but must be named `<svc-name>.<svc-namespace>`.

`--template` doesn't do anything yet, but I'm imagining that there will be different ways to generate service profiles in the future:

```
linkerd profile --template
linkerd profile --swagger=myapi.swagger
linkerd profile --proto=myapi.proto
linkerd profile --interactive
```

comments.author: grampelberg
comments.body:
Ahhh, that explains a lot, thank you!

Is it a hard requirement to have the profile in the *controller* namespace? That seems like an odd decision.

comments.author: adleong
comments.body:
Not a hard requirement but it's the way things are currently implemented.

This was intended to simplify things when one service is calling another across namespaces.  For example, if A is calling B, where should we look for B's service profile?  If we look in A's namespace, then we potentially need to duplicate B's service profile for each calling namespace.  If we look in B's namespace then there is no way for A to create a service profile on B if A doesn't have write access to B's namespace.  If we look in both, then we need some precedence rules for deciding which to use.

By putting the service profile in the controller namespace, we sidestep the issue.

comments.author: grampelberg
comments.body:
Hmm, I'll ask folks some questions and installs. As a service owner, it is likely you also own the controller namespace. As a platform owner, it is unlikely any service owners have access. 

Purely from a k8s resource perspective, I would assume that it should be in the same namespace as the service. Obviously. that only makes sense when it is a profile for *my* service. Everything falls down a little bit when a profile is used in anger. We've talked about using "external" services before, maybe that's the solution (I'm thinking about stuff like having a profile for `github.com` as well).

Feels like the right decision for now, lemme play with it a little bit and get some feedback from other folks to see if we should change it around to something else entirely.

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
I don't think this example is quite right. Should it be:

```
linkerd profile web-svc --namespace emojivoto --template > web-svc-profile.yaml
```

review_threads.author: klingerf
klingerf
review_threads.body: Should this func check to make sure that the `--template` flag is set, and output something useful if it's unset? As written it will print the template regardless of whether `--template` is passed on the CLI.

review_threads.author: klingerf
adleong
review_threads.body: just for my education, why is returning a pointer to the struct preferred over returning the struct directly?

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
I see both approaches in use, but typically initializer functions such as this one return a pointer, rather than initializing the struct and then immediately copying it back to the caller.

Also, given go's error handling, I find pointer return types to be more ergonomic. For instance in the previous implementation, you had:

```
	return templateConfig{}, err
```

Whereas with a pointer return type you could write that as:

```
	return nil, err
```

review_threads.author: dadjeibaah
review_threads.body:
More of a readability nit: I am not entirely sure how `classNames` interprets statements like `this.state.drawerOpen && classes.appBarShift` but I found it a little difficult to comprehend. I tried rewriting the statement like so:
```jsx
className={classNames(classes.appBar, {[`${classes.appBarShift}`]: this.state.drawerOpen})}>
```
And that seemed to work the same way.

review_threads.author: rmars
review_threads.body:
Hahahah, what that line is actually doing is a combination of cool es6 tricks:

First, it's using the `&&` operand to return the string name of the class if `drawerOpen` is true ([docs](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Logical_Operators#Logical_AND_())).
(The js `&&` operand will return the latter of the provided values if the first expression is truthy). Example:
```
>> false && "foo"
>> false

>> true && "foo"
>> "foo"
```

Then, it's using the fancy object assignment to assign `appBarShift`'s className to the object if provided:
```
>> let a = "a_string";
>> let obj = { a }

>> obj
{a: "a_string"}
```

So this is equivalent to providing an object whose key is `classes.appBarShift` and value is `this.state.drawerOpen` as you've written. I'll rewrite it to be less trick-y!

review_threads.author: dadjeibaah
review_threads.body: Oh my gosh! so much sorcery! That is pretty cool. it's a TIOLI so feel free to do whatever you think is best.

review_threads.author: rmars
review_threads.body:
Hahaha, yeah I think readable > cool, so I'll change them to more traditional args. 
It's a pattern I see popping up a lot in the material examples, so maybe we can change later.

review_threads.body: Could this line be moved to the `appBar` style object?

title: Make service profile validation a warning instead of an error
body:
The existence of an invalid service profile causes `linkerd check` to fail.  This means that it is not possible to open the Linkerd dashboard with the `linkerd dashboard` command.  While service profile validation is useful, it should not lock users out.

linkerd-api[kubernetes]: control plane can talk to Kubernetes..............[ok]

title: Use fqdn for service profile name
body:
Service profiles must be named in the form `"<service>.<namespace>"`.  This is inconsistent with the fully normalized domain name that the proxy sends to the controller.  It also does not permit creating service profiles for non-Kubernetes services.

We switch to requiring that service profiles must be named with the FQDN of their service.  For Kubernetes services, this is `"<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local"`.

This change alone is not sufficient for allowing service profile for non-Kubernetes services because the k8s resolver will ignore any DNS names which are not Kubernetes services.  Further refactoring of the resolver will be required to allow looking up non-Kubernetes service profiles in Kuberenetes.

Signed-off-by: Alex Leong <alex@buoyant.io>
author: adleong

title: Remove the proxy-api container
body:
A container called `proxy-api` runs in the Linkerd2 controller pod.  This container listens on port 8086 and serves the proxy-api but does nothing other than forward gRPC requests to the destination container which listens on port 8089.

We remove the proxy-api container altogether and change the destination container to listen on port 8086 instead of 8089.  The result is that clients still use the proxy-api by connecting to `proxy-api.<ns>.svc.cluster.local:8086` but the controller has one fewer containers.  This results in a simpler system that is easier to reason about.

Signed-off-by: Alex Leong <alex@buoyant.io>
author: adleong

comments.author: olix0r
comments.body: Should we call the _destination_ container _proxy-api_? Perhaps as a followup?

review_threads.body: Is there a reason we are no longer using `127.0.0.1`? I am sure it's not a big deal but just curious

review_threads.author: adleong
review_threads.body:
Yeah, I didn't make this change at first and it took me hours to figure out what was wrong.

This causes the destination server to listen on all interfaces instead of just localhost.  If it only listens on localhost then the proxy can't connect to it.

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body: My (somewhat arbitrary) preference is to continue to run the proxy-api's admin server on 9996. The rest of our controller executables use that convention (e.g. `public-api` runs on 8085 / 9995; `tap` runs on 8088 / 9998, etc.).

* Change "IsSuccess" to "is_failure"

title: Increase retry timeout for retryable tests, refactor RetryFor
body:
When running integration tests in a Kubernetes cluster that sometimes takes a little longer to get pods ready, the integration tests fail tests too early because most tests have a retry timeout of 30 seconds. 

This PR bumps up this retry timeout for `TestInstall` to 3 minutes. This gives the test enough time to download any new docker images that it needs to complete succesfully and also reduces the need to have large timeout values for subsequent tests. This PR also refactors `CheckPods` to check that all containers in a pods for a deployment are in a`Ready` state. This helps also helps in ensuring that all docker images have been downloaded and the pods are in a good state.

Tests were run on the community cluster and all were successful.

Fixes #1735, #622 

Signed-off-by: Dennis Adjei-Baah <dennis@buoyant.io>

title: add control plane check before running proxy test assertion
body:
This PR adds a check before the `TestCheckProxy` executes the CLI command to make sure the control plane has installed all its pods. This avoids the situation where the test would fail because the pods are retrying the data plane check.  The PR's base is #1835 but will switch to master once that PR merges.

Relates to PR #1835 
Fixes #1733 

Signed-off-by: Dennis Adjei-Baah <dennis@buoyant.io>
author: dadjeibaah

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
This code unfortunately won't fix #1733. The failure described in that issue is caused by the linkerd-proxy containers in the "smoke-test" namespace not being in the ready state by the time `linkerd check --proxy` is run. But this code is only checking the pods in the "linkerd" namespace, not the "smoke-test" namespace.

Since you're adding the `--wait=0` flag, I think the easiest fix for the issue is to just retry running the check command until it succeeds. Something like this:

```
	var out string
	err := TestHelper.RetryFor(30*time.Second, func() error {
		var err error
		out, _, err = TestHelper.LinkerdRun(
			"check",
			"--proxy",
			"--expected-version",
			TestHelper.GetVersion(),
			"--namespace",
			prefixedNs,
			"--wait=0",
		)
		return err
	})
```

That's pretty similar to how `TestCheckPostInstall` is already setup in this file. Ideally this test and that test would be almost identical, save for the `--proxy` and `--namespace` flags. Speaking of which, we should add the `--wait=0` flag to the `TestCheckPostInstall` test, too.

review_threads.body: I think we should use a tighter timeout here, since I would consider it a bug if it takes the proxies 2 minutes to reach the ready state. For the other check test, we're using 30 seconds. Mind updating this timeout to match?

title: Allow stat summary to query for multiple resources
body:
Howdy folks,

This will allow us to query multiple resources of different types in a single call (#1487), like
```
linkerd stat deploy/web po/emoji-694f94cdff-j44qs
```
or multiple resources of the same type by specifying the type at the beginning:
```
linkerd stat po emoji-694f94cdff-j44qs vote-bot-546746cb47-fswth voting-5f6b976c9f-krtsm
```
- The first commit prepares `util.BuildResource` to be able to deal with multiple resources.
- The second commit updates the `linkerd stat` cli help text.
- The third commit is the real implementation, consisting on firing parallel requests to the controller api, one for each resource. This stroke me as a much simpler approach than generalizing the controller api to accept multiple resources. I couldn't notice any performance degradation through preliminary testing.

Still pending is merging the tables in the results; currently each resource is producing a separate table even if they're of the same resource type. And adding more test cases for this of course :-) I'll wait for your feedback before I tackle those.

title: Fix stat filtering for `--from` queries
body:
# Problem
When we add a `--from` query to `linkerd stat au` we get more rows than if we would have just run `linkerd stat au`.

Destination query labels are now appended to `labels` so that those labels can be filtered on.

title: Add routes command
body:
Add a routes command which displays per-route stats for services that have service profiles defined.

```
$ bin/linkerd routes webapp --from deploy/traffic
               ROUTE   SUCCESS      RPS   LATENCY_P50   LATENCY_P95   LATENCY_P99   TLS
/authors/{id}/delete     5.64%   7.4rps          37ms         247ms         695ms    0%
  /books/{id}/delete     5.75%   7.2rps          29ms         160ms         680ms    0%
              /books    44.64%   1.9rps          71ms        1300ms        1860ms    0%
         /books/{id}   100.00%   0.8rps          75ms         470ms         494ms    0%
     /book/{id}/edit    50.00%   0.8rps         138ms         265ms         293ms    0%
       /authors/{id}   100.00%   0.4rps          30ms          95ms          99ms    0%
            /authors   100.00%   0.4rps          30ms          90ms          98ms    0%
```

This change has three parts:
* A new public-api RPC called `TopRoutes` which serves per-route stat data about a service
* An implementation of TopRoutes in the public-api service.  This implementation reads per-route data from Prometheus.  This is very similar to how the StatSummaries RPC and much of the code was able to be refactored and shared.
* A new CLI command called `routes` which displays the per-route data in a tabular or json format.  This is very similar to the `stat` command and much of the code was able to be refactored and shared.

The easiest way to test this change is to do the following:
1. install Linkerd off this branch
1. inject and deploy the books app (https://run.linkerd.io/booksapp.yml)
1. apply this service profile: https://gist.github.com/adleong/1f2d1d79f93f621cdd64f852f720fa16
1. run `bin/linkerd routes webapp --from deploy/traffic`

Note that as of the currently targeted proxy version, only outbound route stats are supported so the `--from` flag must be included in order to see data.  This restriction will be lifted in an upcoming PR once we add support for inbound route stats as well.

title: Add new iptable rule to for outbound traffic
body:
When requests from a pod send requests to itself, the proxy properly redirects traffic from the originating container in the pod through the outbound listener of the proxy. Once the request ends on the inbound side of the proxy, it skips the proxy and calls the original container that made the request. This can cause problems for containers that serve HTTP as the proxy naively tries to initiate an HTTP/2 connection to the destination of a request.  (See #1585 for a concrete example)

This PR adds a new iptable rule, coupled with a proxy [change](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/pull/122) ensure that requests from a that occur in the aforementioned scenario, always redirect to the inbound listener of the proxy first.

fixes #1585

title: Add --open-api option to linkerd profiles command
body:
The `--open-api` flag is an alternative to the `--template` flag for the `linkerd profile` command.  It reads an OpenAPI specification file (also called a swagger file) and uses it to generate a corresponding service profile.

```
$ linkerd profile --open-api pet.swagger pet
apiVersion: linkerd.io/v1alpha1
kind: ServiceProfile
metadata:
  creationTimestamp: null
  name: pet.default.svc.cluster.local
  namespace: linkerd
spec:
  routes:
  - condition:
      method: GET
      path: ^/sample/pet/[^/]*$
    name: GET /sample/pet/{petId}
  - condition:
      method: POST
      path: ^/sample/pet$
    name: POST /sample/pet
```

title: proxy injector: insert at end of arrays
body:
When using `--proxy-auto-inject` with Kuberntes `v1.9.11`, observed auto
injector incorrectly merging list elements rather than inserting new
ones. This issue was not reproducible on `v1.10.3`.

For example, this input:
```
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: vote-bot
        command:
        - emojivoto-vote-bot
```

Would yield:
```
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: linkerd-proxy
        command:
        - emojivoto-vote-bot
      - name: vote-bot
        command:
        - emojivoto-vote-bot
```

This change replaces json patch specs like
`/spec/template/spec/containers/0` with
`/spec/template/spec/containers/-`. The former is intended to insert at
the beggining of a list, the latter at the end. This also simplifies the
code a bit and more closely aligns with the intent of injecting at the
end of lists.

Signed-off-by: Andrew Seigner <siggy@buoyant.io>

title: Adjust proxy, Prometheus, and Grafana probes
body:
High `readinessProbe.initialDelaySeconds` values delayed the controller's
readiness by up to 30s, preventing cli commands from succeeding shortly after
control plane deployment.

Decrease `readinessProbe.initialDelaySeconds` in the proxy, Prometheus, and
Grafana to the default 0s. Also change `linkerd check` controller pod ordering
to: controller, prometheus, web, grafana.

Detailed probe changes:
- proxy
  - decrease `readinessProbe.initialDelaySeconds` from 10s to 0s
- prometheus
  - decrease `readinessProbe.initialDelaySeconds` from 30s to 0s
  - decrease `readinessProbe.timeoutSeconds` from 30s to 1s
  - decrease `livenessProbe.timeoutSeconds` from 30s to 1s
- grafana
  - decrease `readinessProbe.initialDelaySeconds` from 30s to 0s
  - decrease `readinessProbe.timeoutSeconds` from 30s to 1s
  - decrease `readinessProbe.failureThreshold` from 10 to 3

Fixes #1804

Signed-off-by: Andrew Seigner <siggy@buoyant.io>
author: siggy

comments.author: siggy
comments.body: Relates to #1121 and #1168.

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body: Given the [readiness probe defaults](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-probes/#configure-probes), won't this only give the prometheus pod 20 seconds to start? Is that enough time in clusters that are resource-constrained? How would you feel about setting `failureThreshold: 7` on this probe, to give prometheus a full minute to start?

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body: I believe pods start as unready and then become ready as soon as they pass their readiness probe. Since the default `successThreshold` is 1, starting the readiness probe immediately will not delay a pod's readiness at startup time, nor will early readiness failures put the pod at risk of restart.

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body: Same question here as above -- won't this only give the grafana pod 20 seconds to start? Maybe we can set `failureThreshold: 7` on this probe as well?

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body: Unrelated to your change, but I realized the the grafana pod's liveliness probe does not include an initial delay, whereas the prometheus pod's liveliness probe includes `initialDelaySeconds: 30`. Would you mind updating the grafana pod's liveliness probe to match? I actually wonder if the fact that we haven't previously had an initial delay for the grafana pod's liveliness probe could be the cause of #1747.

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body:
Good idea around setting `initialDelaySeconds: 30` for Grafana liveness, PR updated.

We should keep this technique in mind if we encounter liveness failures/restarts at startup time, for control or data plane. There's not much harm in increasing `livenessProbe.initialDelaySeconds`.

type caused a panic.

Fix panic when unknown type specified as a `--from` or `--to` flag.

Fix `job` label from `linkerd-proxy` overwriting Prometheus `job` label at
collection time. This caused all metrics collected by proxy sidecars in
Kubernetes jobs to be collected into an incorrect Prometheus job, rather than
the expected `linkerd-proxy` Prometheus job.

Fix `unsupported resource type` tap error message incorrectly printing the
target resource rather than the destination.

Set `--controller-log-level debug` in `install_test.go` for easier debugging.

Expose `slow-cooker`'s metrics via a k8s service in the tap integration test, to
validate proxy requests with a job as destination.

Fixes #1872
Part of #627

I'm worried that adding an additional `linkerd check` command with a `--wait` flag in this test will paper over misconfigured readiness checks. We already block test execution until all pods have entered their ready state, on line 104 of this file. Once the pods are ready, my expectation is that the `linkerd check` command will succeed immediately. If that's not the case, then I'd rather be explicit about retrying the `linkerd check` command that we're testing, rather than adding a new check command to run before it. Something like:

```diff
diff --git a/test/install_test.go b/test/install_test.go
index 31ac4f15..85816038 100644
--- a/test/install_test.go
+++ b/test/install_test.go
@@ -118,24 +118,17 @@ func TestVersionPostInstall(t *testing.T) {
 }

-	// Wait for everything to fully come up
-	out, _, err := TestHelper.LinkerdRun(
-		"check",
-		"--proxy",
-		"--expected-version",
-		TestHelper.GetVersion(),
-		"--wait=60s",
-	)
-	if err != nil {
-		t.Fatalf("Check command failed\n%s", out)
-	}
-
-	out, _, err = TestHelper.LinkerdRun(
-		"check",
-		"--expected-version",
-		TestHelper.GetVersion(),
-		"--wait=0",
-	)
+	var out string
+	err := TestHelper.RetryFor(60*time.Second, func() error {
+		var err error
+		out, _, err = TestHelper.LinkerdRun(
+			"check",
+			"--expected-version",
+			TestHelper.GetVersion(),
+			"--wait=0",
+		)
+		return err
+	})
 	if err != nil {
 		t.Fatalf("Check command failed\n%s", out)
 	}
```

review_threads.body: Same comment here as above. It's true that `linkerd check --proxy` might fail if metrics haven't propagated to Prometheus, but in that case I'd rather add an explicit `time.Sleep(10 * time.Second)`, to match the Prometheus collection window.

title: Move the determining of display order into the cli query module

title: Rework routes command to accept any resource
body:
We rework the routes command so that it can accept any Kubernetes resource, making it act much more similarly to the stat command.

When no additional flags are given, the routes command displays all incoming routes for the given resource.  Depending on the resource, this may includes routes from multiple different services:

```
$ bin/linkerd routes ns/default
ROUTE                                                      SERVICE   SUCCESS      RPS   LATENCY_P50   LATENCY_P95   LATENCY_P99   TLS

GET /                        webapp.default.svc.cluster.local:7000   100.00%   0.3rps         250ms         295ms         299ms    0%
GET /authors.json           authors.default.svc.cluster.local:7001   100.00%   0.3rps          10ms          29ms          30ms    0%
GET /authors/{id}            webapp.default.svc.cluster.local:7000   100.00%   0.3rps          75ms         185ms         197ms    0%
GET /authors/{id}.json      authors.default.svc.cluster.local:7001   100.00%   0.8rps           9ms         255ms         291ms    0%
GET /books.json               books.default.svc.cluster.local:7002   100.00%   1.0rps          35ms         180ms         196ms    0%
GET /books/{id}              webapp.default.svc.cluster.local:7000   100.00%   0.6rps         100ms         850ms         970ms    0%
GET /books/{id}.json          books.default.svc.cluster.local:7002   100.00%   1.3rps          12ms          36ms          39ms    0%

```

If the `--to-all` flag is given, the routes command instead shows all OUTGOING routes from the resource.

```
$ bin/linkerd routes deploy/webapp --to-all

```

Finally, if the `--to-service` flag is given, the routes command will show outgoing routes from the resource to give service specified by the flag.

```
$ bin/linkerd routes deploy/webapp --to-service authors
ROUTE                                                      SERVICE   SUCCESS      RPS   LATENCY_P50   LATENCY_P95   LATENCY_P99   TLS
DELETE /authors/{id}.json   authors.default.svc.cluster.local:7001   100.00%   0.4rps          75ms         185ms         197ms    0%

[UNKNOWN]                   authors.default.svc.cluster.local:7001     0.00%   0.0rps           0ms           0ms           0ms    0%
```

`--to-service` and `--to-all` are mutually exclusive.

This PR also adds a `--to-external` flag for querying routes to external services, but additional controller work is required to make this work and will be completed in a follow-up.

adleong
review_threads.body: All we get from Prometheus is the dst label, which the proxy sets to the authority.  So I could see calling it authority instead of dst, possibly.  But we'd have to do a bunch of reverse engineering to construct a Resource from that string.  i.e. create a Service resource if the dst matches the Kubernetes service DNS pattern, otherwise create an Authority resource.

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
This new set of flags doesn't feel congruous with the `linkerd stat` command. My preference would be to use `--to` and `--to-namespace` flags, similar to how stat is handled.

## Examples

To query route stats for requests from the webapp deployment to the books service:

```
linkerd routes deploy/webapp --to svc/books
```

To query route stats for requests from all deployments to all services:

```
linkerd routes deploy --to svc
```

To query route stats for requests to the "linkerd.io" domain:

```
linkerd routes ns/default --to au/linkerd.io
```

review_threads.author: adleong
review_threads.body: My thinking is that `--to` can ONLY be an authority (or an authority constructed from a service).  By encoding this restriction into the type of the flag, we avoid invalid inputs like `--to deploy/foo`.  We can gate against those cases with input validation, but I had hoped that naming the flags this way made it more immediately clear what inputs were valid.

title: proxy: Update for debug logging

commit 68f42c337f2580f3b33ddab2e01540f6849d0d1a (HEAD -> master, origin/master)
Author: Oliver Gould <ver@buoyant.io>
Date:   Tue Dec 4 07:45:20 2018 -0800

    Log discovery updates in the outbound proxy (#153)

    helpful to get a narrow set of logs out to determine whether the proxy

title: proxy-api: Expose a flag to control auto-h2-upgrade
body:
When debugging issues, it's helpful to disable HTTP/2 upgrading to
simplify diagnostics.

This change adds an `enable-h2-ugprade` flag to _proxy-api_. When this
flag is set to false, the proxy-api will not suggest that meshed
endpoints are upgraded to use HTTP/2.

As a follow-up, a flag should be added to `install` to control how the
proxy-api is initialized.

If you inverted it, then you could disable protocol upgrade with `-disable-h2-upgrade` (no argument). And that would be more consistent with the flag that you're adding in #1926.

title: install: Add a -disable-h2-upgrade flag
body:
The proxy-api service _always_ suggests that two meshed pods communicate
via HTTP/2 (i.e. via transparent protocol upgrading, if necessary).
This can complicate debugging and diagnostics at times, so it's
important that we have a way to deploy linkerd without this auto-upgrade
behavior.

This change adds a `-disable-h2-upgrade` flag to the `linkerd install`
command that disables transparent upgrading for the whole cluster.

title: Support service profiles for external authorities
body:
This is branched off of https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/pull/1921

Add support for service profiles created on external (non-service) authorities.  For example, this allows you to create a service profile named `linkerd.io` which will apply to calls made to `linkerd.io`.

This is done by changing the `LINKERD2_PROXY_DESTINATION_PROFILE_SUFFIXES` to `.` so that the proxy will attempt to lookup a service profile for any authority.  We provide the `--disable-external-profiles` proxy flag to revert this behavior in case it is a problem.

We also refactor the proxy-api implementation of GetProfiles so that it does the profile lookup, regardless of if the authority looks like a Kubernetes service name or not.  To simplify this, support for multiple resolves (which was unused) was removed.

Signed-off-by: Alex Leong <alex@buoyant.io>
author: adleong

Based on my reading of prometheus/prometheus#3441, it looks like the pod is already configured to run as a non-root user:

uid=65534(nobody) gid=65534(nogroup)

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
I don't think we can set `securityContext` at the pod level, and instead we'll need to set it at the container level. Setting it at the pod level applies to all containers in the pod, including init containers, and as far as I can tell the `linkerd-init` init container will exit silently with an error if it's not run as root.

To repro with this branch, I ran:

```
bin/fast-build
bin/linkerd install | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl -n linkerd logs deploy/linkerd-controller linkerd-init
2018/12/07 23:38:38 Tracing this script execution as [1544225918]
2018/12/07 23:38:38 State of iptables rules before run:
2018/12/07 23:38:38 > iptables -t nat -vnL
2018/12/07 23:38:38 < iptables v1.4.21: can't initialize iptables table `nat': Permission denied (you must be root)
Perhaps iptables or your kernel needs to be upgraded.

2018/12/07 23:38:38 Aborting firewall configuration
Error: exit status 3
Usage:
  proxy-init [flags]

Flags:
  -h, --help                                help for proxy-init
      --inbound-ports-to-ignore intSlice    Inbound ports to ignore and not redirect to proxy. This has higher precedence than any other parameters.
  -p, --incoming-proxy-port int             Port to redirect incoming traffic (default -1)
      --outbound-ports-to-ignore intSlice   Outbound ports to ignore and not redirect to proxy. This has higher precedence than any other parameters.
  -o, --outgoing-proxy-port int             Port to redirect outgoing traffic (default -1)
  -r, --ports-to-redirect intSlice          Port to redirect to proxy, if no port is specified then ALL ports are redirected
  -u, --proxy-uid int                       User ID that the proxy is running under. Any traffic coming from this user will be ignored to avoid infinite redirection loops. (default -1)
      --simulate                            Don't execute any command, just print what would be executed
```

Moving this `securityContext` attribute to each of the containers fixes the issue, but that also means that the `linkerd-init` container will continue to run as root, in which case this branch won't be a complete fix for #1930. But I'm not sure it's going to be possible to run the init container under a different UID, since it mucks with iptables.

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body:
Note that the `linkerd-init` container already sets its security context as follows:

```
        securityContext:
          capabilities:
            add:
            - NET_ADMIN
          privileged: false
```

review_threads.body: Good catch! I have updated the initContainer to `runAsUser: 0`, `runAsGroup: 0` and `runAsNonRoot: false`. This looks like it fixes the startup problem you saw. I will amend the issue: #1930 to recognize that the `initContainer`s will need root no matter what, until #1887 is resolved.

review_threads.author: klingerf
siggy
review_threads.body:
With Go, I typically use structs unless there is an explicit reason to use a pointer, such as modification by a callee, or large memory footprint. My understanding is that pointers in Go tend to put more pressure on GC, specifically escape analysis, and that outweighs memory allocation caused by copying small structs.

That said, I can change this back to be consistent with the other cli commands, though if we just want consistency I'd be inclined to move all these `new*Options` off of pointers.

A few references:
https://github.com/golang/go/wiki/CodeReviewComments#pass-values
https://segment.com/blog/allocation-efficiency-in-high-performance-go-services/
https://medium.com/@vCabbage/go-are-pointers-a-performance-optimization-a95840d3ef85
https://flaviocopes.com/golang-methods-receivers/

review_threads.author: klingerf
review_threads.body: Right, my strong preference is to keep this consistent across all of our commands. Plus, I find pointers easier to reason about, and those performance concerns don't apply in the same way to the CLI. Until the CLI is suffering from performance issues, I would really like to keep things the way they are.

title: Set proxy-injector resources at container level on install
body: In the process of reviewing #1929, I realized that the project-injector deployment was setting its resource request at the pod level instead of the container level when the `--enable-ha` flag is specified. All of the other controller components set their resource requests at the container level, and it looks like our install command silently drops resource requests at the pod level. Am moving the proxy-injector resource requests to the container to fix.
author: klingerf

title: Fix proxy-api handling of named target ports
body:
The proxy-api wasn't properly handling named target ports. When resolving a service with a named target port, it was using the _pod's_ target port name to look up the port in the endpoints API response, but the endpoints API response uses the _service's_ port name when listing ports.

This means that named ports were working for services that used the same service port name and target pod port name. For example (from the linkerd install YAML itself):

```
kind: Service
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  name: linkerd-proxy-injector
  namespace: linkerd
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  ports:
  - name: proxy-injector
    port: 443
    targetPort: proxy-injector
```

But named ports were not working for services that used a different service port name and target pod port name. For example (from #1853):

```
kind: Service
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  name: linkerd-debugging-receive
  namespace: default
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  ports:
    - name: svc
      port: 8080
      targetPort: app
```

This branch fixes that issue and cleans up some of the other code related to how we handle service ports.

Fixes #1853.

title: Disable serivce profiles in single-namespace mode
body:
Service profiles are backed by a CRD, which requires cluster-wide permissions to create. Since users running in single-namespace mode don't have cluster-wide permissions, I'm disabling service profiles when linkerd is installed with the `--single-namespace` flag. This branch conditionally removes the CRD from the install YAML, adjusts RBAC permissions accordingly, modifies pre-flight permission checks to stop checking for permission to create CRDs, updates the destination service to not watch sp resources and to close `GetProfile` streams, and updates the web UI to not prompt users to create service profiles.

Fixes #1847.
Fixes #1890.
