comments.body: @alpeb Nice catch re: this flag not being on `linkerd install config`. I've pushed an update that puts the flag on both stages, since it affects the RBAC resource in `linkerd install config`, but also affects the flags stored in `linkerd-config` as part of `linkerd install control-plane`. It's not ideal that users must be careful to set this flags on both stages, but we were already in that situation with the `linkerd-cni-enabled` flag, and I've updated the code to couple the behavior of these two flags and make it explicit what's going on.

comments.author: siggy
comments.body:
@ihcsim Good questions re: the rbac stuff.

> 1. Why not use `RoleBinding` for `linkerd-linkerd-web-admin`?

My understanding is that since the `tap.linkerd.io` group contains non-namespaced resources., we need ClusterRoleBinding:
https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/rbac/#rolebinding-and-clusterrolebinding

> 2. Will the `linkerd-controller` needs this permission too?

If the `linkerd-controller`'s Public API was calling the new Tap APIService, we would, but with the Tap APIService, our clients (CLI, web) no longer go through the Public API for Tap. Instead it's client -> K8s API -> TAP ApiServer (in the tap pod).

> 3. Why is `--restrict-dashboard-privileges` necessary? Can we just default to installing the `linkerd-linkerd-web-admin` the `ClusterRoleBinding`?

We do default to installing `linkerd-linkerd-web-admin`, but thought it prudent to offer users a more locked-down approach option.

title: Fix invalid `l5d-require-id` for some tap requests
body:
PR #3154 introduced an `l5d-require-id` header to Tap requests. That
header string was constructed based on the TapByResourceRequest, which
includes 3 notable fields (type, name, namespace). For namespace-level
requests (via commands like `linkerd tap ns linkerd`), type ==
`namespace`, name == `linkerd`, and namespace == "". This special casing
for namespace-level requests yielded invalid `l5d-require-id` headers,
for example: `pd-sa..serviceaccount.identity.linkerd.cluster.local`.

Fix `l5d-require-id` string generation to account for namespace-level
requests. The bulk of this change is tap unit test updates to validate
the fix.

title: Enable tap-admin ClusterRole privileges for `*`
body:
The `linkerd-linkerd-tap-admin` ClusterRole had `watch` privileges on
`*/tap` resources. This disallowed non-namespaced tap requests of the
form: `/apis/tap.linkerd.io/v1alpha1/watch/namespaces/linkerd/tap`,
because that URL structure is interpreted by the Kubernetes API as
watching a resource of type `tap` within the linkerd namespace, rather
than tapping the linkerd namespace.

Modify `linkerd-linkerd-tap-admin` to have `watch` privileges on `*`,
enabling any request of the form
`/apis/tap.linkerd.io/v1alpha1/watch/namespaces/linkerd/*` to succeed.

Fixes #3212

review_threads.author: adleong
review_threads.body: Is this actually deprecated?  Isn't this the interface that the tap pod serves? (albeit as proto-over-http instead of gRPC)

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body:
As of this PR, it's true that the `TapByResource` endpoint in Tap's gRPC server is still accepting requests. In a followup PR, the plan is to remove that gRPC server.

Current request flow:
CLI -> K8s API Server -> Tap API Server -> Tap gRPC Server -> Proxy

The plan:
CLI -> K8s API Server -> Tap API Server -> Proxy

review_threads.author: adleong
review_threads.body:
Maybe this is splitting hairs but I would say this grpc service definition here defines the contract of the Tap API server.  i.e. it takes a TapByResourceRequest as input (encoded as proto-over-http) and returns a stream of TapEvents (encoded as proto-over-http).

Even though none of the grpc bindings generated from this IDL are used, I still wouldn't call it deprecated because it describes the server's interface.

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body:
It's true that there still exists a server endpoint that takes a proto-over-http `TapByResourceRequest` and returns `TapEvent`'s, but I don't think it accurately describes the server's interface, since it's not a gRPC server, and there is not going to be an endpoint called `TapByResource`.

I agree about documenting our API contracts. In that case, we would document the HTTP interface for the TAP APIService. This could be a starting point:
https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/4d01e3720e6d113efc36df52c515f9ad1406bf28/controller/tap/handlers.go#L72-L104

review_threads.author: adleong
review_threads.body: Yeah.  I guess this is weird either way.  At the least, we should add comments to `TapByResourceRequest` and `TapEvent` to indicate that these structs are used by the tap API, since these structs are otherwise not used in any non-deprecated gRPC service.

review_threads.author: kleimkuhler
review_threads.body: @adleong Good point--I added some comments that clarify they are only used by the tap APIServer right now. In the future when we are able to re-expose this to authorized users through the gRPC interface, the comments can be updated.

title: Check in gen deps
body:
Go dependencies which are only used by generated code had not previously been checked into the repo.  Because `go generate` does not respect the `-mod=readonly` flag, running `bin/linkerd` will add these dependencies and dirty the local repo.  This can interfere with the way version tags are generated.

To avoid this, we simply check these deps in.

Note that running `go mod tidy` will remove these again.  Thus, it is not recommended to run `go mod tidy`.

review_threads.author: alpeb
review_threads.body:
The `helm delete` command right before this starts the deletion of Linkerd whose namespace is indeed `$linkerd_namespace-helm`, and we wanna wait till that is gone.
The line immediately below calls `helm reset` which does remove Tiller at the `$tiller_namespace` namespace.

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body:
Thanks this is helpful. I didn't understand the relationship between `helm delete` vs. `helm reset` and `$linkerd_namespace-helm` vs. `$tiller_namespace`.

Mind adding a couple comments around this:

```diff
diff --git a/bin/test-run b/bin/test-run
index 18db3a0e..07b8dfb0 100755
--- a/bin/test-run
+++ b/bin/test-run
@@ -92,12 +92,14 @@ function run_helm_test() {
 function helm_cleanup() {
     (
         set -e
+        # `helm delete` deletes $linkerd_namespace-helm
         $helm_path --kube-context=$k8s_context --tiller-namespace=$tiller_namespace delete --purge $helm_release_name
         # `helm delete` doesn't wait for resources to be deleted, so we wait explicitly.
         # We wait for the namespace to be gone so the following call to `cleanup` doesn't fail when it attempts to delete
         # the same namespace that is already being deleted here (error thrown by the NamespaceLifecycle controller).
         # We don't have that problem with global resources, so no need to wait for them to be gone.
         kubectl wait --for=delete ns/$linkerd_namespace-helm --timeout=40s
+        # `helm reset` deletes the tiller pod in $tiller_namespace
         $helm_path --kube-context=$k8s_context --tiller-namespace=$tiller_namespace reset
         kubectl --context=$k8s_context delete clusterrolebinding ${tiller_namespace}:tiller-cluster-admin
         echo $tiller_namespace
```

title: Remove gRPC tap server listener from controller
body:
### Summary

As an initial attempt to secure the connection from clients to the gRPC tap
server on the tap Pod, the tap `addr` only listened on localhost.

As @adleong pointed out #3257, this was not actually secure because the inbound
proxy would establish a connection to localhost anyways.

This change removes the gRPC tap server listener and changes `TapByResource`
requests to interface with the server object directly.

From this, we know that all `TapByResourceRequests` have gone through the tap
APIServer and thus authorized by RBAC.

### Details

[NewAPIServer](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/ef90e0184f238cbe79987a84f36d4eb91cbcda46/controller/tap/apiserver.go#L25-L26) now takes a [GRPCTapServer](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/f6362dfa805de9a009188014256ecd66e7dc3bfc/controller/tap/server.go#L33-L34) instead of a `pb.TapClient` so that
`TapByResource` requests can interact directly with the [TapByResource](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/f6362dfa805de9a009188014256ecd66e7dc3bfc/controller/tap/server.go#L49-L50) method.

`GRPCTapServer.TapByResource` now makes a private [grpcTapServer](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/ef90e0184f238cbe79987a84f36d4eb91cbcda46/controller/tap/handlers.go#L373-L374) that satisfies
the [tap.TapServer](https://godoc.org/github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/controller/gen/controller/tap#TapServer) interface. Because this interface is satisfied, we can interact
with the tap server methods without spawning an additional listener.

review_threads.author: siggy
adleong
review_threads.body:
It's worth considering if we want to continue having this implement the TapByResource gRPC interface.  Since we only call these methods directly, it's not strictly necessary to continue to implement that interface.  Continuing to implement the interface would make it easier in the future if we ever were to split this back out into a gRPC server again.  On the other hand, breaking that interface would allow us to greatly simplify this code and remove the need for the ServerStream boilerplate.

My preference would be to break the interface and simplify the code, but it's worth considering the tradeoffs.

review_threads.author: adleong
review_threads.body:
GRPCTapServer implements the TapServer interface which is autogenerated from the (deprecated) protobuf service definition.  Since this is not used as a gRPC server, nothing uses this interface.  

My suggestion is that we change the signature of TapByResource to be more ergonomic (for example by taking a channel instead of a `pb.Tap_TapByResourceServer`) but this would mean that we no longer implement the TapServer interface.

title: Sorting the expected response for trafficsplit test
body:
This PR implements sorting for the mock Public API StatSummaryResponse object for `linkerd stat trafficsplit`. This ensures that the order of the expected rows is always consistent when running `stat_summary_test.go`.

Today @kleimkuhler discovered that `stat_summary_test.go` was occasionally failing. Though we have sorting for traffic split rows in `stat_summary.go`, `GenStatTsResponse` in `test_helper.go` -- which generates a mock Public API StatSummaryResponse object -- was *not* being sorted. Thus the `expectedResponse` passed into `testStatSummary` was sometimes swapping the leaf order, causing a test failure. This should resolve the problem.

title: Introduce integration tests into all ci runs
body:
The integration tests under `/test` were run separately via l5d-bot,
lacking the feedback and job management provided by ci.

Enable integration tests in ci, via a docker build and kind clusters
executed on a remote DOCKER_HOST.

CI runs are now broken into two stages, run serially. Each stage is
composed of jobs run in parallel:
- Setup stage
  - Validate go deps
  - Remote docker build
  - Kind cluster setup (deep)
  - Kind cluster setup (upgrade)
  - Kind cluster setup (helm)
- Test stage
  - Go unit tests
  - Node.js unit tests
  - Kind integration tests (deep)
  - Kind integration tests (upgrade)
  - Kind integration tests (helm)

This PR also modifies `bin/test-run.sh` to always set `--failfast` for
Go tests.

Also introduce `bin/docker` and `bin/kubectl` scripts, to ensure
cacheable, pinned executables in ci.

The existing integration tests for master merges and docker pushes,
running against GKE, remain in place.

Signed-off-by: Andrew Seigner <siggy@buoyant.io>

title: Require go 1.12.9 for controller builds
body:
Netflix recently announced a security advisory that identified several
Denial of Service attack vectors that can affect server implementations
of the HTTP/2 protocol, and has issued eight CVEs. [1]

Go is affected by two of the vulnerabilities (CVE-2019-9512 and
CVE-2019-9514) and so Linkerd components that serve HTTP/2 traffic are
also affected. [2]

These vulnerabilities allow untrusted clients to allocate an unlimited
amount of memory, until the server crashes. The Kubernetes Product
Security Committee has assigned this set of vulnerabilities with a CVSS
score of 7.5. [3]

[1] https://github.com/Netflix/security-bulletins/blob/master/advisories/third-party/2019-002.md
[2] https://golang.org/doc/devel/release.html#go1.12

title: Add unit test for edges API endpoint
body:
Fixes #3052.

This PR adds a unit test for the `edges` API endpoint. 
* `linkerd edges` does not query the K8s API, it just returns Prometheus data, so we do not need k8s configs.
* Because it is important to test specifying a namespace (i.e. `linkerd edges deploy -n emojivoto`), `GenEdgesResponse` now accepts an `edgeRowNamespace` string. This affects both the CLI and API unit test for edges.  
* To maintain consistent test results we add sorting both to the returned edge rows in `api/public/edges.go` and the expected edge rows in `/api/public/test_helper.go`.
* Because I reuse `expectedStatRPC` and `newMockGrpcServer` I generate a single `MockPromResponse` that contains both SRC and DST responses, although `linkerd edges` actually makes 2 separate Prometheus queries. This seemed more efficient than creating multiple new functions based on `newMockGrpcServer` but I'm open to feedback on that.

title: Have the proxy-injector emit events upon injection/skipping injection
body:
Fixes #3253

Have the proxy-injector emit an event whenever a injection happens, or
when injection is skipped for some reason (also added that reason into
the proxy-injector logs). The level is associated to the parent workload
(it can't be associated to the pod because at this point the pod hasn't
been persisted).

The event recorder was setup at the `webhook/server.go` level and passed
to the proxy-injector's `Inject` function. The sp-validator thus also
has access to the event recorder, but for now it's not using it.

Related changes:

- Refactored `api.GetOwnerKindAndName()` to have it return a more
generic object.
- Refactored `report.Injectable()` to also have it return the reason why
a workload is not injectable.

I dug a bit further and the function that ends up handling the event is this one:
https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/master/kubernetes/typed/events/v1beta1/event_expansion.go#L40-L57
If we set the namespace there when defining the sink, then the objects associated to the event will be restricted to that namespace. So to be able to send events to objects in all namespaces, we need to leave that as an empty space. I'll add a comment.

```bash
github.com/spf13/cobra.(*Command).execute(0xc0003fd200, 0xc00030cb50, 0x1, 0x1, 0xc0003fd200, 0xc00030cb50)
```

there's some discussion of this issue here:
https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/981f5bc85dd84aa02524c3cd822bdd9a2c1c0756/pkg/healthcheck/healthcheck.go#L278-L284

i think the most straightforward way to address this is to simply include `KubernetesAPIChecks` in all the checks:
```diff
diff --git a/cli/cmd/install.go b/cli/cmd/install.go
index 7c0c8e3c..f4da6f2d 100644
--- a/cli/cmd/install.go
+++ b/cli/cmd/install.go
@@ -247,6 +247,7 @@ resources for the Linkerd control plane. This command should be followed by
                                os.Exit(1)
                        }
                        if err := errAfterRunningChecks(options, []healthcheck.CategoryID{
+                               healthcheck.KubernetesAPIChecks,
                                healthcheck.LinkerdPreInstallGlobalResourcesChecks,
                        }); err != nil && !options.ignoreCluster {
                                fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, errMsgGlobalResourcesExist, err)
@@ -292,6 +293,7 @@ control plane. It should be run after "linkerd install config".`,
                                os.Exit(1)
                        }
                        if err := errAfterRunningChecks(options, []healthcheck.CategoryID{
+                               healthcheck.KubernetesAPIChecks,
                                healthcheck.LinkerdPreInstallGlobalResourcesChecks,
                        }); err == nil && !options.skipChecks {
                                fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, errMsgGlobalResourcesMissing, controlPlaneNamespace)
@@ -355,6 +357,7 @@ control plane.`,
                                os.Exit(1)
                        }
                        if err := errAfterRunningChecks(options, []healthcheck.CategoryID{
+                               healthcheck.KubernetesAPIChecks,

                                fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, errMsgGlobalResourcesExist, err)
```

the downside to this approach is we're initalizing a `kubeAPI` client twice.

a longer-term approach (for this PR if you have the time, or down the road) could involve a Healthcheck-specific error type:

```go
// caution: totally untested, never-compiled code
type CategoryError struct {
	CategoryID CategoryID
	Err    error
}

func (c *CategoryError) Error() string {
	return c.Err.Error()
}

if err := errAfterRunningChecks(options, []healthcheck.CategoryID{
	healthcheck.KubernetesAPIChecks,
	healthcheck.LinkerdPreInstallGlobalResourcesChecks,
}); err != nil && !options.ignoreCluster {
	if cErr, ok := result.Err.(*healthcheck.CategoryError); ok {

		os.Exit(1)

	os.Exit(1)
}
```

also there's an existing `ResourceError` type already in the `healthcheck` package, i'd expect that would need some changes as well if we went down this road.

comments.author: alpeb
comments.body:
Good catch @siggy :eye: 
According to k8s' API conventions, it appears the casing we adopted for Kinds is wrong:
["Resource collections should be all lowercase and plural, whereas kinds are CamelCase and singular."](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-architecture/api-conventions.md#types-kinds)
It would be a large refactoring touching the CP, the CLI and whatnot to have our code conform.
So I think the best approach is to undo the `GetOwnerKindAndName` refactoring, so it continues to return the pair of strings in the casing that we need.

review_threads.body:
Great question. Because trafficsplit metrics are now being returned from the Stat API endpoint, the current `processMultiResourceRollup` can erroneously return trafficsplit leaf services as "upstream" or "downstream" of a selected resource in the Octopus graph.

This line checks if the statTable contains trafficsplit data and returns early if the selected resource is not "all" or "trafficsplit", since any other resource should not include trafficsplit metrics.

I updated the comment to reflect this. The better longterm solution would be to refactor `processMultiResourceRollup` so that `upstream` and `downstream` are handled separately. I'd like to do that in a separate PR.

title: Introduce Github Actions CI workflow
body:
The existing Travis CI setup requires additional integrations and
permissions with Github, and also lacks some flexibility around job
dependency management.

Introduce a new CI workflow based on Github Actions. This initial
workflow performs the same CI work that Travis does, and will iniitially
run in parallel:
- Go unit tests
- JS unit tests
- Go lint
- Validate Go deps
- Integration tests (deep, upgrade, helm)

Signed-off-by: Andrew Seigner <siggy@buoyant.io>
author: siggy

comments.author: siggy
comments.body: @olix0r Correct re: artifact publishing. For the moment Travis will continue to handle that. I'd like to get Github Actions in place just for pull request CI, then later take on artifact publishing and release automation.

comments.author: siggy
comments.body:
@alpeb Re: Dependencies between jobs, I'd like to avoid introducing dependencies unless a job actually depends on a previous job. The goal is to minimize the total time for all jobs to complete, and also make clear what jobs depends on other jobs. While `validate_go_deps` takes only ~8s, `go_lint` takes ~4m, and `go_unit_tests` takes ~5m.

Fortunately the Github PR and Actions UIs provide feedback when individual jobs fail, prior to the full workflow completing, so the user gets feedback asap.

For reference, right now the critical path is:
[docker_build | kind_setup] -> kind_integration -> kind_cleanup

review_threads.body: fwiw, `steps` within a job shares the [same workspace filesystem](https://help.github.com/en/articles/virtual-environments-for-github-actions#filesystems-on-github-hosted-machines). If we ever need to add `-x`, we can use shell to write the secrets to files on the filesystem, and refer them (e.g. `scp -i`) in subsequent steps.

review_threads.body: Is there a way to make this step more common? Is there a sandbox shared between all the steps?

review_threads.body:
Yeah, it's unfortunate we're doing this `Docker SSH setup` step across 4 different jobs. Each job runs in a separate VM so not great shared option.

From a performance perspective, this step only takes 1 second.

From a maintenance perspective, I agree it's less than ideal. We solved this in Travis using YAML aliases, but this is not supported in Github Actions.

review_threads.author: grampelberg
review_threads.body: If the kind cluster doesn't exist, does this succeed? Or, does it even matter?

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body: If the cluster doesn't exist, this command will fail. This is probably fine because if we've gotten this far and the cluster does not exist, a previous job must have failed.

review_threads.author: alpeb
review_threads.body: We also had this in Travis, but I've never known what it is for...

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body:
Good question! It's to mitigate rate-limiting when pulling go dependencies:
https://github.com/golang/go/issues/12933#issuecomment-148098906

The good news is we should be able to remove this when Go 1.13 lands, as Google will run a module mirror:
https://proxy.golang.org/

review_threads.author: ihcsim
review_threads.body: By default, `kind` doesn't wait for the cluster to be ready, before returning, right? Shall we add a `--wait <duration>` here, or some sort of retry check in the `kind_integration` job?

review_threads.author: ihcsim
review_threads.body: Just wondering if the steps in `kind_setup`, `kind_integration` and `kind_cleanup` can all be merged into one job? If anything, it reduces the amount of YAML the human readers have to parse, and eliminate the usage of `needs`. I do think the current setup provides better reporting on the UI though.

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body:
Agree that combining `kind_setup`, `kind_integration`, and `kind_cleanup` would reduce the YAML complexity significantly.

The motivation for the current setup:
- `kind_setup` can run in parallel to `docker_build`, saving time in the critical path
- `kind_integration` depends on both `kind_setup` and `docker_build`
- `kind_cleanup` should always run, regardless of what happened in `docker-build`, or across all matrix variants of `kind_setup` and `kind_integration`

review_threads.author: ihcsim
review_threads.body: I'm curious about the error reporting in `run`. So if e.g., the `scp` command fail, does `run` terminate immediately? And does the UI show which shell command fail? Or do we need `-e`? Setting `-x` is probably not a good idea here, because of the secret env var.

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body:
Fail fast is on by default:
https://help.github.com/en/articles/workflow-syntax-for-github-actions#jobsjob_idstepsrunshell

I believe the UI highlights which command fails.

title: Add support for k8s 1.16
body:
Fixes #3356

1.16 removes some api groups that were already deprecated. From k8s blog
post (https://kubernetes.io/blog/2019/07/18/api-deprecations-in-1-16/):

```
- PodSecurityPolicy: will no longer be served from extensions/v1beta1 in
v1.16.
    Migrate to the policy/v1beta1 API, available since v1.10. Existing
    persisted data can be retrieved/updated via the policy/v1beta1 API.
- DaemonSet, Deployment, StatefulSet, and ReplicaSet: will no longer be
served from extensions/v1beta1, apps/v1beta1, or apps/v1beta2 in v1.16.
    Migrate to the apps/v1 API, available since v1.9. Existing persisted
    data can be retrieved/updated via the apps/v1 API.
```

Previous PRs had already made this change at the Helm templates level,
but we still needed to do it at the API calls and tests.

The integration tests ran fine for k8s 1.12 and 1.15. They fail on 1.16
because the upgrade integration test tries to install linkerd 2.5 which is not
compatible with 1.16.

title: Remove broken thrift dependency
body:
The repo depended on a (recently broken) thrift package:

```
github.com/linkerd/linkerd2
 -> contrib.go.opencensus.io/exporter/ocagent@v0.2.0
  -> go.opencensus.io@v0.17.0
   -> git.apache.org/thrift.git@v0.0.0-20180902110319-2566ecd5d999
```
... via this line in `controller/k8s`:

```go
_ "k8s.io/client-go/plugin/pkg/client/auth"
```

...which created a dependency on go.opencensus.io:

```bash
$ go mod why go.opencensus.io
...
github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/controller/k8s
k8s.io/client-go/plugin/pkg/client/auth
k8s.io/client-go/plugin/pkg/client/auth/azure
github.com/Azure/go-autorest/autorest
github.com/Azure/go-autorest/tracing
contrib.go.opencensus.io/exporter/ocagent
go.opencensus.io
```

Bump contrib.go.opencensus.io/exporter/ocagent from `v0.2.0` to
`v0.6.0`, creating this new dependency chain:

```
github.com/linkerd/linkerd2
 -> contrib.go.opencensus.io/exporter/ocagent@v0.6.0
  -> google.golang.org/api@v0.7.0
   -> go.opencensus.io@v0.21.0
```

Bumping our go.opencensus.io dependency from `v0.17.0` to `v0.21.0`
pulls in this commit:
https://github.com/census-instrumentation/opencensus-go/commit/ed3a3f0bf00d34af1ca7056123dae29672ca3b1a#diff-37aff102a57d3d7b797f152915a6dc16

...which removes our dependency on github.com/apache/thrift

review_threads.body: It looks like this package is coming from k8s' client-go library but we are using this in the prometheus package. What is the reasoning behind switching this from the custom type `WrapTransport` to the k8s provided transport? I would think that we'd still want to keep using `WrapTransport` so we have control over the type.

review_threads.body: I agree that having this prometheus package depend on client-go is a bit weird.

review_threads.body:
curiously, this change was motivated because our `prometheus.WrapTransport` type was no longer compatible with client-go's `config.WrapTransport` type:
```
pkg/k8s/api.go:48:23: cannot use prometheus.ClientWithTelemetry("k8s", wt) (type prometheus.WrapTransport) as type "k8s.io/client-go/transport".WrapperFunc in assignment
pkg/k8s/api.go:48:56: cannot use wt (type "k8s.io/client-go/transport".WrapperFunc) as type prometheus.WrapTransport in argument to prometheus.ClientWithTelemetry
```

config.go in client-go changed from `v10.0.0` to `v12.0.0`:
```diff
-WrapTransport func(rt http.RoundTripper) http.RoundTripper
+WrapTransport transport.WrapperFunc
```

...with this in `v12.0.0`:
```go
type WrapperFunc func(rt http.RoundTripper) http.RoundTripper
```

i agree the client-go dependency in our prometheus package is not great, i'll find a way to remove that.

title: Add TapEvent headers and trailers to the tap protobuf
body:
### Motivation

In order to expose arbitrary headers through tap, headers and trailers should be
read from the linkerd2-proxy-api `TapEvent`s and set in the public `TapEvent`s.
This change should have no user facing changes as it just prepares the events
for JSON output in linkerd/linkerd2#3390

### Solution

The public API has been updated with a headers field for
`TapEvent_Http_RequestInit_` and `TapEvent_Http_ResponseInit_`, and trailers
field for `TapEvent_Http_ResponseEnd_`.

These values are set by reading the corresponding fields off of the proxy's tap
events.

The proto changes are equivalent to the proto changes proposed in
linkerd/linkerd2-proxy-api#33

Closes #3262

Signed-off-by: Kevin Leimkuhler <kleimkuhler@icloud.com>
author: kleimkuhler

title: Fix injector timeout under high load
body:
Fixes #3358

When retrieving a pod owner, we were hitting the k8s API directly because
at injection time the informer might not have been informed about the
existence of the parent object.
Under a large number of injection requests this ended up in the k8s API requests
being throttled, the proxy-injector getting blocked and the webhook requests
timing out.

Now we'll hit the shared informer first, and hit the k8s API only when
the informer doesn't return anything. After a few injection requests for
the same owner, the informer should have been updated.

## Testing

Scaling an emoji deployment to 1000 replicas, and after waiting for a
couple of minutes:

Before:
```bash
# a portion of the pods doesn't get injected
$ kubectl-n emojivoto get po | grep ./1 | wc -l
109

kubectl -n kube-system logs -f kube-apiserver-minikube | grep
failing.*timeout
.... (lots of errors)
```

After:
```bash
# all the pods get injected
$ kubectl -n emojivoto get po | grep ./1 | wc -l
0

kubectl -n kube-system logs -f kube-apiserver-minikube | grep
failing.*timeout
# no errors
```
author: alpeb

review_threads.author: KIVagant
review_threads.body: Just if you have time, could you explain what the pinning does? Thank you.

review_threads.author: alpeb
review_threads.body:
The call below (`t.Run(fmt.Sprintf("%d/retry:%t", i, retry), func(t *testing.T)`...) uses `retry` inside the closure in that second argument. If we don't "pin" that variable, when those two closures run it's possible they will use the current value of `retry`, which in this case would be the last value of the array, `true`. If we "pin" it, then each closure will instead grab a copy of that value, a different copy for each iteration.
I've created a simpler example [here](https://play.golang.org/p/W0imMglYA-U).

review_threads.author: KIVagant
review_threads.body: So I got it right and it's to avoid race conditions but just the name of the var within the closure visibility scope is the same as the name of the var created outside of the visibility scope. And Golang allows to define both of them together.

review_threads.author: KIVagant
review_threads.body: Actually this is amazing comparing to other languages even though it looks tricky first. When I got the same situation in Groovy I had to define a new variable with a new name within the `{}` brackets. Thank you for the explanation.

title: Trace Control Plane components using OC
body:
This PR uses OpenCensus Libraries especially `ocgrpc` & `ochttp` to trace the major grpc and http calls. 

We introduce two new flags with the defaults:

`trace-collector`:          This specified the URL at wihch these spans are sent.
`sampling-probability`: This specifies the rate at which sampling has to be done. 0.1 imples to collect 1 in every 10 (0 implies none, and 1.0 includes all spans)

These installation flags are also part of the helm chart values. The probability will default to 0, i.e to collect no spans. 
These flags are added to the command args in the `linkerd/charts/templates` folder.

These values can be overriden by 
```
linkerd install --trace-collector "oc-tracing:5434" --trace-probability 1
```
As the installation flags are stored in the `linkerd-config` cm Upgrades, etc work as expected.

**How does this work:**

- We use a new function `flags.AddTraceFlags(cmd)` which adds the above mentioned flags and returns their values to be used.
- We also use `util.InitialiseTracing("linkerd-destination", *traceCollector, *probabilisticSamplingRate)`, which registers exporters and also initialises the trace config as per the flags.

Both of these functions are used in the `main` functions of the components.


**Components Traced:**

- All the server side components i.e `linkerd-web`, `linkerd-destination`, `linkerd-tap`, `linkerd-public-api`, `linkerd-identity` that use `prometheus.newGrpcServer()` will have the `ocgrpc` handler added, which automatically sends the request spans.
- As `linkerd-public-api` and `linkerd-web` components have http handlers, they are also traced using `ochttp` handler at the server side. Along with `public-API's` http client to pass the context further.
- Prometheus queries are also traced whenever  `queryProm()` is called.


**Questions**

- As grpc calls especically that of `Identity`, `Destination` are not adding any contextual information.  Are the initial request spans useful? If not, we can remove them. Contextual information is added by using interceptors which would be another PR.
- Is the Information in the prometheus query spans enough? If not, what can be added?

**What doesn't work:**
- The spans from `linkerd-web -> linkerd-tap` are seen as induvidual spans i.e spearate traces because the http client from the `linkerd-web` component uses the k8s transport for communication, so we cant attach the ochttp transport.
 

To be reviewed by, @adleong @grampelberg @ihcsim @alpeb

title: Increase the Grafana dashboards refresh interval
body:
This PR increases the refresh interval of all workload dashboards from 5s to 10s. For dashboards that query for cluster-level or non-Linkerd resources, I set the refresh interval to 1m, following the default of the Prometheus and Prometheus benchmark dashboards.

See Grafana [docs](https://grafana.com/docs/reference/dashboard/#json-fields) for field description.

Fixes #3456.

author: ihcsim

comments.author: alpeb
comments.body:
I was checking whether this interval had anything to do with the `datasources.jsonData.timeInterval` property in Grafana's `datasource.yaml` config file (currently set at 5s), and it turns out that's just for specifying the resolution of the returned series (e.g. a sample every 5s).

Tapping `linkerd-prometheus` with Grafana opened proved me that the `refresh` property modified in this PR does indeed control how frequently the Prometheus API query endpoints get called :+1:

title: Redesign of sidebar
body:
Fixes #3400. 

Simplifies dashboard. Major changes are:
* Workloads are viewed by namespace.
* Individual resources are not listed on the sidebar.
* User can select "All Namespaces".
* If user is looking at `/namespaces/linkerd/pods`, which shows a list of all pods in `linkerd`, and selects the `emojivoto` namespace from the sidebar, they should see `/namespaces/emojivoto/pods`. (Their view should not change if they are looking at resource detail page.)
* Sidebar collapses completely with narrow width.
* New Kubernetes SVG icons for workloads.

Since this redesign involves changes to routing and paths, help is wanted in confirming that all of the data display pages are intact.

**Note on Context in React**
Although we already use React’s [Context API](https://reactjs.org/docs/context.html) to pass information down throughout the app, we are using it in a new way because the user can now update the `selectedNamespace` via the `Namespace` button, which is propagated to all components. 

In order to update context from the bottom up, I restructured `index.js` to pass `<AppContext.Provider value={this.state}>`
into the app. Previously we passed a static `context` object. 

Passing `{this.state}` into the app as context allows us to pass down `updateNamespaceInContext()`.

I am moderately sure I structured this in the correct way, and I modeled it on the React docs, but I would love feedback on this. I was getting an `eslint-plugin-react` `no-unused-state` error on line 44 of `index.js` when I structured state like so:
```
 this.state = {
      ...appData,
      api: ApiHelpers(pathPrefix),
      productName: "linkerd",
    };
```
I found [a Github issue](https://github.com/yannickcr/eslint-plugin-react/issues/1910) about this but there didn't seem to be a clear resolution, since this is the pattern explicitly suggested by the React Context docs. To work around the lint error I put the different state variables on different lines but I am researching a better solution.

title: proxy: Update to v2.73.0
body:

sampling of its own, but is capable of emitting spans to an OpenCensus
collector when an application has chosen to sample a given request.

* ci: Run integration tests on dedicated host (linkerd/linkerd2-proxy#358)
* Add http metadata to spans as annotations (linkerd/linkerd2-proxy#359)
* Instrument the opencensus exporter (linkerd/linkerd2-proxy#362)

title: Introduce Tracing Annotations
body:
This PR introduces two proxy config annotations named `config.linkerd.io/trace-collector` and `config.alpha.linkerd.io/trace-collector-service-account`, to support per-pod tracing. These annotations are translated into two new proxy environment variables.

Note that these annotations work on both the pod template and namespace levels.

The proxy injector logs and events have been updated to include `tracing enabled` events.

## edge-19.9.4

This edge release introduces a redesigned sidebar in dashboard! The goal of the
redesign was to reduce load on Prometheus and simplify navigation by providing
top-level views centered around namespaces and workloads.

* CLI
  * Introduced a new `--cluster-domain` flag to the `linkerd install` command
    that allows setting a custom cluster domain (thanks @arminbuerkle!)
  * Fixed the `linkerd endpoints` command to use the correct Destination API
    address (thanks @Pothulapati!)
  * Added `--disable-heartbeat` flag for `linkerd` `install|upgrade` commands
* Controller
  * Instrumented the proxy-injector to provide additional metrics about
    injection (thanks @Pothulapati!)
  * Added support for `config.linkerd.io/admission-webhooks: disabled` label on
    namespaces so that the pods creation events in these namespaces are ignored
    by the proxy injector; this fixes situations in HA deployments where the
    proxy-injector is installed in `kube-system` (thanks @hasheddan!)
* Web UI
  * Workloads are now viewed by namespace, with an "All Namespaces" option, to
    improve dashboard performance
* Proxy
  * Added experimental distributed tracing support

title: Trace Control plane Components with OC
body:
This PR uses OpenCensus Libraries especially `ocgrpc` & `ochttp` to trace the major grpc and http calls. 

We introduce two new flags with the defaults:

`trace-collector`:          This specified the URL at wihch these spans are sent.
`sampling-probability`: This specifies the rate at which sampling has to be done. 0.1 imples to collect 1 in every 10 (0 implies none, and 1.0 includes all spans)

**How does this work:**

- We use a new function `flags.AddTraceFlags(cmd)` which adds the above mentioned flags and returns their values to be used.
- We also use `util.InitialiseTracing("linkerd-destination", *traceCollector, *probabilisticSamplingRate)`, which registers exporters and also initialises the trace config as per the flags.
Both of these functions are used in the `main` functions of the components.
- `prometheus.NewGrpcServer()` called by components to create a grpc server with telemetry, also now adds grpc request traces using `ocgrpc` handler.
- `prometheus.WithTelemetry()` which is used to instrument HTTP server components, now also adds `ochttp` trace handler.
- All the components, that have `client.go` which are used by other components to call these components are instrumented to use `ochttp` transport to propogate the trace headers.


**Components Traced:**

- All the server side components i.e `linkerd-web`, `linkerd-destination`, `linkerd-tap`, `linkerd-public-api`, `linkerd-identity`
- The prometheus queries in the `linkerd-public-api` component are also traced.

**Questions**

- As grpc calls especically that of `Identity`, `Destination` are not adding any contextual information.  Are the initial request spans useful? If not, we can remove them. Contextual information is added by using interceptors which would be another PR.
- Is the Information in the prometheus query spans enough? If not, what can be added?

**What doesn't work:**
- The spans from `linkerd-web -> linkerd-tap` are seen as induvidual spans i.e spearate traces because the http client from the `linkerd-web` component uses the k8s transport for communication, so we cant attach the ochttp transport.
 

To be reviewed by, @adleong @grampelberg @ihcsim @alpeb

title: Control plane debug
body:
This pr fixes a problem where control plane component cannot be injected with a debug sidecar. The problem was stemming from the fact that during inject, the control plane components are stripped from all `linkerd.io` metadata. This later on causes inconsistency when the proxy is injected again and leads to invalid yaml being produced causing an error in the form of: 

`The Deployment "linkerd-tap" is invalid: spec.template.metadata.labels: Invalid value: map[string]string(nil): `selector` does not match template `labels``

In addition to that this pr introduces a check that ensures that we can run `inject` on control plane components only if the `--manual` flag is present. 

Fixes #3396
author: zaharidichev

comments.author: grampelberg
comments.body:
This doesn't appear to be working for `emojivoto`:

```bash
$ kubectl -n emojivoto get deploy -o yaml | bin/go-run cli debug-sidecar inject -
deployment "emoji" skipped
deployment "vote-bot" skipped
deployment "voting" skipped
deployment "web" skipped
```

I suspect it is because of the mix of auto-injection via annotation and manual. It probably isn't the end of the world if this doesn't work, as you can just use `linkerd inject` to fix it. I think we'll want to change the command name in that case though. Some brainstorming:

```bash
linkerd internal debug-sidecar -
linkerd dev add-debug-sidecar -
linkerd diagnose control-plane-debug -
```

@olix0r what's your thinking? We're starting to introduce a set of commands like this that are for internal diagnosis.

comments.author: zaharidichev
comments.body:
Most likely, will take a look. Emoji is meshed, right ? 

So yes @grampelberg  I actually did not realize that when the proxy is autoinjected, it does not  actually appear in the yaml that we are processing, so my requirement for injecting a debug sidecar is that there is a proxy container running. This can be changed to also check whether there is `"linkerd.io/inject":"enabled"` annotation present.  I am not sure whether that poses any kind of race conditions. If injection autoinjection is enabled with debug sidecar and we try to do debug-sidecar inject, can we end up stepping on our own toes?

comments.author: grampelberg
comments.body: Not by default, just pass it through `linkerd inject`.

comments.author: adleong
comments.body:
Can you explain what the bug is that prevents the debug container from being injected into control plane components and how it is fixed?

I'm confused as to why we need a new linkerd CLI command to inject the debug container into control plane components.  What doesn't linkerd inject work for this?  Can we fix that rather than introducing a new command?

comments.author: grampelberg
comments.body:
@adleong see #3396

- `inject` strips out the control plane labels.
- Updating `inject` to work with control plane components is far more complicated than it seems.
- As this will be used as an internal tool, keeping the scope down to just adding a new command that can *only* manage control plane components instead of solving the general problem.

comments.author: zaharidichev
comments.body: @adleong There was a problem where the uninject was removing some annotations from the control plane component when uninjecting and that was causing the buggy behavior. This has been fixed in this commit, [right here](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/pull/3507/commits/50b8b3577e1c0854c572a17d6cfd27bdcd6a252c#diff-c0c87cb3cf40f8acc005ef36cf5d9fb3R71). Adding a separate command is the result of having a discussion with @grampelberg around introducing a family of commands that only run on the control plane components and are used for more advanced level debugging.

comments.author: adleong
comments.body:
If this is just an internal tool, I'd rather solve this problem with instructions for how to manually edit manifests or something like that rather than adding the technical debt of a new subcommand.

If you're unfamiliar with the complications of the implementation, it's unclear why this would be a separate command and whether the functionality is overlapping.

comments.author: zaharidichev
comments.body: @adleong I am fine with just scratching the whole separate command part and just fixing the problem that was preventing the debug sidecar injection into the control plane components. I think @grampelberg might also have an opinion on the matter.

comments.author: adleong
comments.body:
I think @grampelberg was just trying to keep the scope narrow here so that this didn't balloon into a huge amount of work.  But if you already have a fix that makes `linkerd inject` work properly for control plane components, that seems like the more correct change to me.  

@grampelberg does that sound right to you?

comments.author: grampelberg
comments.body:
What are the implications of adding it to `inject`? Is there a way that a user could shoot themselves in the foot with it there? The one that comes to mind immediately is `inject` without `--manual` on control plane components. That'd be easy to solve with some special code and an error, but I'm wondering if there are others there.

>  I'd rather solve this problem with instructions for how to manually edit manifests

It has been useful while helping folks debug issues to ask them to add the debug container to a control plane component and the run a command. So far, the instructions for doing it manually have been extremely hit and miss. I'm looking for something that is easy to explain and get the data back from.

comments.author: adleong
comments.body:
If I understand correctly, running `linkerd inject` on a control plane component without using the `--manual` flag will always result in weirdness, since this will strip out the manually injected proxy.  This is true regardless of the debug container.  If someone tries to run `linkerd inject` on a control plane component without using the `--manual` flag, we should return an error.

With that established, I don't think we need a new command here.

comments.author: zaharidichev
comments.body: Alright then, I will remove the new command and we take it from there.

comments.author: zaharidichev
comments.body: Removed the additional command and left just the fix for the original bug that @grampelberg found. If you decide the command is needed, I can add it back. Up to you :)

comments.author: adleong
comments.body:
I just tried this using this command:

```
$ k -n linkerd get deploy/linkerd-destination -o yaml | bin/linkerd inject --enable-debug-sidecar - | k apply -f -
```

However, since the auto-injector skips pods in the control plane namespace, this had the effect of stripping the proxy out of the pod:

```
linkerd-destination-8b76849f6-k76vt     1/1     Running   0          21s
```

I think, as we discussed above, running `inject` on a control plane component without the `--manual` flag should return an error.

review_threads.body:
This is pretty confusing so I think it warrants a more extensive comment explaining the context.  Control plane components must only ever be manually injected, so they will never have the `linkerd.io/inject` annotation.  Furthermore, since these components are part of linkerd itself, we don't want to strip off the other `linkerd.io/*` annotations such as `linkerd.io/created-by` when uninjecting.

Yes, I will amend that, good call. Wrt to the `linkerd.io/proxy-version` my view is that there is no need to remove it. I assume if the value of the annotation has changed before the nject, then it will be updated. Isn't that correct? 

Also, just to confirm my understanding, from end user perspective, `uninject` as a command would probably never be used on control plane components by a user, correct. Its only used as part of `inject`, which in turn is used not to really inject anything, but to update the injected container such as in the case of adding a debug sidecar. I wonder whether I am the only one who finds all that a bit confusing.

title: If tap source IP matches many running pods then only show the IP
body:
When an unmeshed source ip matched more than one running pod, tap was
showing the names for all those pods, even though they didn't necessary
originate the connection. This could be reproduced when using a pod
network add-on such as Calico.

With this change, if more than one running pod matches the source, only
use the IP as source without attaching any of the pods' metadata.

Fixes #3103 

#### Tested using GKE with Network Policy enabled (Calico), with emojivoto without vote-bot, but the readiness probe hitting the web deployment:

Before:
![Screenshot from 2019-10-02 08-22-02](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/554287/66066655-8c24c180-e50f-11e9-8c8d-57f25185d934.png)

After:
![Screenshot from 2019-10-02 12-12-25](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/554287/66066694-a2328200-e50f-11e9-9af4-a40c915e0185.png)
author: alpeb

comments.author: adleong
comments.body: I'm a bit confused as to how the screenshot relates to the code change.  Is tap data really used in the octopus graph?  I thought that was purely based on metrics data.  Also, if I'm reading the old code correctly, it looks like it would return the first running pod that it finds with the ip address, not a list or set of pods.  Am I missing something?

comments.author: alpeb
comments.body:
@adleong Correct, the Octopus (at least the unmeshed resources part) is fed from tap data. 
This is where the Octopus component is rendered:
https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/9e287ace3b178601b47bd4cf4a3e14b2b519dbf4/web/app/js/components/ResourceDetail.jsx#L342-L346
That `unmeshedSources` property comes from here:
https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/9e287ace3b178601b47bd4cf4a3e14b2b519dbf4/web/app/js/components/TopModule.jsx#L265-L271

You're also right about the old code behavior. Using my example screenshot above, all those pods (ip-mask, calico, etc) have the same IP `10.128.0.11`. The tap backend asks for the first running pod for that IP, each time a tap event is processed. But apparently that first running pod returned is not always the same; it could be any of the many living in that IP, so they start accumulating in the UI. Makes sense?

comments.author: grampelberg
comments.body:
Specifically, this problem arises when there are pods that use the host network on a node. Traffic external to the cluster has the IP address of the local node. When any pods with host networking have been scheduled to that node (calico, fluentd), they have the same IP address as the node. As we're looking up simply pod IP addresses, it ends up selecting pods that are not associated.

The midterm solution here would be to look at nodes first and then pods. That way, we'd label it as a node. The long term solution would be to be aware that it is external traffic and label it that way.

comments.author: alpeb
comments.body:
@grampelberg I like the idea of explicitly labeling as "node" traffic. That'd imply granting tap RBAC access to the `nodes` resource to figure the ip. Tap already has a ton of privileges anyway.

Note that I can only observe this situation when there's a network add-on like Calico installed.
If not, any pod with `hostNetwork: true` will indeed take the node's IP, but connections originating from it , or from outside the cluster through ingress, appear to k8s's API as comming from some other IP that I can't figure out what it corresponds to. For example in a node with a pod CIDR `10.52.0.0/24` that ip is `10.52.0.1`. Still digging...

Edit: Removed note about unmeshed sources and added note about ingress.

comments.author: alpeb
comments.body:
I could reproduce that non-Calico scenario I described above in Minikube. That IP (10.1.0.1 in this case) turns out to be the ipam gateway in the cni config file:
```bash
$  cat /etc/cni/net.d/k8s.conf 
{
  "cniVersion": "0.3.0",
  "name": "rkt.kubernetes.io",
  "type": "bridge",
  "bridge": "mybridge",
  "mtu": 1460,
  "addIf": "true",
  "isGateway": true,
  "ipMasq": true,
  "ipam": {
    "type": "host-local",
    "subnet": "10.1.0.0/16",
    "gateway": "10.1.0.1",
    "routes": [
      {
        "dst": "0.0.0.0/0"
      }
    ]
  }
}
```
I think it'll be enough for now to just figure the node's ip, and return its metadata if there's a match, and return just the ip otherwise.

comments.author: alpeb
comments.body:
The last push changes this so if a node's internal IP matches, it is displayed like so:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/554287/66965025-f07e6f80-f03d-11e9-9044-2e73903bdcb3.png)
If no node matches, we proceed to look for a matching pod. If exactly one running pod matches we return it. Otherwise we return just the IP.

Tests will followup after this approach is validated.

comments.author: alpeb
comments.body:
> Is the screenshot below indicating that there is a pod with hostNetwork: true talking to my controller? I'd read it as the node is sending some traffic to my controller though.

It could be that, or the kubelet in the node sending probes for example. Unless we start looking into the requests themselves, we can't tell apart those two scenarios. I'm open to suggestions on how to maybe make that more explicit, but I think the current PR at least makes things a little clearer than they were before, saying that "something in that node" is sending traffic, instead of showing random pods that didn't necessarily originate the traffic.

comments.author: ihcsim
comments.body: Thanks for the additional unit tests. Still LGTM!

review_threads.author: ihcsim
review_threads.body:
Will this cause the dashboard to output non-deterministic graphs? E.g., on first load, if there is only one pod that is running, this will return a non-nil `singleRunningPod`. But on refreshing the dashboard if more than one pods are running, then the previous pod won't show up in the dashboard, right?

Now that we explicitly handle node internal IP, will it still be possible for multiple running pods to have the same IP? Is it bad to just issue a warning with the names of the pods if `len(pods) > 0`, and just `return nil, nil`?

review_threads.author: alpeb
review_threads.body:
> Will this cause the dashboard to output non-deterministic graphs? E.g., on first load, if there is only one pod that is running, this will return a non-nil singleRunningPod. But on refreshing the dashboard if more than one pods are running, then the previous pod won't show up in the dashboard, right?

Yes. On the first load the pod would have been interpreted as a regular unmeshed pod, and on the second run that assumption would have been proven wrong. In your second run those pods would have `hostNetwork: true` and their IP wouldn't match the node's, which is a possible scenario depending the network config (see [comment above](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/pull/3513#issuecomment-538145228)).

> Now that we explicitly handle node internal IP, will it still be possible for multiple running pods to have the same IP?

Multiple running pods with the same IP is indeed the case when they all have `hostNetwork: true`. 

> Is it bad to just issue a warning with the names of the pods if len(pods) > 0, and just return nil, nil?

What would the dashboard show in that case? Currently in this branch, if that happens and the IP matches the node, we just say "something in that node" is sending unmeshed traffic. If the IP doesn't match the node, we say "IP/1.2.3.4"

review_threads.author: ihcsim
review_threads.body:
> those pods would have hostNetwork: true and their IP wouldn't match the node's

Ah.. somehow k8s API sees it as the CNI gateway IP (e.g. in minikube), instead of the pod IP?

> Multiple running pods with the same IP is indeed the case when they all have hostNetwork: true.

If there are multiple pods sharing the same host IP, wouldn't the change in [`controller/tap/server.go`](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/9a4d97675303bfbf2db60fa75859cb847f2264a8/controller/tap/server.go#L619-L622) be `true` and return?

> What would the dashboard show in that case? 

Not sure tbh :stuck_out_tongue:. Ideally, it will be nice to separate pods using host network from say kubelet traffic. But yeah, we don't need to tackle this here. We can check with @grampelberg if we want to open a separate issue for it.

review_threads.author: grampelberg
review_threads.body: I think we're getting about as good as we can with this method. It'll be interesting to flesh out something more comprehensive, but I think we need to look at it more deeply first.

title: Health check: check if proxies trust anchors match configuration
body:
If Linkerd is reinstalled or if the trust anchors are modified while
proxies are running on the cluster, they will contain an outdated
`LINKERD2_PROXY_IDENTITY_TRUST_ANCHORS` certificate.

This changeset adds support for `linkerd check`, so it checks if there
is any proxy running on the cluster, and performing the check against
the configuration trust anchor. If there's a failure (considered non
fatal), `linkerd check` will notify the user about what pods are the
offenders (and in what namespace each one is), and also a way to
remediate the issue (restarting the pods).

Fixes #3344

Signed-off-by: Rafael Fernández López <ereslibre@ereslibre.es>

title: Control Plane Trace configuration
body:
Fixes #3487 

This PR adds the Control Plane Trace configuration, to make the Control Plane components emit spans along with the proxy spans to the collector. 

This adds the following Trace Configuration values, 
```
# Control Plane Trace Configuration
ControlPlaneTrace:
  Enabled: false
  ProxyTrace:
    CollectorSvcAddr: linkerd-collector.linkerd-tracing:55678 # leave blank to disable tracing
    CollectorSvcAccount: linkerd-collector.linkerd-tracing
```

Installation is done by,
```
linkerd install --control-plane-tracing | k apply -f -
```
This will enable `ControlPLaneTrace.Enabled` flag and also configures the control-plane proxies to use the default values as specified in the config.

For helm installation, Users will have to set the `Proxy.Trace` values to the values as specified above.

Once the installation is done, the collector and jaeger can be installed by running 
```
kubectl apply -f https://gist.githubusercontent.com/Pothulapati/245842ce7f319e8bcd02521460684d6f/raw/39bacaa657255eca59de768fefef10da2835e966/linkerd-tracing.yaml
```

The BUILD.md docs will be updated, with the above manifest to let users install the tracing components once it is enabled.

**Note**

This PR can only be merged after https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/pull/3495

title: Re-add the destination container to the controller spec
body:
This PR re-adds the `destination` container back to the `controller` to ensure backward compatibile upgrade. It retains the previous selector of the `linkerd-destination` service, and adds a new `linkerd-dst` service to front the new `Destination` deployment.

This fix is necessary to avoid data plane downtime during an upgrade to 2.6. 

In summary, after a 2.5 control plane is upgraded to 2.6, 

all existing 2.5 proxies will continue to send their requests to these 2.5 resources:
Deployment: `linkerd-controller`
Service: `linkerd-destination`
Service account: `linkerd-controller`

then, on restart the proxies will be upgraded to 2.6, in which cases all requests will be sent to these 2.6 resources:
Deployment: `linkerd-destination`
Service: `linkerd-dst`
Service account: `linkerd-destination`

Fixes https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/issues/3537.

Signed-off-by: Ivan Sim <ivan@buoyant.io>
author: ihcsim

comments.author: ihcsim
comments.body:
@adleong Unfortunately, changing the service, service account and deployment name isn't as straightforward. It causes a series of integration test failures. I ended up having to make changes to these tests, to a point where I'm not 100% sure if I'm fixing or "altering" the tests.
```
test/endpoints/endpoints_test.go
test/get/get_test.go
test/install_test.go
test/routes/routes_test.go
test/stat/stat_test.go
```
E.g. the [log test](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/c5d68ecb1611aa3e09269c9b9101b71662982403/test/install_test.go#L507-L529) relies on the deployment name and `control-plane-component` label to be the same. If I changed the deployment name, it causes further downstream test failures. And the label is used as a Prometheus label, so not something I want to change here.

Unless we have more time to investigate these test failures, I prefer not renaming these resources now.

review_threads.author: adleong
review_threads.body: I think we should also update line 84 in this file to point the public-api at the new linkerd-dst service

title: Switch from using golangci fmt to using goimports
body:
CI currently enforcing formatting rules by using the fmt linter of golang-ci-lint which is invoked from the bin/lint script.  However it doesn't seem possible to use golang-ci-lint as a formatter, only as a linter which checks formatting.  This means any formatter used by your IDE or invoked manually may or may not use the same formatting rules as golang-ci-lint depending on which formatter you use and which specific revision of that formatter you use.  

In this change we stop using golang-ci-lint for format checking.  We introduce `tools.go` and add goimports to the `go.mod` and `go.sum` files.  This allows everyone to easily get the same revision of goimports by running `go install -mod=readonly golang.org/x/tools/cmd/goimports` from inside of the project.  We add a step in the CI workflow that uses goimports via the `bin/fmt` script to check formatting.

Some shell gymnastics were required in the `bin/fmt` script to work around some limitations of `goimports`:
* goimports does not have a built-in mechanism for excluding directories, and we need to exclude the vendor director as well as the generated Go sources
* goimports returns a 0 exit code, even when formatting errors are detected

Signed-off-by: Alex Leong <alex@buoyant.io>
author: adleong

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body: i don't think `GITCOOKIE_SH` or `GOGC` should be necessary. `GITCOOKIE_SH` mitigates rate-limiting issues when downloading go dependencies, and `GOGC` is a special tuning to prevent golangci-lint from OOM'ing.

review_threads.body: Probably less a concern as I wouldn't expect that install command to download many deps, but yeah I guess it doesn't hurt to leave `GITCOOKIE_SH` in for now. FWIW we should be able to remove this in Go 1.13.

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body:
i may not have my paths set up correctly, but this doesn't work out of the box in my env:
```bash
$ bin/fmt
bin/fmt: 13: bin/fmt: goimports: not found
```

rather than relying on (and modifying) the user's Go env, can you follow the pattern in `bin/lint` and other scripts to download the `goimports` binary into `./target/bin`?

i think it's fine to leave instructions in `BUILD.md` to enable folks to set up their env to use our blessed version of goimports, but this script should be less env-dependent.

review_threads.author: adleong
review_threads.body:
The `bin/lint` tool is downloaded differently, it downloads an install shell script and pipes it to sh which creates a binary in the current working directory.  Since we rely on go modules to install the correct version of this tool, I think we're stuck with whatever the behavior of `go install` is.

We could potentially run `mv $GOPATH/bin/goimports ${targetbin}/.goimports` after install, but I'm not sure if that's better.  

Does this work on your machine if you change the the `goimports` invocation to `$GOPATH/bin/goimports`?

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body:
It's true `bin/lint` is a bit different given the pipe to shell pattern, but we're pretty consistent about wrapping tool downloading and execution this way:

```bash
$ grep "target/bin" bin/*
bin/docker:targetbin="$( cd $bindir/.. && pwd )"/target/bin
bin/goimports:targetbin="${rootdir}"/target/bin
bin/helm:targetbin="$( cd $bindir/.. && pwd )"/target/bin
bin/kind:targetbin="$( cd $bindir/.. && pwd )"/target/bin
bin/kubectl:targetbin="$( cd $bindir/.. && pwd )"/target/bin
bin/lint:targetbin="${rootdir}"/target/bin
bin/protoc:targetbin="$( cd $bindir/.. && pwd )"/target/bin
```

We can still leverage `go.mod` versioning while installing `goimports` into a specific location, by temporarily setting `GOBIN`. Recommend breaking out installing `goimports` from  `bin/fmt` into a new `bin/goimports` script:

`bin/goimports`:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

set -eu

cd "$(pwd -P)"

bindir="$( cd "$( dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}" )" && pwd )"
rootdir="$( cd $bindir/.. && pwd )"
targetbin="${rootdir}"/target/bin

GOBIN=$targetbin go install -mod=readonly golang.org/x/tools/cmd/goimports

goimportsbin=${targetbin}/goimports

exec $goimportsbin "$@"
```

...and then `bin/fmt` can simply call `bin/goimports`:

```diff
diff --git a/bin/fmt b/bin/fmt
index b3e0eabf..b9ea373e 100755
--- a/bin/fmt
+++ b/bin/fmt
@@ -2,19 +2,17 @@

 set -eu

-go install -mod=readonly golang.org/x/tools/cmd/goimports
-
 # go list will exclude the vendor directory.  We use grep to exclude generated
 # code.
 dirs=$(go list -f \{\{.Dir\}\} ./... | grep -v controller/gen)
 # go list will list all subdirectories and goimports acts recursively.  This
 # results in certain files being reported multiple time.  Therefore, we must
 # dedup them.
-files=$(goimports -l $dirs | sort | uniq)
+files=$(bin/goimports -l $dirs | sort | uniq)

 if [ ! -z "$files" ]; then
   for file in $files; do
-    goimports -d "$file"
+    bin/goimports -d "$file"
   done
   exit 64
 fi
```

review_threads.author: siggy
review_threads.body:
i think if we're going to do this check (which is great to avoid the download/installation hit), we should version the binary somehow, otherwise when we bump `golang.org/x/tools/cmd/goimports` in `go.mod`, this script won't pick it up.

if that's too much of a pain, we can just install every time.

title: Faster `linkerd install --ignore-cluster`
body:
The `linkerd install` `--ignore-cluster` and `--skip-checks` flags
enable generating install manifests without a connection to a k8s
cluster. Unfortunately these flags were only checked after attempted
connections to a k8s cluster were made. This satisfied the use case of
`linkerd install` "ignoring" the state of the cluster, but for
environments not connected to a cluster, the user would have to wait for
30s timeouts before getting the manifests.

Modify `linkerd install` and its subcommands to pre-emptively check for
`--ignore-cluster` and `--skip-checks`. This decreases `linkerd install
--ignore-cluster` from ~30s to ~1s, and `linkerd install control-plane
--ignore-cluster --skip-checks` from ~60s to ~1s.

Signed-off-by: Andrew Seigner <siggy@buoyant.io>

## before

```
$ time bin/go-run cli install --ignore-cluster > /dev/null

real	0m35.948s
user	0m5.518s
sys	0m2.085s

$ time bin/go-run cli install control-plane --ignore-cluster --skip-checks > /dev/null

real	1m3.408s
user	0m2.723s
sys	0m1.979s
```

## after

```
$ time bin/go-run cli install --ignore-cluster > /dev/null

real	0m4.140s
user	0m3.887s
sys	0m2.027s

$ time bin/go-run cli install control-plane --ignore-cluster --skip-checks > /dev/null

real	0m3.237s
user	0m2.631s
sys	0m1.938s
```

title: Add APIService fake clientset support
body:
The `linkerd upgrade --from-manifests` command supports reading the
manifest output via `linkerd install`. PR #3167 introduced a tap
APIService object into `linkerd install`, but the manifest-reading code
in fake.go was never updated to support this new object kind.

Update the fake clientset code to support APIService objects.

Fixes #3559

Signed-off-by: Andrew Seigner <siggy@buoyant.io>
author: siggy

comments.author: siggy
comments.body:
@adleong 

> Do we have concerns about this approach being sustainable? We will need to add a fake client set for any API group in our install manifest, even if we never plan to read that object from the real or fake API.

I'm not particularly concerned about the sustainability. Thus far we have special-cased `CustomResourceDefinition` and `APIService`.

> An alternate approach would be to have the upgrade --from-manifest code parse the manifest directly rather than constructing a fake API. Has this already been considered?

When implementing #2697 I did consider this approach, but realizing we already had `NewFakeClientSets` in place for testing, re-using that code, which uses Kubernetes libraries to parse manifests, seemed a more sustainable approach.

> Anyway, I'm sure this is fine. It just feels weird that we need to build fake client sets for apigroups that we never interact with.

I had two motivations for this branch:

#### 1. Upgrading from a complete install manifest

Our install/check/upgrade/cli ux is extremely clear and often called out as a favorite feature by users. Without this change, the upgrade from manifest flow requires the user to understand which k8s objects are required for upgrade:

```bash
linkerd install > linkerd-install.yaml
cat linkerd-install.yaml | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl -n linkerd get \
  secret/linkerd-identity-issuer \
  configmap/linkerd-config \
  -oyaml > linkerd-manifests.yaml
cat linkerd-manifests.yaml | linkerd upgrade --from-manifests - | kubectl apply -f -
```

... this change allows for a more user friendly upgrade process:

```bash
linkerd install > linkerd-install.yaml
cat linkerd-install.yaml | kubectl apply -f -
cat linkerd-install.yaml | linkerd upgrade --from-manifests - | kubectl apply -f -
```

#### 2. Testing completeness

The `fake` module in `pkg/k8s` is used heavily in our testing infrastructure. Anecdotally I find that when there is existing test infrastructure in an area I'm working in, I'm more likely to add more tests during development. If no testing infrastructure is present (for example, if `NewFakeClientSets` does not support `APIService`), the barrier to getting tests implemented is much higher, particularly for a small change.

title: Updating clean-webpack-plugin and other webpack dependencies
body:
I’m encountering an issue with `clean-webpack-plugin` that may be related to #3573. `clean-webpack-plugin` is supposed to remove all old webpack bundles when webpack builds a new bundle. However, in certain situations, it is not removing old bundles, leaving two sets of bundles in the `/dist` directory.

(History: #2058)

Solution: I updated `clean-webpack-plugin` to `3.0.0` (from `1.0.0`) and turned on the option `protectWebpackAssets: false`. This seems to remove *all* webpack assets, even in the case of an interrupted build. I also updated versions of `webpack` and the other related dependencies.

**To replicate the current problem**
1. While in this branch, run `bin/web/setup` from `/linkerd2`
2. In `webpack.config.js`, comment out `protectWebpackAssets: false`
3. Run `bin/web dev` and view contents of `/dist`.
4. Make a change to a JSX file. Let webpack rebuild as normal. Confirm that there is only one set of bundled JS files in `/dist`.
5. Make another file change. While webpack rebuilds, `^C` to kill the build. You’ll see two sets of `main.HASHNAME.js` in the `/dist` folder.
6. Run `bin/web dev` again. You’ll still see both sets of files.
7. Make another change to a file. You’ll see that both sets of files persist.
8. Uncomment `protectWebpackAssets:false` and run steps again. You should see only one set of webpack bundles in the `/dist` folder.

title: Keep old releases in Helm repo index
body:
When building the Helm repo index file, keep the references to the old
releases. Also rename and keep the old index file in case
something goes wrong when generating the new one.

Fixes #3561
author: alpeb

comments.author: alpeb
comments.body:
> I'm guessing that the helm charts themselves are already versioned and present, but prior to this change, the index file only pointed to the most recent release? So this change merges the previous index file with the current one so that all versions are referenced?

Correct.

> It looks like only the previous index.yaml is downloaded, whereas the current and previous indices are uploaded. This means that exactly one previous index version will ever be stored. Is that intended?

No, unless I'm mistaking somewhere. 
- The github action downloads `index.yaml` (with `gsutil cp`)
- `bin/helm-build package` renames it as `index-pre-$version.yaml`
- The github action uploads the merged `index.yaml` and that `index-pre-$version.yaml`. The older `index-pre-$version.yaml` files with the previous `$version` should remain in that google storage folder.

title: Support pod ip and service cluster ip lookups in the destination service
body:
Fixes #3444 
Fixes #3443 

## Background and Behavior

This change adds support for the destination service to resolve Get requests which contain a service clusterIP or pod ip as the `Path` parameter.  It returns the stream of endpoints, just as if `Get` had been called with the service's authority.  This lays the groundwork for allowing the proxy to TLS TCP connections by allowing the proxy to do destination lookups for the SO_ORIG_DST of tcp connections.  When that ip address corresponds to a service cluster ip or pod ip, the destination service will return the endpoints stream, including the pod metadata required to establish identity.

Prior to this change, attempting to look up an ip address in the destination service would result in a `InvalidArgument` error.

Updating the `GetProfile` method to support ip address lookups is out of scope and attempts to look up an ip address with the `GetProfile` method will result in `InvalidArgument`.

## Implementation

We do this by creating a `IPWatcher` which wraps the `EndpointsWatcher` and supports lookups by ip.   `IPWatcher` maintains a mapping up clusterIPs to service ids and translates subscriptions to an IP address into a subscription to the service id using the underlying `EndpointsWatcher`.

Since the service name is no longer always infer-able directly from the input parameters, we restructure `EndpointTranslator` and `PodSet` so that we propagate the service name from the endpoints API response.

## Testing

This can be tested by running the destination service locally, using the current kube context to connect to a Kubernetes cluster:

```
go run controller/cmd/main.go destination -kubeconfig ~/.kube/config
```

Then lookups can be issued using the destination client:

```
go run controller/script/destination-client/main.go -path 192.168.54.78:80 -method get -addr localhost:8086
```

Service cluster ips and pod ips can be used as the `path` argument.
author: adleong

title: Cert manager support
body:
This pr introduces the ability to use external cert manager via the --identitiy-external-issuer=true flag upon install. Currently the flag is persisted so its easier to figure out which kind of secret is being used during upgrade. The slight complication comes from the fact that cert-manager is storing the data in the secret using different keys than our own implementation. Whether we persist this flag or not is a matter of further discussion I guess but for now you can just go ahead and test this change manually (there are also unit tests) by following these steps: 


**Install Cert Manager**
1. `kubectl create namespace cert-manager`
2. `kubectl apply -f https://github.com/jetstack/cert-manager/releases/download/v0.11.0/cert-manager.yaml`

**Create cert manager resources.** 
1. Create the [root certs](https://linkerd.io/2/tasks/generate-certificates/) and create a secret with them

```
kubectl create secret tls linkerd-trust-anchor \
   --cert=ca-crt.pem \
   --key=ca-key.pem \
   --namespace=linkerd
```

2.  Create a cert manager issuer: 
```
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1alpha2
kind: Issuer
metadata:
  name: linkerd-trust-anchor
  namespace: linkerd
spec:
  ca:
    secretName: linkerd-trust-anchor
```

3. Create a cert manager certificate: 
```
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1alpha2
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: linkerd-identity-issuer
  namespace: linkerd
spec:
  secretName: linkerd-identity-issuer
  duration: 1h
  renewBefore: 55m
  issuerRef:
    name: linkerd-trust-anchor
    kind: Issuer
  commonName: identity.linkerd.cluster.local
  isCA: true
  keyAlgorithm: ecdsa
  usages:
  - cert sign
  - crl sign
  - server auth
  - client auth
```

**Inspect the setup**
You can take a look at your secret: 
`kubectl get secret linkerd-identity-issuer -o yaml -n linkerd`

Now, you can install linkerd with proxy configured with a short issuance lifetime to see the whole process in action: 
[bin/linkerd install  --identity-external-issuer=true --controller-log-level=debug --identity-issuance-lifetime=2m  | kubectl apply -f -](url)

With this configuration cert manager rolls the certificate every approximately every five minutes. Proxy sends a CSR every two minutes.  You can take a look at the logs of `identitiy-service`, `cert-manager` as well as the proxies to make sure that all certs are being updated accordingly.

IIUC, almost feels like this should be expressed differently from whether `linkerd install` need to output the issuer secret YAML or not. I'm gonna take a stab here:

`linkerd install`  translates to: 

* `IdentityContext.Issuer=auto`
* `IdentityContext.Issuer.Scheme=linkerd.io/tls`

`linkerd install --identity-*` translates to:

* `IdentityContext.Issuer=manual`
